en: Preface to the *Complete Collection of the Pure Land* I have heard that those who aspire to be reborn in the Pure Land must first purify their minds; for when the mind is pure, the land is pure.
Those who wish to purify their minds must apply themselves single-mindedly to the Dharma; for when the Dharma is practiced with focused devotion, one’s merit becomes pure. Rebirth...

The scriptures on the Pure Land are indeed vast and numerous; yet, in terms of the single-mindedness of holding the Name and the refinement of its practice, none surpasses Wang Longshu’s *Pure Land Texts*.
In the past, I frequently read this work and would sigh with admiration each time I closed the volume.

Desiring to promote its wide circulation, I wish that throughout the nine provinces and four seas, among both monastics and laypeople, and both men and women, there may arise a sense of weary detachment from this Sahā world.

While suffering extreme misery, those who joyfully aspire to the supreme bliss of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang Jile) shall all be able to encompass hundreds of thousands of millions of samādhis within a single Buddha-Recitation Samādhi.

Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, it is pure and unmixed; it is concise and easy to practice, requiring little effort yet yielding double the merit. Its efficacy is swift and its fulfillment certain; upon the blossoming of the lotus, one beholds the Buddha and is forever liberated from the cycle of saṃsāra. Thus, this book is truly a means of... [to break through... (Note:

The final character "破" (pò) appears to be an incomplete or truncated term, likely intended as "破除" (pochú - to shatter/overcome) or "破障" (pózhàng - to break through obstacles). As the source text ends with "破," I have translated it literally while noting the probable intent.)
It is a vanguard against the obstacles, a sharp blade for severing delusions, a precious raft for the pure realm, and the essential ford for entering the state of sainthood.
Together with the lay practitioner Master Yu Hui, who dwells here by the water and hails from Longshu, he has extensively studied the sūtras and śāstras and compiled them into this complete work.

Having thus benefited himself, he has simultaneously benefited others. Observing his direct and straightforward faith and aspiration, as well as his vast and profound resolve, it is truly worthy of praise.
It is said that one must enter the sea to obtain the moon-pearl and ascend a mountain to gather the "linked cities" jade; there is nothing that surpasses this.
Once the carving was completed, he requested a word from me to serve as a preface. I have long known that when the Dharma is focused, one's achievement becomes pure;

when achievement is pure, the mind becomes pure; and when the mind is pure, the ground becomes pure. It will not be long—whether by morning or evening—that he shall encounter it. How could it be otherwise?
It is merely a matter of accumulating many roots of goodness, much merit, and numerous causes and conditions.
Written in the second month of autumn in the third year of the Kangxi era by the Baeon Monastery monk, Dharma Master Hyu,
as the preface to the *Complete Collection on the Pure Land*.
The Prince of the Dharma from the Land of Peaceful Nurturing said: "If pure mindfulness continues without interruption, one attains *samādhi*;
this is precisely the mind of the Pure Land—it need not be the physical land itself. He replied:

"When the Bodhisattva Śrīkṣetra enters within a single atom and turns the fundamental wheel of Dharma, one realizes that the formation and abiding of the Pure Land have a cause. The Great Master of Caoxi said: "People of the East..."
One seeks rebirth in the Western Land. If those in the West seek rebirth in yet another land, would that not mean that seeking rebirth does not necessarily result in being born there? The answer is:

The Patriarch Lu, fearing that people within the single realm of ultimate truth (*eka-tattva-dhātu*) would give rise to disputes over "self" and "other," clarified that the Pure Land can be reached with a mere step.

For this reason, it makes no difference whether one is a child or an elder; it makes no difference whether one lives in a grand mansion or a thatched hut; it makes no difference whether one is active or at rest.
Do not concern yourself with time. There is no person who is not a person of Buddha-remembrance; there is no place that is not a land of Buddha-remembrance;
there is no moment that is not a time of Buddha-remembrance. Thus, all people are originally the people of the Buddha, and all lands are the birthplaces where the Buddha descended.
"At all times, this is the time of the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment; every sound is the Buddha’s voice; every thought is the Buddha’s mindfulness.
Layman Longshu suddenly arose from the Samādhi of the Pure Land, joined his palms with joy, and said to me:
'In Qishui Shanli, there is a great elder who has manifested a pure and clear body and is sharing a seat to preach the Dharma with me, [the person named] So-and-so, enabling him to...'"
All sentient beings shall practice the conduct of the Buddhas together, uphold the vows of the Buddhas together, realize the mind of the Buddhas together, and be born together in the Buddha-lands.
The Old Man of Mount Ling will serve as their witness; I, this mountain monk, cannot help but dance with hands and feet in joy. I respectfully inscribe these words at the beginning of this scroll.
Preface to the Complete Collection of the Pure Land Teachings, inscribed by Hongli of Lingyin Monastery in the hall of Zhizhi on the first day of winter in the Jiachen year of the Kangxi era.

Since the Zen school was transmitted from the West by Bodhidharma, its lineages have spread through five generations and its lamp has continued for a thousand years. Among them, those of great wisdom and insight...

Regarding the faculties: while there are certainly many who, upon hearing [the Dharma] once, attain thorough awakening and realize the sublime, unsurpassed state, for those of ordinary capacity whose faculties are dull and rigid, although the seeds of Bodhi are fully present within their own bodies, they are shrouded by deep clouds and heavy mists that cannot be dispelled.
To confront such "fools" with staffs and shouts to awaken them is like using one blind person to guide another; it will remain obscure for kalpas.

In what sense, then, can he be called the Great Compassionate Father? Śākyamuni Tathāgata specifically expounded the single sūtra of Amitābha, pointing exclusively to rebirth through the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

Former sages such as Huiyuan first established the Lotus Society, and Zhongfeng deeply cherished the Pure Land, extensively propagating the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation and yearning for the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
For the most part, these practices stem from the attachments of ordinary beings.
Wherever it is applied, it provides a sudden and skillful guidance; those who understand do not dare to deem it wrong, while those who are ignorant take great pleasure in it.
Indeed, it is a path of extreme convenience for both the wise and the foolish alike.

Alas, however, as the Dharma of the Final Age gradually declines and its fundamental source becomes increasingly obscured, people may know that reciting the Buddha’s name can lead to rebirth in the Pure Land, yet they ultimately fail to recognize which Buddha they are reciting. Consequently, this causes the West...

The distance is as vast as hundreds of millions of leagues; the ocean of suffering offers no joy of turning back. How could one know that what is called "reciting the Buddha's name" is not merely a matter of teeth and tongue?
Every thought is the mind; every thought is the Buddha. As soon as a single thought arises, the Western Land immediately manifests before one.
As soon as it manifests, this is named the World of Ultimate Bliss. Thus, through the recitation of the Buddha’s name, one attains rebirth there.
This teaching—what is it not the very same as the principle of "mind itself is Buddha"? To take this as the core tenet: if one is free from discursive thought, where else could one seek the core?

To take this as direct realization: if one sets aside the Buddha, what else could serve as the realization? Thus we know that when the successive patriarchs transmitted the lamp, they transcended birth and death instantaneously;
when sentient beings have deep faith, they consequently escape the cycle of saṃsāra. Their ultimate aim is one and the same. Recently, the Great Master Lianchi [Yunqi Zhuhong] has once again...
He opened a swift path and enlightened the ignorant and deluded; yet now, as time has grown distant, his teachings have been obscured.

Herein, the gentleman Bao Lian Yu, concerned that the Pure Land of Peaceful Nurturing remains a mere abstraction and pitying the sentient beings as numerous as motes of dust who remain unawakened, looked up to the sublime instructions of Longshu and extensively consulted the fundamental commentaries of the sutras and treatises.
He compiled them into this single work; its prose is vast yet not prolix, and its meaning is comprehensive yet concise.
There is no concealment here; it is surely intended to propagate the supreme teaching and extensively receive the multitudes of the ignorant so that the Dharma shall not fall into ruin.
Being of dull wit, I have read through the entire work from beginning to end and am suddenly filled with joy, and thus I write these words.

Preface to the Complete Collection of the Pure Land Teachings, written by Shi Da-cheng, the Dragon Head Graduate (Zhuangyuan) of Shiding, on the fifteenth day of the second month in the year of Yisi of the Kangxi era.
Regarding the doctrine of the Pure Land: it originated with Amitābha Buddha, whose great compassionate vows were widely proclaimed by Śākyamuni Buddha.

The Buddha specifically told Ānanda that his words were not false; therefore, the teachings were transmitted from the Western Land and flowed into China, where they were followed and believed with such unanimity that it was like an echo responding to a sound.

When the Jin dynasty master Huiyuan and his associates, including Liu Yimin and others, established the Lotus Society with over a hundred members, they practiced with sincere faith and single-minded devotion.
Among them, there were those who experienced the Buddha coming to welcome them and were reborn in the Pure Land.
Shengquanji followed; subsequently, Zhiyi appeared in the Sui dynasty, Tanyuan in the Wei dynasty, and Shandao at Wuhui and Taiyan in the Tang dynasty, greatly revitalizing the school’s tradition.

Reaching the Song dynasty, masters such as Shengchang of Yongming and Cizhao further encouraged the practice of recitation. When Master Wang Longshu arrived, his aspiration became even firmer and his cultivation more earnest;

he passed away in a standing posture, [attesting to] the Pure Land— Please note that the provided text fragment ends abruptly. If you provide the full passage, I shall complete the translation accordingly.
The account is now clear. He composed thirteen volumes of *Zhujing tuwen* (Texts on Adorning the Pure Land) to benefit himself and others, and to instruct future students.
Over time, the woodblocks became obscured by dust. Lü Yuanyi re-engraved them for publication, wishing to ensure their long-term transmission.

When the engraving reached the ninth and tenth blocks of the fourth volume, three *śarīra* relics emerged from the wood. This is recorded in the preface written by Master Lü; it may be verified chapter by chapter.
All of these are manifestations of spiritual power brought about by sincere devotion and the display of supernatural faculties. Who would say that the Buddha-dharma lacks miraculous efficacy?
Master Master Lianchi also frequently guided people toward rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha, and his teachings spread somewhat widely. I was born late in life [to encounter them].
In the past, I have privately heard his teachings, yet I did not fully grasp their essential meaning. Recently, I obtained the *Longshu Jingtuwen* (Pure Land Texts of Longshu);

having reverently recited and carefully examined it, I was suddenly struck by the Master’s single-minded compassion. It is truly a compassionate vessel for crossing the world, a treasure among the Dharma.
However, this work primarily aims to guide those of middling and inferior capacities; its text is vast and extensive, and I fear that those of dull faculties—

Unable to achieve a sudden, clear realization of faith, I have ventured, without presuming upon my own abilities, to summarize the essential principles and draft a definitive manual for the Pure Land.
I have carved it into printing blocks for circulation and universally exhorted both monastics and laypeople.

Yet, fearing that the treasury of the Pure Land teachings was not yet fully complete, I have further extensively gathered materials from various sutras as well as the discourses of other venerable masters, compiling them into this comprehensive work to broaden one’s understanding and experience. This is why...

To inspire faith in others, to shatter their doubts, to rouse the will for progress, and to provide the steps for vigorous advancement—I consider myself to have roughly fulfilled these duties as a predecessor.
I hope that the sentient beings of this Sahā world shall each turn their faith toward the lotus ponds of the seven treasures, so that lotuses may bloom there day by day;
thus, may the single gate of the Pure Land be propagated eternally throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Thus it is. Written respectfully by the Lotus-Adorned Practitioner Yu Xingmin on the middle month of summer in the third year of the Kangxi era, the Jiachen year.
Preface to the Exhortation for Cultivating the Pure Land.
I humbly consider that for a beginner in the study of Buddhism, the Great Compassion is the seal of the Bodhisattva’s own mind;

as for the practice of benefiting others, it is the supreme cause for inducing progress in pure karma. The multitude of sages in the land of Jin vowed to be reborn together in Sukhāvatī; the ocean-like assembly of beings throughout the ten directions should likewise be gathered and uprooted from Saṃsāra.
Lamenting that birth and death are difficult to escape, and sighing that impermanence is exceedingly swift, how could I not look up to this with reverence?
The former sages have proclaimed for the future, exhorting one person until many, spreading the Dharma-gift of the śramaṇas;
from mindfulness of one Buddha to ten billion Buddhas, they provide the compassionate vessel for reaching the Pure Land. I urge my fellow practitioners to deeply plant the roots of goodness.
We shall constantly act as companions on the Path and diligently cultivate true merit. If one person falters through indolence, we shall exert our combined strength to rouse and support them;

if one child ascends far toward liberation, we shall join together to guide and lead them forward. Thus, we hope that sentient beings will not remain forever stranded on the path of delusion, and that all those with faith in the good may rejoice in ascending to the Precious Abode.
If one merely knows the Way but fails to practice it, their descendants will sink perpetually into the Black Hells. If one merely pushes [the burden onto others]...
Having already set forth to transform others through his teachings, he manifests his very body as Amitābha. I venture to hope that his vast benevolence will further awaken me;

may I immediately take the first step and suddenly turn back my head. Thus, in this single lifetime, I shall attain the rank of a Buddha, remaining unstained by even a speck of dust throughout kalpas of eternity.
This is truly the swift path for transcending saṃsāra and the broad highway for rushing directly to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī). —By the Practitioner of the Precious Lotus.
I respectfully offer this preface to the *Jingtu wen* (Text on the Pure Land).
Amitābha Tathāgata, by means of his great power of vows, gathers in all classes of beings; the practice of mindfulness is exceedingly simple, yet the realization of the fruit is profound.

[The interlocutor] was quick to respond, yet some remained doubtful. I have once explained to them: "Amitābha Buddha is none other than your own nature; the Land of Ultimate Bliss is none other than your own mind.

Sentient beings turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of sensory objects, thus sinking into the seven realms of existence. They establish a self that is as far removed from the Buddha as heaven is from earth.
For this reason, the Buddha, out of compassion and through skillful means, reveals, awakens, and leads them, manifesting all manner of immeasurable [qualities]."

The Samādhi Like an Illusion adorns that land, making it exquisitely beautiful and magnificent. Furthermore, through eloquent wisdom, he expounds the Dharma for all sentient beings, causing them to rejoice and find delight.
Within their daily activities, they are able to give rise to even a single thought, recollecting that Tathāgata.
If one desires to be born in that land, this single thought of pure firmness is itself the inherent nature; it is no different from that of the Buddha.
At the moment of this thought, without rising from one's seat, the entire Pure Land of Amitābha Buddha appears before one.
Practice in this manner until it reaches full maturity. When the illusory body perishes, this nature does not perish; [one is reborn upon] a golden lotus pedestal.
Born from the nature-seed (*prakṛti-gotra*), one is reborn therein as if returning to one’s own dwelling. All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are my own kin, for their nature is no different from mine;
thus, they naturally love one another. My friend Wang Xuzhong of Longshu was upright, serene, simple, and pure.

He was widely versed in the multitude of books, having lectured and transmitted several hundred thousand words on the Six Classics and the various schools of thought (*zhǐzǐ*). One day, he cast them all aside, saying: "All of these..."
Karmic habits are not ultimate dharmas; my destination is the West. From then on, he practiced with diligence, contemplating only the Buddha.

Approaching sixty years of age, wearing plain clothes and subsisting on simple vegetables, he traveled a thousand *li* with calluses on his feet, teaching others in this manner regardless of wind, rain, cold, or heat.

He never neglected his solitary retreats; he performed a thousand prostrations daily and did not retire to bed until midnight. His face was radiant with light, such that those who beheld him believed him to be a man of the Way.
In the autumn of the *Xin-si* year of the Shaoxing era, he visited my father in Xuancheng and stayed for two months;
it was then that I first saw his *Pure Land Text*, including all the methods of cultivation and the recorded accounts of spiritual responses.

This work possesses both beginning and end; seeking to propagate the Way of the Buddha, it has been carved into woodblocks for transmission. The author requests that I provide a preface for this book, and thus I have composed this brief introduction at its head.
Written by Xu Zhong, named Ri-hou, on the first day of the tenth month. Prefaced by the Grand Marshal Zhang Xiaoyang of Liyang.
Preface to the Reprinted *Longshu Jingtuwen* (Pure Land Texts of Longshu):
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit; it nurtures all roots of goodness.
Now, regarding what the world calls the cultivation of the Pure Land, one cannot afford to lack faith. The Pure Land is none other than the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
As for that world, its various and sublime adornments are recorded in detail in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Amitābha is the Buddha therein. Prior to his attainment of Buddhahood, he made forty-eight vows, each vowing to deliver sentient beings.
For sentient beings who wish to be born in that land, by reciting its name even once, they will be reborn there according to their mindfulness.
For people of the final age, after life has ended and breath has ceased, one should cause others to recite it ten times; this is called "ten recitations. What benefit does this bring?
It is not known whether, during ordinary days, they refrained from all evil and practiced all good, remaining inseparable from these thoughts in every moment.
In the Pure Land of the West, one should, in every thought-moment, vow to behold that Buddha Amitābha until the end of life, without deviation or distraction.
Thus, one will certainly be born by transformation upon a lotus pedestal in the highest grade, never again entering this world of the five turbidities and evil.
Only those who are icchantikas do not believe in its existence; obscured by their own evil karma, they are unable to cultivate it themselves and further obstruct others from doing so.

To enter this hell is like being struck by an arrow; it is truly to be pitied. It is, for example, like people from distant lands and remote regions whose dwellings and sustenance are utterly desolate;
how could they know of the wealth, honor, and happiness of the Central Kingdom?
If one were ever to speak of it to them, they would all consider it a fabrication. Among them, not even a single person would listen with faith and longingly yearn for the Central Kingdom.
In this land, there are many who deeply detest that realm and vow to be reborn there after their bodies perish. Among those currently born in the Central Kingdom, are there not such as these?
Within this world, are there not distant lands and remote frontiers? Since there exists Jambudvīpa, there must likewise exist the Western Pure Land.
To abandon this life and be born there is simply the constant order of principle; how could one not believe it? All [should understand].
The Buddha speaks no falsehoods; the Buddha’s words do not deceive people. Among the sages of antiquity and the patriarchal masters of the Chan school, many also cultivated the Pure Land.
Only Layman Wang of Longshu believed in it with such sincerity and practiced it with such diligence that right mindfulness manifested before him and he remained lucid at the time of his death.
His return to the Pure Land is beyond doubt. For the sake of benefiting both himself and others, he further composed the *Ten Essays on the Pure Land*.
This work consists of three fascicles. It cites scriptures and treatises of the Three Teachings as evidence, providing expedient means for benefit and guidance for future generations;

it may truly be said that "one thought lasts ten thousand years. However, over the long course of time, the woodblocks have become obscured and are no longer fit for perusal. My nephew Lü Yuanyì, whose self-style is Xunzhai, [has undertaken this task].
The recluse of Mount Kāṅ-lu was the son of my late elder brother, the Vice President Dao-shan. Having planted the roots of goodness in former lives, he was born into our family.

In his conduct and self-cultivation, he never failed to abide in the Way. He constantly provided relief for those suffering from hunger, cold, and illness. He printed and distributed various sutras of both the Daoist and Buddhist traditions for the benefit of others.
Cultivating pure karma, he alone understood the resolve that had arisen within him; thus, he once again commissioned the carving of woodblocks for these works, desiring—
May its transmission endure. May all sentient beings return entirely to the Pure Land.

When carving up to the ninth and tenth blocks of the fourth fascicle, the iron chisel encountered an obstruction; three śarīra relics were ejected, embedded deep within a fissure, their radiance brilliant and dazzling.

The multitude was struck with wonder and marvel at this. All of this is due to the manifestation of the compassionate wisdom of Amitābha Buddha, the unceasing power of the vows of the Layman of Longshu, and the firm faith of my nephew.
How could one say that the Buddha-dharma lacks spiritual efficacy, or that there is no Pure Land in the West?
On the Mid-Autumn Festival of the third year of the Yan-you era, in the year of Bingchen, the lay devotees who practice the Pure Land together respectfully [recorded this].
Written at the Xintang (Hall of Trust) in his lodging in Xunyang by Lü Shishuo of Gusou, former Vice-Commissioner of the Fiscal Administration Commission for the Huai,
Jiang, and other regions, and Instructor of the Grand Masters.
Preface to the Reprint of the *Longshu Jingtuwen* (Pure Land Texts of Longshu):

I have previously read the *Longshu Jingtuwen* and thereby came to know the aspirations of Layman Wang. He sought to universally deliver all beings while simultaneously encompassing those of the three vehicles;
yet his merit in guiding those of middling and inferior capacities was the greatest. Why is this? It is because this matter...
It is primordially manifest and does not depend upon cultivation or realization; yet, as soon as one engages with conceptual thought, one falls into the secondary meaning.

Since people of the world do not all possess superior faculties and sharp intelligence, were it not for showing them the method of cultivation through the arousal of faith and providing evidence through accounts of responses in the present life, there would be few who could remain free from objective conditions and resolve their minds [upon awakening]. This is the Pure Land...

This text is a shortcut for spiritual practice. If one is willing to believe and accept it with sincerity, then regardless of whether one's faculties are sharp or dull, or whether one's cultivation is shallow or deep, one will attain realization both in this life and at the end. It is truly something that the world cannot do without.

Some may fear that ten recitations of the Buddha’s name are insufficient to enter deeply into samādhi, or that their visualization will not be pure, and thus they may not necessarily [attain realization] at the moment of death.
They continue to enjoy [the fruits of their practice] until the end, yet fail to realize that the world arises entirely from conceptualization and thus constitutes a phantom-like existence.

How much more so for those who exclusively cultivate the Pure Land—how could it be that they worship and maintain focused mindfulness throughout their lives, yet fail to attain rebirth according to their wishes?
Such a thing is logically impossible. Only those practitioners who directly cut through to the root and suddenly empty all phantoms have no need for this; as for everyone else...
For practitioners on the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), to abandon this is like being blind; unable to rely on a staff, they wander aimlessly, not knowing where to go.
Therefore, I say that the merit of the Layman (*upāsaka*) in guiding those of middling and inferior faculties is the greatest. This book must never be absent from any place or situation.
Written on an auspicious day in the middle month of autumn in the second year of the Wanli era, the year of Jiashu (1574), by one from Mount Ziyun, a follower of the Zen school.
Regarding the study of the scriptures on maintaining integrity:
the *Buddhabhāṣita-drumaghoṣarāja-sūtra* states that in the distant past, eons ago, there was a land named Abhirati and a king named Kauśika.
Kāśyapa, his grandfather was King Śuddhodana of the Pure Land, his father was the Cakravartin King Candrābha, and his mother was Queen Viśeṣamukhī.
The queen gave birth to three sons: the eldest was named Candraprabha, the second Kausika, and the third Indrasena.
At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata. Kausika renounced his royal position and went forth as a monk under the Buddha.

He was named the Bhikṣu Dharmākara. Standing reverently before the Tathāgata, he made forty-eight kinds of vast and great vows and practices to universally deliver all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
He vowed that if even a single vow were not fulfilled, he would never become a Buddha.
At that time, the devas scattered flowers, the earth shook violently, and voices from the sky praised him, saying: "You shall certainly attain Buddhahood (with the title Amitābha)."
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: In a past kalpa, there was a universal monarch named Araṇemin, whose spiritual friend was the minister Ratnasāgara.
Together, they made vows before the Buddha Ratnagarbha. The universal monarch said:
"When I become a buddha, I shall dwell in the world of Pure Bliss and gather in all sentient beings. The minister said: "When I become a buddha..."
In this world of the five turbidities and suffering, Amitābha Buddha is the King A-raṇemin who delivers all sentient beings, and the Great Minister Ratnasāgara is Śākyamuni Buddha.
This harmony between such a sovereign and minister is called the "Two Gates of Gathering and Subduing. Therefore, Amitābha Buddha receives [beings] in that Pure Land.
To attract sentient beings: Śākyamuni Buddha resides here in this Sahā world to teach and transform them.

For those who are soft and submissive, he should transform them through the Dharma-gate of compassionate reception, such as by speaking of the meritorious adornments of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). For those who are stubborn and self-satisfied, he should deliver them through the Dharma-gate of subduing, such as by speaking of the sufferings, hardships, and fluctuations of rising and falling in the Sahā world.
The *Bodhisattva-piṇḍapātra-karuṇāpuṣpa-sūtra* further states: At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha again addressed the eldest prince Animiṣa (the son of the universal monarch):
"I shall now bestow upon you the name Avalokiteśvara. When Amitāyus Buddha enters parinirvāṇa (here translated as 'entering quiescence')," [you shall succeed him].
"In the future, you shall attain the Way of the Buddha, and your name shall be the Tathāgata Universal Radiance Merit Mountain. Furthermore, he addressed the second nun, Prince Ma, saying:
'Next, you shall become a Buddha, and your name shall be the Tathāgata Well-Abiding Merit Jewel King. By the power of your vows, you shall take up a pure land;
furthermore, I shall name you Mahāsthāmaprāpta.'"
The *Sūtra of the Great Amitābha* states: The Buddha said, "When that Buddha (namely Amitābha) reaches parinirvāṇa (namely nirvāṇa), the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara shall then become a Buddha.

He will grasp the power of transformation and teach and deliver all devas and humans throughout the worlds of the ten directions, even down to the species of crawling and flying insects, causing them all to attain the Way of Nirvāṇa. It continues:
They teach, transform, and deliver beings, exactly as the Great Master Amitābha Buddha does, without end.
Only after further incalculable kalpas do they enter parinirvāṇa. Next, Mahāsthāmaprāpta becomes a Buddha;
he wields the power of transformation to teach, transform, and deliver beings, exactly as Amitābha Buddha does, passing through kalpas without ever having a time of parinirvāṇa.

The Complete Collection of Pure Land Texts, Volume One.
Composed by Mr. Wang Longshu, Jinshi of the National Academy of Song;
recompiled by the junior scholar Yu Xingmin, courtesy name Hengongfu.
The *Prāthama-sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra* states:
"The Western Pure Land is adorned with the seven treasures; it is eternally pure and spontaneous, devoid of all impurities and defilements, and is therefore called a 'Pure Land.
Its inhabitants are all born from within lotus flowers; they enjoy eternal life without aging, and its seasons are ever-constant."
In spring, there is no longer cold or heat; one receives great joy and is free from all suffering and affliction.
Therefore, it is named the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). As for that Buddha’s name in the Sanskrit language, *Amitābha*, this translates as "Immeasurable.

Because the light of our Buddha illuminates the worlds of the ten directions without limit, and because there are no sentient beings who recite his name whom he does not know, it is also called [Amitābha].
The Buddha of Immeasurable Light. The lifespan of our Buddha and the lifespans of the people in his land are both without limit;
even for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they would never be exhausted. For this reason, he is also called the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.

Our Buddha possesses great vows (to be seen later) for the salvation of beings, and his majestic spiritual power is inconceivable. Therefore, one should recite with a sincere heart of faith and devotion.
As for his name: within a pool of the seven treasures in the western quarter, a single lotus flower shall immediately arise.
On another day, he shall take birth therein, directly transcending the cycle of saṃsāra and further attaining *avaivartika* (in Chinese, "non-retrogression").

The *Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra* states: "In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there are sevenfold railings, sevenfold jeweled nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all made of the four precious substances, which surround it on every side.
Furthermore, there are ponds of the seven treasures, filled with water of eight meritorious qualities;
the bottom of these ponds is entirely covered with golden sand, and the steps along the four sides are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal."
It was completed. Above it were multi-storied pavilions, likewise adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, red pearls, and agate.

In the ponds, lotuses were as large as chariot wheels; those that were blue emitted blue light, those yellow emitted yellow light, those red emitted red light, and those white emitted white light—subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure.
Furthermore, celestial music constantly played, and the ground was made of gold.
Six times throughout the day and night, *māndārava* flowers rain down from the sky.
Furthermore, there are various wondrous birds of diverse colors—white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śārikas, kalaviṅkas, and jīvañjīvakas. These various birds...

Six times throughout the day and night, they emit harmonious and elegant sounds. These sounds expound and clarify the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and such dharmas as these.
When the sentient beings of that land hear these sounds, they all mindfully recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
These various birds are not born as a result of karmic retribution for transgressions; rather, they are all produced by the will of Amitābha Buddha.

It causes the sound of the Dharma to resound. Through these miraculous transformations, gentle breezes blow upon the rows of jewel-trees and the jeweled nets, producing a subtle and wondrous sound, like hundreds of thousands of kinds of music performed simultaneously. Those who hear this sound—
Spontaneously, they all give rise to thoughts of mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Saṅgha.
It further says: "If good men or good women hear the teaching of Amitābha Buddha and uphold his name—whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days."
With single-mindedness and without distraction, when that person approaches the end of life, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy beings,
will appear before them. At the time of death, this person’s mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "In the land of Amitābha Buddha, the ground consists entirely of natural seven treasures interspersed with one another, or sometimes a single treasure forms the ground.
Its radiant colors shine brilliantly; it is wondrous, pure, and surpasses all worlds throughout the ten directions.
That land is vast and expansive, beyond measure; the ground is everywhere level and even, and Mount Sumeru does not exist there."
There are no mountains, nor the Vajra-encircling mountains, nor any other peaks; there are neither great oceans, small seas, pits, hollows, wells, nor valleys.
There are no places of gloom or darkness. There are no hells, hungry ghosts, or animals, down to the smallest of crawling and flying creatures.
There are no dragons or spirits. There is neither rain nor dew, but only naturally flowing springs. There is neither cold nor heat.
The climate is perpetually like spring; it is pure, refreshing, bright, and beautiful, beyond description.
Amitābha Buddha’s lecture halls and monasteries are all spontaneously formed from an intermingling of the seven treasures.

Furthermore, there are seven treasures used for the towers and railings, and again, seven treasures are fashioned into necklaces and pendants suspended along their sides. Moreover, there are white pearls, moon-pearls, and maṇi jewels.
Jewels were interlaced as cross-strings, covering its entire surface; it was so exceptionally wondrous and beautiful that words could not fully describe it.
The palatial residences of the other bodhisattvas and śrāvakas were likewise so.
For those devas and worldlings, clothing, food and drink, flowers, incense, necklaces, parasols, canopies, banners, and exquisite music appeared at will. Their palatial residences...
The celestial palaces correspond to their respective forms and colors; whether high or low, large or small, they are all manifested through one, two, or even immeasurable varieties of jewels.
Furthermore, these palatial residences may be as tall or vast as one desires, floating in mid-air.
As for those that are like clouds and vapors, they cannot rise as high as one wishes and remain upon the earth, just like those of the mundane world.
The reason for this is none other than this: those who can act according to their will have, in previous lives while seeking the Way, practiced compassion and diligence, performing many good deeds;
this is the result of their profound virtue. Those who cannot act according to their will are such because, while seeking the Way, they did not practice compassion and diligence, and lacked virtue.
This is due to the degree of their cultivation. Thus, there are distinctions in their diligence and indolence, and differences in the magnitude of their virtues, as manifested for all to see.
Furthermore, both within and without, there are natural flowing springs and various ponds that arise together with the seven natural treasures.

There are some pools consisting of a single type of treasure; even the sand at their bottom consists of that same single treasure. For instance, if it is a pool of gold, the sand at its bottom is of white silver.
As for the crystal ponds, their bottoms consist of lapis lazuli sand. As for the coral ponds, their bottoms consist of amber sand.

Where two jewels form a single pond, the bottom sand likewise consists of those two jewels. If three, four, or even up to seven jewels together form a single pond, its bottom is likewise composed of them.
Among these various jewel ponds, some are forty *li* square, and some are fifty [li] square.
The sixty *li* [in circumference] gradually increase in size until they reach twenty thousand four hundred and eighty *li* on each side;
these are all the places where Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and various superior virtuous beings are born and raised. As for those Buddha-pools, their sides are twice this size.
All these pools are filled with water of eight virtues, serene and overflowing, pure, fragrant, and clean, with a flavor like nectar (*amṛta*).

In the countless worlds of the ten directions, all devas and humans, down to the smallest crawling and wriggling insects, who are reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, are all born by transformation within lotus flowers in ponds of the seven treasures.
They grow naturally without being nursed at breast, and all partake of natural food. This includes all the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and other most virtuous beings.
Sometimes he bathes therein. If he intends for the water to reach his feet, the water immediately reaches his feet;
if he intends for it to reach his knees, his waist, or even his neck, the water does likewise. If he intends for the water to become as it was before, it immediately becomes as it was before.
The temperature was perfectly balanced between cold and warm, providing a sense of total comfort and harmony. It awakened the spirit and gladdened the body, cleansing all mental anxieties.
One became clear, bright, and pure, as translucent as if formless. Once they had finished bathing, each sat upon a lotus flower; naturally, a gentle breeze began to stir.
They blew upon the various jewel trees, which produced either musical sounds or the sounds of the Dharma;
they blew upon the various jewel flowers, all of which became extraordinary fragrances and were scattered over the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.

Among those bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, some desired to hear the sounds of the Dharma, some desired to hear the sounds of music, some desired to hear the fragrance of the flowers, and some had no desire to hear anything at all. As for those who desired to hear...
Those who wish to hear it shall immediately hear it alone; those who do not wish to hear it shall remain silent and hear nothing. Each attains their own intent, and they are naturally happy.

As they proceed with their cultivation, there are those on earth who lecture on the sutras, those who recite the sutras, those who explain the sutras themselves, those who orally transmit the sutras, those who listen to the sutras, those who contemplate the sutras, those who reflect upon the Way, those who practice *dhyāna* with single-mindedness, and those who practice according to the sutras. Furthermore...

There were those in the midst of the void who preached the sutras, recited the sutras, expounded the sutras on their own, orally transmitted the sutras, listened to the sutras, chanted the sutras, contemplated the Way, practiced dhyāna with single-mindedness, and practiced according to the sutras.

Among them, there were those who had not yet attained the stage of Srotāpanna, but by means of this they attained Srotāpanna; and those who had not yet attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin, but by means of this they attained Sakṛdāgāmin.
Those who had not yet attained the stage of *anāgāmin* attained the stage of *anāgāmin*;

those who had not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression for a bodhisattva attained the stage of non-retrogression for a bodhisattva. Each obtained what was appropriate according to their own capacity.
Within the various jewel ponds, the waters flowed into one another, neither too fast nor too slow, as infinite, wondrous sounds arose spontaneously from the surging waves.
Some produce the sound of preaching on the Buddha; some produce the sound of preaching the Dharma; some produce the sound of preaching on the Sangha;
some produce the sound of preaching on tranquility; the sound of preaching on emptiness and non-self; the sound of preaching on great compassion; the sound of preaching on the *pāramitās*;

the sound of preaching on the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharmas*); the sound of preaching on the various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms; the sound of preaching on non-action; and the sound of preaching on the non-arising and non-extinction [of phenomena].
They utter the sound of the teaching on the patience of non-arising, up to the sound of the teaching on all sublime dharmas such as the consecration of ambrosia.
Those who hear them experience immeasurable joy and give rise to a pure mind, free from all conceptual discrimination, upright and equanimous, thereby maturing their roots of goodness.
They shall never regress from unsurpassed bodhi. In that world, one shall no longer hear the sounds of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, or yakṣas;
nor shall one hear such evil sounds as killing, stealing, strife, harsh speech, or double-tongued speech.
Such wicked sounds will be utterly non-existent even to be heard, let alone exist in reality. There will be only naturally pure sounds and naturally delightful [sounds].
Because it is a realm of bliss, its land is named Sukhāvatī (Utmost Bliss). Upon the banks of the ponds stand countless sandalwood trees and auspicious fruit trees;
their flowers and fruits are perpetually fragrant, and extraordinary scents waft abroad. There are also celestial utpala lotuses.
There were *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, variegated in color and luxuriantly blooming, covering the surface of the water.

Furthermore, there were trees made of the seven kinds of jewels. As for those trees consisting of a single jewel, their roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were all made of that one jewel alone.
As for those trees consisting of two, three, or even up to seven jewels, their roots, trunks, branches, and leaves [were likewise composed of those respective jewels].
The fruits are likewise so. These various jewel trees each form their own distinct rows; row after row they stand planted together, arranged in hundreds of thousands of tiers.
They are interspersed with jewel ponds in the same manner, extending everywhere throughout the world.

Their brilliant colors and radiant splendor are beyond the power of the eye to fully behold. From time to time, a pure breeze arises, spontaneously producing subtle and wondrous sounds that have no equal.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of spontaneous, wondrous music, the sounds of which are none other than the sublime Dharma—clear, resonant, piercing, subtle, harmonious, and elegant.
When those who have been reborn there partake of food, some desire bowls made of gold or silver;
others desire those made of crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, agate, or alternatively, moonstone, maṇi-jewels, white jade, or purple gold.
As for the bowls, they all appear before them according to their wishes. Within them, food and drink of a hundred flavors are filled;
though much is present, there is no excess, and though little is present, nothing is lacking. Once eaten, they naturally vanish. When one wishes to eat again, they reappear as before.
Whatever clothing one desires arrives immediately upon thought, without the need for cutting, sewing, beating, dyeing, or washing. Thus it is with the various Bodhisattvas.
The assembly of śrāvakas all had countenances that were upright, serene, and handsome; their dispositions were all characterized by wisdom and vigor;

whatever they wished to say, they already understood each other’s intentions; and among the thoughts held in their minds, there was nothing that was not concerned with the Way and its Virtue, which was thus manifested in their speech.
There was nothing that was not a righteous matter; every movement conformed to propriety and righteousness.

They were as harmonious as brothers, instructing and exhorting one another with reverence and joy, their intentions all pure and clear, free from any taint of greed. All traces of lust, anger, and folly were utterly extinguished without remainder.

They delight in following the path of the sutras, illuminating their nature of wisdom and penetrating their past lives. Furthermore, there is a Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment, one thousand six hundred yojanas in height;
its branches and leaves spread out for eight hundred yojanas, and its roots penetrate the jeweled ground for five hundred yojanas.
Furthermore, all manner of precious jewels spontaneously coalesce there, and flowers and fruits flourish, manifesting hundreds of thousands of infinite and exquisite colors.
When a gentle breeze occasionally stirs upon these trees, it produces the sounds of infinite sublime Dharma teachings.
Its sound spreads throughout all Buddha-fields. Sentient beings who hear it attain the profound *dharmakṣānti* (receptivity to the Dharma) and abide on the stage of non-retrogression.
They shall be free from diseases of the ear until they achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*.

If there are sentient beings who see this tree, they shall not suffer from diseases of the eye until they attain Buddhahood; nor shall those who smell the fragrance of the tree suffer from diseases of the nose.
Those who eat the fruits of the trees have no illness of the tongue; those illuminated by the light of the trees have no illness of the body;

and those who contemplate the trees find their minds cooled, becoming free from the diseases of afflictions such as greed. They all attain the profound *dharmakṣānti* and abide on the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, immeasurable jewel nets cover that buddha-field, and there is also a wind of natural virtue.
It moves gently; neither cold nor hot, it is warm, harmonious, and soft;

neither hurried nor slow, it blows through the various jeweled nets and jeweled trees, producing immeasurable and subtle sounds of the Dharma and spreading ten thousand kinds of pure and elegant fragrances of virtue.
Those who hear them find their afflictions and defilements stilled and do not arise naturally. When the wind touches their bodies, they experience spontaneous bliss. Within that space...
Those who wish to become Buddhas are immediately led to cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva until they attain Buddhahood.

Once they have attained Buddhahood, if they possess a prior vow to deliver sentient beings, they will, by virtue of their great vows and merit, enter the realms of birth and death in other directions to roar the lion’s roar, preaching the Dharma to deliver them.
At that time, Amitābha Buddha, through his majestic spiritual power, causes those [beings] to be transformed and taught.

All sentient beings—countless devas and humans throughout the ten directions, down to the smallest of crawling and wriggling creatures—who are delivered and liberated, and who are reborn in that land, are beyond counting.
Those who become śrāvakas and attain the path of nirvāṇa are also beyond counting.
Those who become bodhisattvas and even attain buddhahood are likewise beyond counting. Such is the Jewel...
These lands are all manifested through the boundless power of Amitābha Buddha’s vows, his vast majestic spirit, and his perfected merit;
they appear spontaneously, infinitely and inexhaustibly, beyond the reach of thought. To speak of them for a day and night, or even for an eon, would not suffice;
I have now described them to you only briefly. Among the devas and people of the worlds in the ten directions, those who possess a sincere heart and desire to be born in [Amitābha’s land]...

Regarding the Buddha-field of Amitābha, there are three distinct classes of those who are reborn there. As for those of the highest class who are reborn, they leave their homes and renounce desire to become śramaṇas.
With hearts free from greed or longing, they uphold the sutras and precepts, practice the six pāramitās, and cultivate the deeds of a bodhisattva.
Single-mindedly and exclusively mindful of Amitābha Buddha, they cultivate all manner of meritorious virtues. Such persons shall, within their dreams, behold the Buddha and—
When the lives of various bodhisattvas and śrāvakas are about to end, the Buddha and the assembly of sages will all come to welcome them.
They will then be born through transformation within lotus flowers in ponds of the seven treasures, becoming bodhisattvas of the stage of non-retrogression.

Their residences, palaces made of the seven treasures, are situated in mid-air and are close to where the Buddha resides. As for those born through the middle grade, although they cannot go there [themselves],...

He became a śramaṇa and extensively cultivated meritorious deeds. He constantly believed in and accepted the Buddha’s words, resolved upon the mind of unsurpassed bodhi, and focused exclusively on mindfulness of the Buddha.

According to his capacity, he practiced virtue, observed the fasts and precepts, erected stupas and images, provided food for śramaṇas, hung silk banners, lit lamps, scattered flowers, and burned incense.
He dedicated these merits, vowing to be reborn in that land. When his life was about to end, the Buddha...
He also manifests his body before the great assembly and that person, and together with them, he is reborn there, likewise abiding in the stage of non-retrogression.
Next, regarding those born in the middle grade, as for those born in the lower grade, they are unable to perform various meritorious deeds.
He did not give rise to the aspiration for unexcelled bodhicitta; he merely recited the Buddha’s name ten times each day, vowing to be reborn in that land.
When his life was about to end, he again saw the Buddha in a dream, and subsequently attained rebirth there. His dwelling in the palace of seven treasures was situated solely upon the ground.

One is far removed from the Buddha. If one cannot practice great diligence and meditative concentration, yet fully upholds the sutras and precepts, one must certainly cultivate the ten wholesome actions:
first, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not engaging in sexual misconduct; fourth, not being deceitful; fifth, not drinking intoxicants; sixth, not using double-tongued speech;
seventh, not using harsh speech; eighth, not speaking falsehoods; ninth, not being envious; tenth, not being greedy.
Free from desire, stinginess, anger, and wrong views; steadfast in filial piety and diligent in sincerity and trustworthiness;

faithfully accepting the Buddha’s words and contemplating Amitābha Buddha day and night—such a person, at the end of life, will have no inverted thoughts and shall immediately attain rebirth, never regressing from unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, those who maintain the purity of the precepts and fasts, constantly mindful with a single mind, [shall likewise attain rebirth].
Amitābha Buddha. Those who desire to be born in that land and maintain this practice for ten days and nights without interruption will, at the end of their lives, certainly attain rebirth there.
Even if one cannot do so for ten days and nights, one should sever all anxieties and cast away sorrow; one must not concern oneself with household affairs and must not be near women.

With body upright and mind rectified, severing all craving and desire, maintaining the purity of the fast and precepts, one should with a sincere heart recollect that Buddha and chant His name for a single day and night without interruption. This is superior to practicing virtue for a hundred years within the land of Amitābha.
Why is this? Because the people in that land are entirely virtuous, lacking even a hair’s breadth of evil. If it were like this...

In this world, those who commit evil are extremely numerous, while those who practice goodness are extremely few. One who is able to cultivate and discipline themselves achieves merit far superior to theirs;

at the end of life, such a person shall attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]. If there are good men or good women who give rise to the bodhicitta, uphold the various prohibitive precepts, and steadfastly maintain them without transgression;
who benefit sentient beings and dedicate all the roots of goodness they have cultivated toward enabling others to attain peace and security—[they too shall likewise attain rebirth].

Delighted, they constantly recollect the Buddha and the realms of that land. When such persons pass away, they will be reborn there, surrounded by sages and saints, and will swiftly hear the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma.
All those who are reborn there will be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and will ultimately penetrate deeply into the essential meaning of the wondrous Dharma.
Their faculties will be clear and sharp; even those whose faculties were initially dull will achieve the two types of patience (*kṣānti*), while those of sharp faculties [will achieve more].

They shall attain the incalculable patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). All shall, in a single lifetime, succeed to the seat of Buddhahood. Furthermore, they shall be free from three kinds of faults:
first, their minds shall be free from falsehood; second, they shall abide in non-retrogression; third, their virtues shall not be in vain.
Those who are born there will progress without ever regressing until they attain Buddhahood.

If there are sentient beings who cultivate various merits with the aspiration to be born in that land, yet later develop regret or harbor doubts, and do not believe in the existence of that Buddha-land, [they shall not go].
They do not believe that there are those who attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Although such persons are thus, they continue to maintain a mindful heart;

at times they believe and at times they disbelieve, their will wavering and having no firm foundation. At the moment of death, the Buddha manifests his body so that they may see him with their own eyes.

Though they are unable to speak, their hearts are filled with joy, and they then regret not having exerted themselves to perform various good deeds. Thus, through this repentance, [they are purified].
Therefore, they were also born in that land; however, they were unable to proceed to the presence of the Buddha and instead entered the borderland of that land.
There they saw a city made of the seven treasures and immediately entered it. Within a lotus flower, they received a body and grew naturally to maturity.

Their food and drink were also entirely spontaneous, and their happiness was like that of the gods in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Yet, within that city, for five hundred years, they were unable to [attain...].
They see the Buddha, but do not see the bodhisattvas or the assembly of śrāvakas; having no means to make offerings, they regard this as suffering.
To show them a minor reprimand, that land is called "womb-birth" (garbhaja). One should know that those who give rise to doubt lose great benefit.
The people of this world who, in their previous lives, performed good deeds and constantly practiced the Buddha-way are those who are able to hear the name of Amitābha Buddha;
they are certainly no ordinary persons. Those who do not give rise to faith, nor believe the words of the Buddha, have come from the evil realms with residual karmic retribution yet to be exhausted;
being ignorant and lacking understanding, they are not yet fit for liberation. Furthermore, they dwell amidst extreme wickedness and the most intense suffering.

Amidst these circumstances, they labor their bodies in various enterprises to provide for themselves. Whether noble or base, rich or poor, young or old, male or female, all are anxious over wealth and possessions.
Their thoughts are burdened and their anxieties accumulated; their minds run errands for them, finding no time of rest. Those with fields worry about their fields.
There are those who grieve over their homes; there are those who grieve over their cattle, horses, six domestic animals, slaves, clothing, food, and utensils.

Even the noble, the honorable, and the wealthy suffer from these afflictions, which bind them fast within their hearts. As for the poor and lowly, they are constantly tormented by deprivation and exhaustion.
Having no fields or houses, they worry and desire to possess them; having no oxen, horses, or other livestock, they likewise worry and desire to have them all.
When they finally acquire one thing, they lack another; when they finally obtain one circumstance, they lack another.
Their toil and suffering are such that there is never a moment of rest. They do not attain the Way and its Virtue, but remain lost and submerged in anger, greed, and resentment.

Attached to wealth and sensual pleasures, you shall not attain the Way and will instead enter the miserable realms of suffering, wandering through thousands of billions of kalpas with no time of escape.
This pain is beyond words; it is most pitiable. I now tell you all: among worldly matters, choose what is good and practice it diligently.
Love, desire, glory, and splendor cannot be maintained forever; there is only the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Impure and foul are the secretions; there is nothing therein to be delighted in. You should resolve with determination to maintain upright conduct and perform all manner of wholesome deeds.

Wash away the defilements of the mind, ensure that your words and actions are loyal and trustworthy, and let your inner thoughts correspond with your outward behavior. Having attained self-deliverance, you should further rescue and assist others.
Although the hardships of the present life are but a fleeting moment, one will thereafter be born in the Pure Land, where happiness is infinite.

One shall forever be united with the illumination of the Way and its Virtue, eternally uprooting the very foundation of birth and death. Out of compassion for the people of this world, my instruction is most earnest:

the True Dharma is difficult to hear; you should therefore exert yourselves with diligence and be reborn in the Pure Realm, forever departing from the five destinies. If you do not believe and awaken to this, it will be of no benefit.
When such a person’s life is about to end, what can repentance avail?
Furthermore, it is said that immeasurable and incalculable kalpas ago, there appeared a Buddha named Lokeśvararāja, who transformed and delivered sentient beings.
At that time, there was a great king who went to listen to the Dharma and subsequently attained awakening.
He then renounced his royal position to go forth and practice, becoming known as the Bhikṣu Dharmākara—none other than Amitābha Buddha.
In the presence of the World-Lord Sovereign Tathāgata, he made forty-eight vows, each vowing to deliver sentient beings. Among them, one vow states: "When I become a Buddha, in the ten directions..."
Sentient beings from countless worlds, with sincere hearts, believe and rejoice, desiring to be born in my land.
If they should not be born after ten recitations of my name, may I not attain Buddhahood. This is because I, as a Buddha, have made a personal vow to deliver sentient beings;
it is merely by relying on their ten recitations that I manifest the heart of taking refuge. Therefore, people direct their sincere faith toward me and recite my name.

Such a person will certainly receive blessings and protection in the present life, and all calamities and obstacles will be eliminated. After death, they will surely be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
When reciting the Name, one should single-mindedly visualize the form of Amitābha Buddha. At the time of the end of life...
One will surely behold the true body of the Buddha, who comes forward to welcome and guide them. Furthermore, another vow states:

"If women in the countless worlds of the ten directions hear my name and, with joy, faith, and delight, resolve their minds upon Bodhi and loathe their female bodies, then at the end of their lives they shall be reborn in my land;
their bodies shall no longer be female. This is due to the vast and great majestic power of me, the Buddha."
He is omnipresent. When the thoughts of a person’s mind become fully matured through union with the Buddha, there is a spontaneous resonance;
thus, the Buddha manifests his body.
It is further said that Amitābha Buddha, throughout great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, practiced the bodhisattva path and perfected the power of patience.
Disregarding all sufferings, he constantly benefits sentient beings with a serene countenance and loving speech. He skillfully guards his verbal karma, never deriding the faults of others;
he skillfully guards his physical karma, never failing in his moral discipline (*śīla*); and he skillfully guards his mental karma, remaining pure and untainted.
From his mouth there constantly issues the fragrance of sandalwood, and from all the pores of his body issues the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus. Thus, immeasurable sentient beings...
Those who smell this fragrance all give rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhicitta.

From their hands constantly emerge all kinds of clothing, all kinds of food and drink, all kinds of banners, flags, and precious parasols, as well as all kinds of music and every most excellent requisite.
By bestowing these gifts upon sentient beings, they cause them to experience joy and transform them through such practice; thus, [they attain] the state of non-...
He measured countless sentient beings and caused them to resolve upon unexcelled bodhicitta. Such virtuous practices were immeasurable and boundless, beyond the power of words to fully describe.
Throughout immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, his merit became perfected and his majestic spiritual power blazed forth;
only then did he fulfill his vow and enter the rank of Buddhahood. Therefore, throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions...
From the devas and people of the various realms down to the smallest crawling and wriggling insects, there are none who are not saved.
Thus, by taking refuge in a single thought, they are reborn in that land, all through transformation within lotuses in ponds of the seven treasures.
They all receive naturally pure and ethereal bodies and enjoy infinite lifespans. Throughout that buddha-field, they are all beings of supreme goodness; there are none [of inferior character].
The women all have lifespans of incalculable kalpas; they all possess the power of clairvoyance and clairaudience, seeing one another from afar and hearing one another’s voices from afar.
They all seek the path of goodness and are no different from any other beings.
It is further said that one day the countenance of Śākyamuni Buddha was extraordinary. His attendant Ānanda, finding it strange, questioned him about it. The Buddha said, "Excellent!

What you have asked surpasses the merit of making offerings to all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas throughout a single world-system, as well as the merit of bestowing gifts upon the devas, humans, and even down to the smallest crawling and flying insects, even for the duration of many kalpas. It would still be but a hundred-thousandth part [of the merit of this question].
It is ten thousand times greater; it cannot be equaled. Why is this?

Because all the celestial emperors, kings, and common people, down to the smallest crawling and wriggling creatures, shall all, by virtue of your inquiry, attain the Way of liberation. Viewed from this perspective, [it is immeasurable].
When Śākyamuni Buddha was first about to speak of Amitābha Buddha, his state of mind manifested in his physical appearance as something different from his usual self.
Thus, the way in which Amitābha Buddha moves the various Buddhas is already extraordinary;
how much more so is it when he moves all sentient beings? Observe his initial verse of aspiration, which says: "When I reach..."
When he attains Buddhahood, his fame shall transcend the ten directions; humans and devas will joyfully hear of it and all come to be born in my land.
Even those in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm shall likewise be born within my land.
Thus, it can be known that there is no one within the three realms and the six paths of saṃsāra who is not saved. For this reason, this sutra says: "Amitābha Buddha currently dwells in the West..."

He dwells in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and furthermore, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, he teaches and transforms countless devas and humans, even down to the smallest crawling and wriggling creatures;
there are none who do not attain transcendence and liberation. This is why his vast deliverance of sentient beings is without end.
If a person takes refuge in him with even a single thought, they shall accordingly be born in that land—of this there is no doubt.

Furthermore, it is said: Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, how many bodhisattvas of the stage of non-retrogression in this world will be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha?
The Buddha replied, "In this world, there are seven hundred and two..."
Ten billion bodhisattvas of the stage of non-retrogression will be reborn in that land, as well as countless lesser bodhisattvas who have cultivated only slight merit.
Not only in my own land, but in the buddha-fields of other directions, even throughout the infinite buddha-fields of the ten directions,
those who are reborn there are exceedingly numerous, beyond all calculation.
It is further said: The Buddha declared that within heaven and earth, the five realms of existence are clearly manifest. Vast and expansive, they are boundless;

karmic retributions arise one after another, passed down through successive inheritances. Whether beautiful or foul, whether pleasant or cruel and toxic, all are experienced by oneself. When a person of goodness performs good deeds, they proceed from joy to joy.
From light one enters light; when the wicked commit evil, they enter from suffering into further suffering, and from darkness into deeper darkness.

The people of the world are oblivious to this, and thus the evil paths are never-ending. Consequently, there exist the natural hells, hungry ghosts, birds, beasts, and all classes of crawling and flying creatures.
Transmigrating within this cycle, one has no means of escape for countless kalpas; only by practicing the Pure Land method can one directly transcend it.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "At that time, Vaidehī wept aloud and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'World-Honored One, I pray that you will extensively describe for me the place free from sorrow and affliction, where I may be reborn. I take no pleasure in the turbid and evil world of Jambudvīpa. Thereupon...
The World-Honored One emitted light from between his eyebrows, which shone throughout the Buddha-lands of the worlds of the ten directions, appearing clearly within them all.
When Vaidehī saw this, she addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Although these Buddha-lands are pure and all possess radiance, my sole wish now is to be born in the world of Ultimate Bliss, in the presence of Amitābha Buddha."

Furthermore, it says: Regarding those of the highest grade in the highest birth, if there are sentient beings who wish to be born in that land, they shall attain rebirth provided they give rise to three kinds of mind:
first, the mind of utmost sincerity; second, the profound mind; and third, the mind of dedication and aspiration.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of sentient beings who shall attain rebirth: first, those who possess a compassionate heart and do not kill, fully maintaining all the precepts;
second, those who read and recite the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras; and third, those who practice the six mindfulnesses and dedicate their merit while making vows.
One should vow to be born in that land. Possessing these merits, after one day up to seven days, one will immediately attain rebirth there.

At the time of being born in that land, because this person has been diligent and courageous, Amitābha Tathāgata, along with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus and the assembly of śrāvakas, immeasurable devas, and Avalokiteśvara...
The Bodhisattvas, holding vajra pedestals, together with the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, arrive before the practitioner.
Amitābha Buddha emits a great radiance that illuminates the practitioner’s body; together with the various bodhisattvas, he extends his hand to welcome them. Having seen this, the practitioner...
Filled with joy and leaping for gladness, they saw themselves mounted upon a vajra pedestal, following behind the Buddha. In the time it takes to snap one's fingers, they were reborn in that land.
There they beheld the physical bodies of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, complete with all their marks, as they expounded the sublime Dharma; having heard it, they rejoiced.

He immediately realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). In the space of a mere moment, he attended upon various Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
In the presence of each Buddha, he received successive predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Returning to his own land, he attained immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dharanī-doors.
Those of the highest grade who are born from the middle [level] do not necessarily read or recite the Vaipulya sutras;

yet they skillfully understand their meaning and intent, have deep faith in the primary truth (paramārtha) and the law of cause and effect, and do not slander the Mahāyāna. By virtue of these merits, they dedicate them toward seeking birth in Sukhāvatī.
When their lives are about to end, Amitābha Buddha, surrounded by a vast assembly of followers including Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, will appear before them.
Holding a vajra pedestal, he approaches the practitioner and praises him, saying: "O Son of the Dharma, you practice the Mahāyāna and understand the ultimate truth;
therefore, I have now come to welcome you. Together with a thousand transformation Buddhas, he simultaneously extends his hand. The practitioner sees this for himself.
Seated upon a purple-gold pedestal, in the space of a single thought-moment, one is immediately reborn within the seven-jeweled pond of that land.
This purple-gold pedestal is like a great jewel-flower; it opens after a night has passed. The Buddha and the bodhisattvas simultaneously emit light, illuminating the body of the practitioner.
His eyes immediately opened and became clear. He descended from the golden platform, prostrated before the Buddha with palms joined, and remained thus for seven days.
At that moment, he attained non-retrogression regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that same moment, he was able to fly through the air, traveling everywhere throughout the ten directions to attend upon various Buddhas and cultivate various *samādhis*. After the passing of one small kalpa, he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*).
Regarding those of the highest grade who are born in the lower level: they also believe in cause and effect and do not slander the Mahāyāna;
they merely give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment and, by means of these merits, dedicate them toward seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

When their lives are about to end, Amitābha Buddha, along with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with their retinues, holding golden lotus flowers and manifesting as five hundred Buddhas, come to welcome this person.
Five hundred manifested Buddhas simultaneously extended their hands and praised him, saying, "Son of the Dharma, you are now pure;
having resolved to attain the unsurpassed Way, we have come to welcome you. He then saw himself seated upon a golden lotus flower.
Once seated, the flower closed, and he followed behind the World-Honored One to attain rebirth in the pool of seven treasures. After one day and one night, the lotus flower opened; after seven days—

In the interim, he was able to see the Buddha; yet, although he saw the Buddha’s body, his mind was not clear regarding its various marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa*). After twenty-one days, he saw them with perfect clarity.
He traveled throughout the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas, and in the presence of those Buddhas, he heard the most profound Dharma.
After three minor kalpas, he attained the Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas and dwelt in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

Regarding those of middling capacity who are born in the upper grade: if there are sentient beings who uphold the five precepts, do not commit the five heinous crimes, and are free from various faults and afflictions, they dedicate these roots of goodness toward seeking rebirth in the world of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
At the time of their death, Amitābha Buddha, surrounded by his retinue, emits golden light and approaches that person, proclaiming [the truths of] suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
The constant absence of self; praising renunciation, by which one attains liberation from all suffering. Upon seeing this, the practitioner’s heart is filled with great joy.

He beholds his own body seated upon a lotus pedestal, with supple and tender hands joined in *añjali*, prostrating before the Buddha. Before his head has even been raised, he immediately attains rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
The lotus flower then opens; at the moment it blooms, he hears various sounds extolling [the virtues of the Buddha].
They praised the Four Noble Truths. At that very moment, they attained the path of Arhatship, endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.

As for those born in the middle grade: if there are sentient beings who, for one day and one night, observe the eight precepts of the fast, or for one day and one night, observe the śrāmaṇera precepts, or for one day and one night, observe the full precepts (upasaṃpadā) without deficiency in their dignified conduct—by means of these...
Dedicate these merits toward seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

When one’s life is about to end, one will see Amitābha Buddha together with his retinue, emitting golden light and holding seven-jeweled lotus flowers, appearing before the practitioner. The practitioner will hear for themselves:
A voice resounded from the sky, praising him: "O son of good family! Since you, a virtuous person, have followed the teachings of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, I have come to welcome you.
The practitioner saw for himself that he sat upon a lotus flower, which then closed;
he was born in the world of Sukhāvatī within a jeweled pond. After seven days had passed, the lotus flower finally opened. He opened his eyes and, with palms joined, offered praise.
They praised the World-Honored One; hearing the Dharma, they rejoiced and attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. After half a kalpa had passed, they became *arhats*.

As for those of middle capacity who are born in the lower grade: if there are good men or good women who filially support their parents and practice worldly benevolence and kindness, at the time when their lives are about to end, they encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who extensively expounds for them the bliss of Amitābha Buddha’s land.
He also recounted the forty-eight vows of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara. Having heard this account, he immediately passed away;
in the time it takes a strong man to extend or contract his arm, he was reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss. Seven days after his birth there, he encountered Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
hearing the Dharma, he rejoiced and, after the passing of one small kalpa, became an Arhat.
Regarding those born in the lower grade of the superior level: there may be sentient beings who have committed various evil deeds.
Although such foolish people do not slander the Vaipulya sutras, they have created much evil karma and lack a sense of shame or remorse.

When their lives are about to end, they encounter virtuous friends who recite for them the titles of the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna scriptures. By hearing the names of these various sutras, [they attain rebirth].

Therefore, the most grievous evil karma of a thousand kalpas is eliminated. Furthermore, the Wise One instructs that one should join the palms and, with hands clasped, recite the name "Namo Amitābha Buddha.
