By reciting the Buddha’s name, the offenses of fifty billion kalpas of birth and death are eliminated.

At that time, that Buddha immediately dispatches manifested Buddhas, as well as manifested Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, to the presence of the practitioner, who praise him, saying: "Good son, you..."
"By virtue of reciting the Buddha’s name, all transgressions are extinguished. I shall come to welcome you. The practitioner will then see the light of the manifested Buddha filling his room;
he will immediately pass away, mount a precious lotus flower, follow behind the manifested Buddha, and be born within a precious pond.

After seven weeks had passed, the lotus flower finally blossomed. At the moment of its blooming, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion emitted a great radiance and stood before that person, preaching the profound twelve divisions of the sūtras for them.
Having heard this, they attained faith and understanding, and gave rise to the mind set on the unsurpassed path.
After ten minor kalpas, they perfected the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas and entered the first bhūmi.
Regarding those of the middle grade within the lowest category: there may be sentient beings who violate the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the full set of precepts;
who steal the property of the Sangha or the property of the monks present; who preach the Dharma with impurity;
and who lack shame and remorse, adorning themselves with various evil karmas. Such offenders, on account of their evil karma, ought to fall into hell; yet when their lives are about to end,

When the various fires of hell simultaneously converge upon them, they encounter a spiritual friend who, out of great compassion, explains for them the ten powers and majestic virtue of Amitābha Buddha.
This friend extensively praises that Buddha’s radiant supernatural power and likewise extols his precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Upon hearing this, the person eliminates the offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas; thus, the fierce fires of hell [are extinguished].
It transforms into a cool breeze that blows upon celestial flowers. Upon each flower are transformed Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who welcome this person.
In the space of a single thought-moment, they attain rebirth within a lotus flower inside a pond of the seven treasures. After six kalpas have passed, the lotus flower finally opens.
Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta comfort the person with their Brahma-voices and preach for them the profound Mahāyāna.
Regarding the profound sutras: having heard this Dharma, they immediately give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment at that very moment.
As for those of the lowest grade and lowest birth: there may be sentient beings who commit unwholesome deeds—the five heinous crimes and the ten evil acts—possessing all manner of unwholesomeness.
Such foolish people, on account of their evil karma, ought to fall into the evil realms and undergo suffering for many kalpas.

"Alas! Such a foolish person, at the time of death, may encounter a virtuous friend who offers various forms of consolation and explains the sublime Dharma, instructing them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Yet, this person, being oppressed by suffering, has no leisure to practice mindfulness. The virtuous friend tells them:

'If you are unable to practice mindfulness, you should instead invoke the name of Amitāyus Buddha. Thus, with a sincere heart, they cause the sound of the invocation to be uninterrupted for ten [moments]."
Recite: "Namo Amitābha Buddha. By reciting the name of the Buddha, in every moment of thought, one eliminates the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death.
At the time of death, one will see a golden lotus flower, like a sun-disk, appearing before that person.
In the space of a single thought-moment, one attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Within the lotus flower, for twelve full...

After a great kalpa, the lotus flower finally opens. Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, with voices of great compassion, extensively expound for them the true reality of all dharmas and the methods for eliminating sinful karma.
Having heard this, they rejoice; at that very moment, they immediately resolve to attain bodhicitta.
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "After my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Gopaka in the kingdom of Northern India.

Having cultivated immeasurable and various most excellent roots of merit for bodhi, he will pass away and be reborn in the West, in the Land of Immeasurable Life, beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds.
There, in the presence of that Buddha, he will plant various roots of merit. Afterwards...
"He shall become a Buddha named Vimalaprabha.
The *Bodhisattvajanmabhūmi-sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "At that time, Makhādeva attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Five hundred laymen and twenty-five laywomen all attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). When their lives ended, they were all reborn together in the Immeasurable [Life]."

Regarding the Pure Land of the Buddha of Longevity, the *Jingtu zhuan* (Biographies of the Pure Land) states: "Amitābha Buddha, together with the two Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, out of compassion for sentient beings, board the vessel of great vows to navigate the sea of birth and death.
Within this Sahā world, they call out to and lead sentient beings [to liberation]."
Board the great vessel of the supreme vow and be conveyed to the Western Land. If one has faith and is willing to go, even if they possess evil karma, they will certainly attain birth in that land.
As the Sūtra says: "The Buddha can deliver all sentient beings, but he cannot deliver those who lack faith.

This is because faith is but a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*). At the moment the body perishes, there is only this single thought-moment. When one reaches that destination by means of a single thought-moment, then—
There is nothing they cannot reach; how much more so for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who further invite others to be reborn there?
The *Avatamsaka Sūtra*, Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra, says: "When such a person approaches the end of life, at the final moment, all their faculties will completely disintegrate;
all kinsmen and relatives will be left behind; and all power and influence will utterly fade away."
"Even though elephants, horses, chariots, precious jewels, and all other things shall no longer follow him, this King of Vows alone shall not abandon him, but shall lead him from behind at all times.
Within a single kṣaṇa, he shall attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Therefore, upon hearing this King of Vows, you must not harbor doubts; you should receive it with earnest attention."
The "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" states: "If one hears this sutra and practices according to its teachings, at the end of life in this world,
one will immediately go to the Land of Peace and Bliss, to the dwelling place of Amitābha Buddha surrounded by a multitude of great bodhisattvas,
and be born within a lotus flower upon a precious throne."
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "If a person with a distracted mind enters a stupa or temple and calls out 'Namo Buddha' even once, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha is the unsurpassed Dharma King, and the great Bodhisattvas serve as his ministers of the Dharma. [The text continues: "All..."
That which I, your servant, hold in the highest esteem is solely the Buddha, the King of Dharma.

There are certain bodhisattvas who, reflecting upon their own past, realized that because they had slandered the *prajñāpāramitā*, they fell into the evil realms and underwent immeasurable suffering. Furthermore, although they practiced other disciplines for immeasurable kalpas thereafter, they were unable to escape the ocean of suffering.
Later, they encountered a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who instructed them to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha; immediately, their transgressions were extinguished.
Obstacles. Transcending birth, one enters the Pure Land. I should now pay homage and offer thanks to Amitābha Buddha. Why is this?
Parents, relatives, friends, kings, and deities cannot deliver me and enable my escape from the ocean of suffering;

only through the power of Amitābha Buddha’s vows and his compassionate reception can I emerge from this ocean of suffering. As the verse says: "If a person aspires to become a Buddha, they should keep Amitābha in mind."
...he immediately manifested his form before me; therefore, I take refuge in him and pay homage.
The eminent Master Yang Jie (Cizong) attained high honors in his youth and was well-versed in the fundamental tenets of the Chan school.

He held that because the faculties of sentient beings vary between sharp and dull, the only path that is both accessible and easy to understand, as well as concise and easy to practice, is the Western Pure Land. It requires only a single...
Regarding the contemplation of the mind: by relying on the power of the Buddha’s vows, one is born directly in An-yang (i.e., the Pure Land).
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* records the words of the Elder’s Son Vimokṣa: "One knows that all Buddhas are like reflections and one's own mind is like water.

If I wish to see the Tathāgata Amitābha in the World of Peace and Bliss, I shall see him immediately at will. From this, it is known that when sentient beings focus their thoughts with concentration, [they attain this realization].
One beholds Amitābha Buddha. If one is born in that land, there will be no manifold sufferings. The *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* states:
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla asked Śākyamuni Buddha, "How can future sentient beings come to see all the Buddhas of the ten directions?
The Buddha instructed him to recollect Amitābha Buddha, whereby they immediately see all the Buddhas of the ten directions. Furthermore, the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*...

The *Sūtra of the Accumulation* states: "If sentient beings from other directions hear the name of the Tathāgata Amitāyus, and are able to give rise to even a single thought of pure faith, rejoicing with delight, and dedicate all their roots of goodness toward the vow to be born in his land, they shall be reborn there according to their wish and attain the stage of non-retrogression.
These are all the words of the Buddha. If one does not believe the words of the Buddha, what words can be believed?"
If one is not born in the Pure Land, what land could one be born in? Su Dongpo said: "In his later years, Cigong served as a high-ranking provincial official.

He had a sixteen-foot image of Amitābha Buddha painted, which he carried with him for worship and contemplation. When the time of his death arrived, he was moved by the Buddha’s coming to welcome him;
he passed away sitting upright. His verse on departing this world says: 'In life there is nothing to cling to; in death there is likewise nothing to fear.'"
It may be abandoned; it is merely something within the great void. To take what is mistaken and proceed with it—this is the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
During the time of Śākyamuni Buddha, there were an old man and an old woman who used one *dǒu* of grain to keep count as they recited the name of Amitābha Buddha, vowing to be reborn in the West.
The Buddha said, "I have another method that allows you to attain the benefit of a single recitation of the Buddha’s name."

Regarding the number of grains of rice: one is taught to recollect the thirty-six trillion, one hundred and eleven thousand, nine thousand five hundred Buddhas named and titled identically as Amitābha in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (as recorded in the *Bao Wang Lun*).

If one were to calculate this using common *xiān* rice, there would be one thousand eight hundred grains in a single *hé*. This number corresponds to the measure of two thousand *shí*. The Buddha himself [established] this...
From this instruction to the two elderly women, it can be known that their merit is exceedingly great. (Regarding the mantra syllables:

they were originally not characters from the Buddha-land, but were employed by the translators of the scriptures. Because people found these characters difficult to recognize and would not recite them, when the Buddha first spoke [the mantra], there was only sound.

Now, we preserve those sounds and substitute them with easily recognizable characters. Furthermore, there are many errors in the punctuation of worldly texts; now, we have used the punctuation from two locations in the Tripiṭaka so that they are identical. One need no longer harbor doubts. For one who recites this mantra, Amitābha Buddha will always be upon their crown, preventing enemies from [harming] them.)

It prevents harm; it brings peace and security in this present life, and at the end of one’s life, one will be reborn according to one’s wish. If one completes two hundred thousand recitations, the sprout of Bodhi will arise. At three hundred thousand recitations, one will soon behold Amitābha Buddha face-to-face.
(This is transcribed here according to the punctuated edition in the Tripitaka.)
Namo Amitābhāya tathāgatāya te dhyeye te amitābhe sudarśanāya amitābhe samantāya amitābhe vikaraṇe amitābhe vikaraṇate gamini.
*Gagana śiti-kāri svāhā*. Regarding this, Longshu (Longshu) said:
"I have perused the Tripitaka and various biographical records in their entirety; taking their essential meaning, I have composed this for the sake of Pure Land [practice]."
As for the writing: there is not a single character that lacks a source. I hope you will not disregard these words because they come from a person of humble station.
Desiring that everyone may understand them together, I have made my speech direct rather than ornate.
The discourse on the Pure Land is frequently encountered in the midst of daily life, yet its residual merit is often perceived only after death.
Those who do not understand this regard it merely as a matter for the life hereafter; they fail to realize that it is of great benefit even during one's lifetime.
Why is this? For that which the Buddha teaches to instruct humanity is nothing other than goodness, just like that of the Confucian tradition.

This is how they instruct others; what is different about this? Therefore, when one takes the Pure Land as their core intention, then whatever appears within the course of daily life—whatever the mind contemplates, whatever the mouth speaks, and whatever the body performs—will invariably be good.
Being good, one becomes a gentleman or a great sage. In this present life, people will respect them and the spirits will protect them; their fortune and merit may thus increase.
One’s lifespan may be prolonged; even an ordinary person who has a slight understanding of Buddhist principles will surely be regarded by the world as a virtuous man—this is its efficacy.
Judging from this, who could say that following the words of the Buddha and taking the Pure Land as one's core concern is of no benefit during one's lifetime?
Someone might ask: "If one follows the words of Confucius and takes Confucianism as one's core concern, would it not likewise be so?"
"If it does not benefit one while alive, why is Pure Land necessary? [The Master] replied:

"This is merely a worldly dharma (*laukika-dharma*), not a world-transcending dharma (*lokottara-dharma*). Worldly dharmas do not transcend saṃsāra; world-transcending dharmas directly liberate one from outside of saṃsāra.
Since Pure Land benefits both while one is alive and after death, it is because it encompasses both the worldly and the world-transcending."
This is because it pertains to worldly dharmas.
The teaching of the Pure Land possesses both principle and manifestation. Regarding its principle, it is seen within the midst of daily activities and is never absent from them;
this is what was discussed in the preceding chapter. Regarding its manifestation, it is seen even in the brief interval of a single cup of tea during the three periods of the day.
It is not necessary to be mired in the practice of the "Ten Recitations" dharma-gate for the entirety of one's life; this is precisely what is meant.

For there are nine grades of dharma-gates for cultivation and practice, all of which can be cultivated by every person. Even those who are sinful and evil are not abandoned by the Buddha, because as soon as they turn their minds toward goodness, they become virtuous.
Even a butcher, upon laying down his cleaver, may also cultivate; therefore, it is for those who practice.
It is not difficult, nor does it interfere with any worldly affairs. Thus, for those in office, it does not hinder their duties;
for scholars, it does not hinder their studies; for merchants, it does not hinder their trade; for farmers, it does not hinder their cultivation;

for those in government service, it does not hinder their attendance upon superiors; and for monastics, it does not hinder their practice of Zen. Whatever one may do, none of these activities are mutually obstructive. Therefore—
It is said: "The practice of this cultivation requires only the brief duration of a single cup of tea during the three periods of the day;
yet it can serve as the foundation for non-destruction throughout ten million kalpas. The effort required is extremely slight, while the achievement is immense.
Why would anyone not cultivate this? To fail to cultivate it now—how lamentable! How lamentable!"
When people suddenly hear of the scenes of the Pure Land, it is not surprising that many do not believe it.
For they dwell in this turbid world of Sahā, knowing only growth from a womb and unaware of the transformational birth within lotus flowers;
knowing only a lifespan of no more than a hundred years, they are unaware of lifespans as vast as the sands of the Ganges; and they know that food and clothing must necessarily result from labor.
They do not know that those beings possess natural clothing and food, nor that their happiness is constantly interspersed with sorrow and affliction;
they do not know that those beings possess singular, pure happiness. Consequently, they equate what the Buddha has spoken to illusions and delusions, and do not believe it.
They fail to consider that the Buddha strictly forbids people from speaking falsehoods, and would certainly not himself speak falsely to deceive others; his words are [reliable].
There is no room for doubt regarding this faith. Thus, the sages of old said: "If one does not believe the words of the Buddha, what words can be believed?
Moreover, from antiquity to the present day, those who have practiced this have experienced many instances of spiritual response; therefore, it is truly unacceptable to disbelieve.
In this world, there are those who are devoted solely to *chán* (meditation) who say: "The Pure Land is but one's own mind; how could there be any further Pure Land? Amitābha is one's own nature;
there is no need to see another Amitābha. These words seem plausible but are actually erroneous. Why is this?

The Western Pure Land possesses both principle (*lǐ*) and phenomena (*jì*). If we discuss its principle, it is because one can purify the mind that all things become pure; thus, it is truly [the Pure Land].
It is the Pure Land of Mind-only. Yet, if one examines its traces, there truly exists the world of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī).

Since the Buddha spoke of it with such earnestness and detail, how could it be a false word? That every person can attain Buddhahood—that which is called the Amitābha of one's own nature—is certainly not false.
Nevertheless, one cannot suddenly reach this state; it is like fine timber that can be carved into the likeness of an object, yet—

It is exceedingly magnificent; it must be fashioned through the labor of carving before it can be completed. One cannot hastily point to fine timber and claim that it already constitutes the ultimate magnificence of all forms.

Furthermore, some may believe in the Pure Land while adhering rigidly to the doctrine of "mind-only," asserting that the present moment is itself the Western Paradise and thus deeming rebirth there unnecessary.
Others claim that by practicing Zen meditation and awakening their nature, they transcend [the need for such rebirth].
The Buddhas transcend the patriarchs; those who find even Amitābha insufficient are all lost. Why is this? These words are exceedingly lofty, and I fear they are not easily reached.
In that Western Pure Land, there is no greed and no attachment, no anger and no delusion. Can my own mind be free from greed, attachment, anger, and delusion?
In that Western Pure Land, one obtains clothing upon thinking of clothing, and obtains food upon thinking of food.
When one wishes to be still, one is still; when one wishes to depart, one departs. If one longs for clothing but has none, cold afflicts the mind.
If one longs for food but has none, hunger afflicts the mind. If one desires stillness but cannot attain it, the multitude of distractions afflicts the mind.
If one desires to depart but cannot do so, entanglements and fetters afflict the mind. This is what is called the "Pure Land of Mind-Only."
Truly, it is not easy to reach that state. That Amitābha Buddha possesses blessings as vast as mountains and seas, and his power encompasses heaven and earth;
he can transform the hells into lotus flowers as easily as turning over one's hand, and he beholds infinite worlds as if they were before his eyes.

Yet, even with my own merit and power, I am unable to achieve this for myself; I constantly fear that my past karma is so deep and heavy that I might fall into hell. How much more so, then, [in the case of others]?
It transforms into a lotus flower; yet one cannot even perceive what occurs on the other side of a wall, let alone behold the infinite worlds.
This is what is called "Amida of Self-Nature," which is truly not easy to reach.
Thus, while my mind can be the Pure Land, it cannot suddenly become the Pure Land; while my nature can be Amida, it cannot suddenly become [Amida].
For the sake of Amitābha, how could one neglect the Pure Land without cultivation, or abandon Amitābha without wishing to behold him?

Therefore, by cultivating the Western Paradise and beholding the Buddha, attaining the Way is exceedingly easy. If one remains only within this world, desiring to practice Chan to awaken the nature and transcend the Buddhas and Patriarchs is exceedingly difficult.
Moreover, for those who cultivate the Pure Land, there is no hindrance to practicing Chan. Why is this so?
Those who practice Chan meditation invariably disparage the Pure Land and fail to cultivate it. The *Great Amitābha Sūtra* states:

"In the ten directions, there are immeasurable bodhisattvas who are reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha. If even those bodhisattvas desire to be reborn there, what kind of person am I that I would not wish to be born there?
Would I truly be superior to all these bodhisattvas? To not rely upon the grace of Amitābha [is surely a grave error].
If, by the power of the Buddha’s compassion, one is reborn in that land, would that fruit not surpass that of Amitābha Buddha?

From this it follows that the doctrine of the "Mind-Only Pure Land" and the "Self-Nature Amitābha" is lofty but yields few practical results; those who have not reached the ultimate stage of cultivation have misled many people.
It is better to tread the ground with reality, maintaining the recitation and practicing the path; then every person will surely be born in the Pure Land and directly attain liberation.
The cycle of saṃsāra and those who speak empty words without substance are as far apart as heaven and earth.
Regarding the *Inquiry on the Pure Land*, it says: "Nowadays, when Chan practitioners see those who practice the Pure Land, they despise them as mere fools and commoners.
This is not a disparagement of fools and commoners; rather, it is a disparagement of Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Aśvaghoṣa, and Nāgārjuna. Why is this so?"
Therefore, the verse by Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva in the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* says: "May I, at the time of my life's end, eliminate all obstacles;

may I behold Amitābha Buddha face-to-face and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. The verse by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva in the "Universal Vow Chapter" (*Guanzhi Pin*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"May I, when I am about to reach the end of my life, completely remove all obstacles and behold him face-to-face."
By reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha, one immediately attains rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).

In the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa demonstrates the most supreme expedient means, stating that by single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha, one immediately attains rebirth and shall never again fall back.
In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the Buddha tells Mahāmati: "The bhikṣu of great name and virtue known as Nāgārjuna first attained the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) and was reborn [in that land]."
The Land of Peace and Bliss. Thus far, I have briefly cited four great bodhisattvas; the other bodhisattvas who cultivate the Pure Land are beyond counting.
How could inferior ordinary beings dare to neglect the Pure Land and fail to practice it?

The single method of Zen meditation is established for the purpose of awakening to birth and death; likewise, the single method of cultivating the Pure Land is also intended to lead sentient beings to awaken to birth and death.
If one attains realization through Zen meditation, one awakens to birth and death in this very life.

If one is born in the Pure Land, one first beholds Amitābha Buddha and subsequently awakens to birth and death; moreover, one may even realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
One dwells on the stage of non-retrogression until the attainment of Buddhahood, at which point it finally comes to an end.
Great spiritual friends have never failed to teach others by means of this. Why, then, do beginners who study the Way disparage the Pure Land and fail to cultivate it?
The *Lianzong baojian* states: "When people of even slightly sharp faculties look down upon the practice of nianfo, they claim it is merely the business of foolish men and women.
They see only those foolish men and women who recite the Buddha’s name with their mouths while their minds wander a thousand miles away;

they do not realize that such people are merely 'reading the Buddha' and are not truly practicing nianfo. True nianfo arises from the mind; it is the mind’s act of mindful recollection without forgetting."
It is called "mindfulness. Yet, when a person’s single mind does not contemplate what is correct, it contemplates what is perverse; when it does not contemplate principle, it contemplates desire.
Nowadays, people are constantly mindful of and recall the five desires, failing to realize their error, and instead regarding the mindfulness of the Buddha as wrong.
Is this not a most extreme form of delusion?
There are those who do not believe in cause and effect, and consequently do not believe in the Pure Land. Now, how can one fail to believe in cause and effect?
One must know that what was the cause in a previous life is what is experienced in this life; one must know that what is created in this life is the fruit in a future life.
If you do not believe these words, why not observe them through the events before your very eyes? This is why human beings...
There are the noble and the wealthy, the poor and the lowly; there is suffering and joy, toil and ease; there is honor and disgrace, longevity and early death.
Thus, their misfortunes and blessings differ in myriad ways. Although this is called "the mandate of Heaven," does Heaven indeed act with partiality toward individuals?

It is simply because the deeds performed by a person in a previous life were either good or evil that they receive retribution as fortune or misfortune in this present life. For this reason, this body is called the "retributive body" (*vipākakāya*). Retribution...

As for the body, it arises because of the retribution for what one did in a previous life. Since the actions performed in that previous life could not be purely wholesome, one cannot receive purely fortunate retribution in this life either.
There are those who possess wealth and status yet suffer from misery and an early death;

there are those who are poor and lowly yet enjoy longevity and happiness; there are those who are honored and prosperous yet meet with decline and disgrace. These follow one like a shadow follows a form.
It is like an echo responding to a sound; there is not even the slightest deviation. Thus it is said: "Planting peach trees, one obtains peaches; planting apricot trees, one obtains apricots.

The time spent planting is brief, while the time of harvest is vast. Therefore, the duration of performing good or evil deeds is extremely small, yet the retribution for receiving calamity or fortune is exceedingly great.
Therefore it is said: "In spring one sows a single grain of millet; in autumn one harvests ten thousand seeds. For human beings, the retribution for good and evil is just like this.
This is indeed the natural principle of the transformative power of the universe (*dharmatā*). If this principle can be trusted, then the teaching of the Pure Land must certainly be trusted.
Why? Because both are the words of the Buddha. Since the Buddha speaks truthfully regarding cause and effect, he would never speak falsely.
Therefore, for those who do not believe in cause and effect and consequently do not believe in the Pure Land, this may resolve their delusions.
Some might doubt, asking:
"If one recites the Buddha's name here in this world, how can a lotus flower immediately arise within the Western Seven-Jeweled Pond?"

[The Master] said: "This is not difficult to understand. It is like a large, bright mirror: whenever anything comes before it, its reflection immediately appears. How could the mirror ever harbor a conscious intention?
It is simply because of its brightness that this occurs spontaneously. The light from within the crown of Amitābha Buddha’s head is pure and perfect;
it spontaneously illuminates and perceives the worlds of the ten directions. Therefore, when one recites the Buddha's name here [in this world], [the response follows]."
In the western direction, a single lotus flower naturally arises within a pond of the seven treasures; of this there is no room for doubt.

Furthermore, those who harbor doubts regarding the practitioners of the mantra for rebirth [in the Pure Land] should know that Amitābha Buddha constantly dwells upon their crowns. As for the sentient beings of the infinite worlds, [the same applies].
If one recites this mantra, how could Amitābha Buddha possibly dwell upon each and every person's crown? It is said: "It is likewise spontaneous.
For example, it is as when there is but one moon in the sky, yet it appears universally in all waters; is this not spontaneous?"
During one's lifetime, one regards as one's own property everything from parents, wives, and children, to houses, fields, and gardens; cattle, sheep, carriages, and horses;
down to desks and stools, utensils, clothing, and even the most minute items such as belts and cords—regardless of size or kind, all are claimed as belonging to oneself.

The storehouses are already full, yet the mind remains unsatisfied; gold and pearls are already abundant, yet the pursuit does not cease. Every movement of the eyes and every step taken is nothing but attachment.
Having stayed abroad for but a single night, one already longs for home; when a single servant has not yet returned, one already worries over their loss.
Among the various affairs of life, there is nothing that does not weigh upon one's mind; yet when the great limit of one’s time arrives, all are cast aside.
Even this body of mine is but a discarded thing, let alone those things external to it. Reflecting on this with a quiet mind, it is as if one were in a dream. As an ancient said:
"Only when impermanence arrives in a single day does one know they were but people in a dream; of the myriad things, nothing can be taken away—only..."
"Karma follows one wherever one goes. How wonderful these words are! I have therefore used the latter two lines to compose this verse in continuation:
Of all things that can be taken away, Only karma follows one's person. Simply recite the name of Amitābha, And you will surely be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Generally speaking, "karma" refers to wholesome and unwholesome karma. Since these are all things that one must carry with one when departing [this life], how could one not take the Pure Land as one's karma?
Formerly, the Buddha asked Ānanda, "Do you wish to see those in the hells? Ānanda replied, "I wish to see them. The Buddha said:
"Those who commit evil through bodily action, speak evil through speech, and harbor evil thoughts in the mind—these are people of the hells.

This refers to the fact that the good and evil of human life do not exceed the three karmas of body, speech, and mind. If all three karmas are evil, this constitutes purely black karma, which is why one enters hell.
If all three karmas are good, this constitutes purely white karma, whereby one is born in heaven. Regarding these three karmas..."
There is one type of karma that is virtuous; it constitutes mixed karma and does not lead to rebirth in hell.

Therefore, even if one’s body and mind are evil, if one recites the Buddha’s name with the mouth, this single virtuous act of karma far surpasses the three types of karma being entirely evil. Moreover, when reciting the Buddha’s name with the mouth, if one can further visualize the Buddha’s form with the mind, then the mental karma is virtuous.
If one maintains a dignified posture with the body while holding a rosary in the hand, then the bodily karma is virtuous.
The karma is wholesome. One who is constantly able to perform these three types of wholesome karma and thereby cultivate the Pure Land will certainly be reborn in the highest grade. Some may say:
"If a person recites the names of the Buddhas continuously without ceasing, it is just like calling out to one person repeatedly;

that person will surely become angry. Therefore, those who exclusively recite the names of the Buddhas cannot be considered truly virtuous. This is not so. Since sentient beings have been without beginning...
The transgressions and evils of one’s verbal karma have accumulated like mountains and seas; one must recite the names of the Buddhas many times to wash them away.
Yet, even then, one fears it may not suffice—how could this possibly be compared to merely calling out the names of ordinary people?

Moreover, the Buddha himself opened this dharma-gate of recitation to guide and assist sentient beings, to purify their verbal karma, and thereby gradually to bring their bodies and minds to goodness. Up to this point...
As for the claim that reciting the Buddha’s name alone is insufficient to be considered virtuous, this is merely the talk of worldly fools;
it is not the teaching of the Buddhas to guide and assist sentient beings. How could it be worth even mentioning?
According to what the Buddha has said, the retribution for the karma of speech is greater than that of the two karmas of body and mind.

This is because an intention formed in the mind does not necessarily manifest outwardly, whereas once it issues from the mouth, its effects are immediately seen. Even when one commits evil with the entire body, there are still times of difficulty and obstruction;

this is not as easy as the manifestation of speech. For instance, if a person utters a single word to praise someone or to exhort them, the effect of those words remains with that person for their entire life.

Receiving such gifts brings blessings upon oneself and one's descendants; yet, a single word that traps another person or incites them to harm can cause that individual to suffer for a lifetime, with the consequences extending even to their descendants.
How grave, then, must be the karma of speech!
One should fully observe the fasts and precepts; furthermore, pay homage to the Buddha and recite his name, read and recite Mahāyāna sūtras, and understand the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Dedicate these merits with the vow to be reborn in the Western Land, where one will certainly attain the highest grade of the highest birth. What is meant by "fast" (*upavāsa*)?

It is not eating meat, not drinking alcohol, not engaging in sexual desire, and not eating the five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*). What is meant by "precepts" (*śīla*)? [It is] abstaining from killing, stealing, and so forth.

Stealing, sexual misconduct, and [killing]—these are called the three karmas of the body. False speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech—these are called the four karmas of the mouth.
Covetousness, malice, and wrong views—these are called the three karmas of the mind. Taken together, these constitute the ten precepts.
If one cultivates the Pure Land and fully observes these ten precepts, adding to them the merits described above, one will certainly attain birth in the highest grade of the highest level.
If one observes the five precepts and cultivates the Pure Land, they will not fail to attain rebirth in the lower-middle grade, or at least the upper-lower grade.
If one is further unable to observe the five precepts, how can one possibly neglect the precept against killing?
Killing is the foremost of the five precepts, the foremost of the ten precepts, and likewise the foremost among the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu.
First: Not killing is a great good; killing is a great evil. Therefore, one must certainly refrain from taking life.

Generally, if one kills living beings merely to provide for the mouth and stomach, how can the desire for food ever be satisfied? After the chopsticks are laid down, the flavor has already vanished, yet the karmic retribution of the act of killing remains intact.
If one kills to entertain guests, the guests—unlike those who have not [been so treated] during ordinary days—[will not truly appreciate it].
To kill [a living being] would likewise incur no blame; moreover, one must bear the consequences of that sin oneself. As the sutra says: "Coming, one comes alone; departing, one departs alone.
One wanders through saṃsāra alone, and alone one receives the retribution. Considering this, how could one kill for the sake of others?
If one were to kill to sacrifice to one's ancestors, why not use vegetarian offerings of pure delicacies? Confucius...
Even if one subsists on simple vegetables, vegetable soup, and melons, one must maintain a state of ritual purity (*zhāi*) during sacrifices. If this is so, what could be impossible?

If one likewise burns incense and recites sutras, relying upon the power of the Buddha to offer merit for the salvation of others, they will naturally attain rebirth in the higher realms; thus, it does not depend on killing living beings.
If one can simply observe this single precept of non-killing to cultivate the Pure Land, one will already not fall into the lower grades of rebirth.
It has been established.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that there are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat. The flesh of sentient beings is fundamentally not fit to be eaten;
yet, because one has become habituated through hearing with the ears and seeing with the eyes, one fails to recognize its impropriety. To be able to sever this habit is truly the highest course.

If one cannot yet renounce them entirely, one should at least reduce one's intake by eating only the three kinds of pure meat—namely, meat that one has not seen being killed, heard being killed, or known to have been killed specifically for oneself.
Just as when eating a meal with various flavors, one might omit one; or if both meals consist of meat, one might make one meal vegetarian.
Since the lifespan allotted to a person is finite, practicing in this way can naturally extend it; one should therefore do so.
If sentient beings recite [the name] as a means of offering for the deceased, it may serve to release grievances and extinguish transgressions.

According to the words of King Yama spoken to Zheng Lin, if one recites the Buddha’s name with utmost sincerity on their behalf, they will certainly attain transcendence and rebirth in the Pure Land. (The *Record of Avalokiteśvara’s Responsive Manifestations* states: "Zheng Lin, a military official in Ruzhou... )

He was mistakenly led to the Netherworld and subsequently released. King Yama informed him, saying: "When you return to the human realm, strive diligently to do good. Whenever you see someone killing a living being, simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;

they shall attain rebirth, and you too shall gain merit. From this it can be inferred that reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha is truly capable of delivering the deceased and increasing their blessings and longevity—not only ensuring their birth in the Western Paradise after death."

Regarding those of the lowest grade of rebirth: even when the manifestations of hell have already appeared at the moment of death, if one can recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha" with a sincere heart ten times, then hell will be transformed into a lotus flower, and one will likewise be born in the Pure Land.

This is truly because the compassion of our Buddha is profoundly deep and his majestic power is exceedingly great; thus he is able to act in this way. Now, as for what is called the "ten recitations," it is [the means of] birth...
One should personally recite the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times before death; it is not that one entrusts others to recite for them after the body has perished.

Because those who recite for themselves during their lifetime will be personally welcomed by the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas at the time of their passing, they will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land.

Someone may ask: "If one who has throughout their life slaughtered sentient beings and cruelly oppressed the people attains rebirth in the Pure Land simply by reciting the Buddha's name at the moment of death, when can the grievances and injustices harbored by those who were killed or tormented ever be resolved? The answer is as follows:
After being born in the Pure Land and attaining the Way, one subsequently delivers all enemies and kin;
is this not far superior to the cycle of mutual vengeance where neither side finds an end?
The *Lianzong baojian* states: "Evil people will certainly not turn their hearts to recite the Buddha's name; those who do so are hypocrites and their recitation is not genuine.
If one can truly recite the Buddha's name with single-mindedness, then even ten recitations at the moment of death will suffice."
They will certainly attain rebirth there; how much more so for virtuous people who recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion—how could they fail to be born in the Western Land?

Since we have already cultivated the Pure Land, our only concern is not reaching the state of "single-mindedness without distraction. If one attains single-mindedness without distraction, [rebirth is assured].
Let others revile you in a thousand ways and slander you in ten thousand ways; remain as majestic and immovable as Mount Tai. What further cause for doubt could there be?

The *Jingtu zhigui* (The Guide to the Pure Land) states: "Those who wish to resolve the matter of birth and death by practicing the pure karma must give rise to ten kinds of faith, maintaining them in mind without forgetfulness, so that they will certainly be born in the Pure Land.
First, have faith in the Dharma preached by the Buddha: these are the sincere words from his golden mouth, true and not false."
1. [One] believes that ordinary beings dwell in delusion and their consciousness-spirits (*vijñāna*) do not perish; they circulate through the six realms of existence without ceasing. 2.
[One] believes that those who practice in this land have not yet attained the fruits of the Path and thus cannot avoid saṃsāra. 3.

[One] believes that even if one is born in the heavens, as long as one has not escaped saṃsāra, one cannot avoid falling back down. 4. [One] believes that for those born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there is never again any retrogression. 5. [One] believes... (Sixth point).
1. Faith that sentient beings who make the vow to be born in the Pure Land will certainly attain rebirth there. 2.

Faith that one recitation of the Buddha’s name by a person at the seventh stage of faith can extinguish the heavy karmic offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas. 3. Faith that Amitābha Buddha, through his supernatural powers and radiant light, embraces and never abandons those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha.
4. Faith that for those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha, the Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges...

The Buddha likewise constantly protects and keeps them in mind through his supernatural power. Once the ten levels of faith have arisen, one’s lifespan in the Pure Land will be immeasurable, and in a single lifetime, one shall attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Yet, regarding these ten [levels], those who cannot believe with deep sincerity and give rise to doubt and confusion will not attain rebirth in the Pure Land despite reciting the Buddha’s name.
Furthermore, there is a common sentiment that reciting the Buddha’s name is a matter for the elderly; only then—

When one is young and strong, there is no leisure for such matters; yet when this single day of impermanence arrives, one’s hands are helpless and reach nothing. Alas! Do not wait until old age to recite the Buddha's name;
most solitary graves belong to those who died in their youth. Now, I shall again provide a skillful means for when one is in the prime of life. When you are young and strong...

One must immediately place one’s faith and orientation [toward this]. Every morning, after completing the ritual washing of the mouth, face west with a devout mind and apply oneself exclusively to the practice of the ten recitations.

Recite the Buddha’s name ten times with single-minded concentration, and then perform the dedication of merit, saying: "May I, at the time of my death, be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
If one maintains this until middle age and increases one's efforts with diligence, one will certainly attain rebirth there.
This book originates from Longshu and propagates the teachings to broaden them, thereby supplementing what was incomplete in the Dharma-treasury.
All you virtuous believers who obtain this book should earnestly embody its spirit.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs extend their great compassion to all fellow practitioners.

Let us exhort one another not to consign this to the high shelves or treat it with indifference, thereby burying the Dharma-treasure and showing irreverence toward the Sages; such a sin would be impossible to escape. Be on guard!
Be on guard! Should there be faithful adherents from afar who wish to propagate its transmission, they may contribute funds to re-carve it for circulation throughout the ten directions.
The merit is immeasurable; rebirth [in the Pure Land] is certain. Exert yourselves, exert yourselves!

The Fixed Form for the Pure Land (performed at the three times of morning, noon, and evening: burn incense, join the palms, prostrate toward the west, and gaze upward with both eyes, maintaining a solemn demeanor).
Beholding the compassionate countenance (first recite the name):
Homage to our original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.
(One prostration) Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. (One prostration)
Homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion (one prostration).
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta (one prostration).
Homage to all Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and all noble and virtuous persons (one prostration).
(After completing the prostrations, again join the palms and pay homage.
Visualize yourself within a lotus flower, facing upward toward the sixteen-foot golden body of Amitābha Buddha, who sits upon a great lotus and golden pedestal.
Between your two eyebrows, visualize an upward-pointing white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) with eight facets and a hollow center. Recite as follows:)
Namo Amitābha Buddha (ten recitations).

(Furthermore, visualize the sixteen-foot golden body of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva within a great lotus flower, with hands extended downward to welcome and guide; recite according to your mindfulness.)
Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (ten times).
(Furthermore, visualize the sixteen-foot golden body of Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva within a great lotus flower, as you recite.)
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta (ten times). (Furthermore, visualize that the assembly of bodhisattvas throughout the entire realm are all within the lotus flowers, as you recollect them.)
Homage to all Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and all noble and virtuous persons (ten recitations). (Then, prostrate once more and recite the verse for praising the Buddha,
repenting of offenses, dedicating merit, and making vows in honor of the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion once.)
The Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, Amitābha is foremost; Delivering sentient beings through the nine grades, their majestic virtue is infinite.
I now take great refuge and repent for the sins of the three karmas;
Whatever merits and virtues I possess, I sincerely dedicate them all, Vowing that I and all fellow practitioners of nianfo May together attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
Responsive manifestations appear according to the moment; at the time of death, the realm of the Western Paradise will clearly appear before one's eyes.

Through seeing and hearing, all shall practice with diligence and together be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Having seen the Buddha, they will bring an end to birth and death, and like the Buddha, deliver all beings.

(Having finished the recitation, the dedication is spoken: "I, disciple [Name], have reverently recited the sacred name, solely seeking that at the time of my death, I may rely upon the compassionate guidance of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. (One prostration. Then, perform the visualization accordingly.
One’s own body, within a lotus flower, proceeds directly to the Western Quarter, where one personally beholds my Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
After a long while, one further recites:
"Namo to the thirty-six trillion, one hundred and eleven thousand, nine thousand, five hundred [Buddhas] of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss."
One hundred times the name and title of Amitābha Buddha (seven recitations completed).
(The Dedication of Merit says: Disciple [Name], having reverently recited this sacred name, solely for the purpose of transcending the realm of suffering and attaining deliverance:
for those of this Jambudvīpa in this life and past lives—ancestors, parents, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, wives, daughters, kinsmen, maternal relatives, servants...
May all those from whom we have received service—servants, teachers, disciples, friends, benefactors, and enemies; those known and those unknown;
even those who have been killed or eaten, and all sentient beings used for silk or cotton—be reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss. (Recite this with each prostration.)
The Great Compassion Mantra (seven times). The Rebirth Mantra (seven times, completed).
The Dedication of Merit says: "May I, at the time of death in this present life, by the power of these two divine mantras, be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
Visualizing myself within a lotus flower, may I go directly to the West and behold [Amitābha] face-to-face."

The *Ten Doubts Treatise* (Shiyi lun) of Tiantai states: "Reciting the Buddha's name at the moment of death is called the 'final mind.

This mind is so fierce and sharp that reciting the Buddha's name even once brings one immediately to birth in the Pure Land. For at the time of impending death, the mind is so fierce, robust, and resolute that it surpasses the power of a hundred years of practice;
thus, it can move the Buddha to come and welcome the practitioner, resulting in immediate rebirth in that land."
Master Lianchi said: "The Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation makes no distinction between male and female, monastic and lay; it makes no distinction between noble and base, wise and foolish;

it makes no distinction between old and young, or the healthy and the infirm. Provided one’s mind is single-minded and undistracted, one will attain rebirth in the nine grades according to the magnitude of one's practice.
Thus, we know that there is not a single person in this world who is incapable of reciting the Buddha’s name. Allow me to speak further for the sake of the assembly."

If one is wealthy and noble, enjoying the fruits of present prosperity, this is precisely the time to practice nianfo. If one is poor, with few family burdens, this is precisely the time to practice nianfo.
If one has children, such that the ancestral sacrifices may be entrusted to them, this is precisely the time to practice nianfo. If one has no children...
To be solitary and free is precisely the time to practice nianfo. If one’s children are filial, and one receives their offerings with peace, this is precisely the time to practice nianfo.

If one’s children are rebellious, and one is spared from feelings of attachment, this is precisely the time to practice nianfo. If one is without illness, take advantage of this physical vigor to practice nianfo.
It is precisely the right time to practice nianfo when one is ill; it is precisely the right time to practice nianfo when death is imminent;

it is precisely the right time to practice nianfo when one is young and the spirit is strong and healthy; it is precisely the right time to practice nianfo when one is old and the remaining years are few.

If a person dwells in seclusion and their mind is free from disturbances, it is precisely the right time to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. If a person dwells in busyness, they should steal moments of leisure amidst that busyness;

it is precisely the right time to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. If a person has left the household life, wandering freely beyond worldly affairs, it is precisely the right time to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. If a person remains at home...

Knowing this to be a burning house, it is precisely the right time to practice nianfo. If a person is intelligent and thoroughly understands the Pure Land, it is precisely the right time to practice nianfo.
If a person is dull-witted and lacks other abilities, it is precisely the right time to practice nianfo. If a person upholds the Vinaya, know that the Vinaya was established by the Buddha.

It is precisely for this reason that one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha. If a person reads the sutras, the sutras are the words of the Buddha; it is precisely for this reason that one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha. If a person practices Chan meditation, Chan is the mind of the Buddha;

it is precisely for this reason that one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha. If a person attains enlightenment, that realization must be certified by the Buddha; it is precisely for this reason that one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

I universally exhort all people of the world: with utmost urgency, recite the Buddha’s name. Through this, one will attain rebirth in the nine grades of the Pure Land; when the lotus flower blooms, one shall behold the Buddha.
Having beheld the Buddha and heard the Dharma, one will ultimately achieve Buddhahood, and only then realize that one's own mind has been the Buddha from the very beginning.
Chan Master Zhenxie Le said: "The shortcut dharma-gate is none other than the recitation of the Buddha's name. Its merit is supreme and its progress easy.

If one seeks liberation without reciting the Buddha’s name, one will ultimately gain nothing. I universally exhort all who hold the pure precepts to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and pray for rebirth;
this is certain and will not fail."

Master Mingjiao said: "I exhort those who study the Way: if you cannot achieve sudden enlightenment, simply take up the single phrase 'Amitābha Buddha' and constantly recollect it, constantly keep it in mind, and constantly maintain awareness and illumination of it. Why is this? Because even if at this time you have not yet attained enlightenment,"
At the time of death, by relying on the power of that Buddha, one will certainly attain rebirth there. Once rebirth has been attained, why worry about not attaining awakening?
O virtuous ones, you should know that this single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha truly transcends all other gates.

The Patriarch Tianru said: "The world is exceptionally ignorant and deluded. When taught to recite the Buddha's name for rebirth in the Pure Land, they always excuse themselves as ordinary beings, wondering how they could dare hope for such a thing and insisting they must wait until future lives to practice again.
They do not realize that in the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation, with a single thought of faith, one can reach the destination in the snap of a finger.
Relying entirely upon the Buddha’s power of guidance, why wait for a future life? As the former masters have said: this...
"If this body is not delivered in this life, in what other life shall it be delivered? These words are truly worthy of repeated reflection three times.
Master Zongben’s *Discourse on the Ease and Difficulty of Chan and Pure Land* states: "People of the present age take up public cases (*gong'an*) to practice."
"One merely aspires to investigate Chan and realize the Way, but does not wish to be reborn in the Pure Land. How is this method? The answer was:

"Those of keen faculties and superior wisdom may directly investigate and truly awaken. Yet, even a slight error leads to a great mistake. Why is this? It is difficult to investigate Chan and realize the Way;
it is easy to recite the Buddha’s name and attain rebirth. As an ancient worthy said: 'In investigating Chan, one must reach a final resolution...'"
In the cycle of birth and death, there is not one in two or three who succeeds; yet in seeking rebirth in the Pure Land through mindfulness of the Buddha, there is not one in ten thousand who fails.

This is precisely what is meant by the saying: "With Chan but no Pure Land, nine out of ten go astray. Although there are indeed eighty-four thousand dharma gates, none are equal to a single recitation of "Amitābha Buddha."
**Encouraging the Cultivation of Pure Land Practice at Lion Peak: The Face of Suchness for Those Deluded by the World** (By Ru Ru Yan Bing;

"The Body is the Root of Suffering—Awaken Early and Practice") As for this very physical body, who would believe that the body is the root of suffering? Everyone greedily pursues worldly pleasures, unaware that such pleasure is the cause of suffering.
This floating life is easily passed; how could it be for long dwelling? This illusory form is not empty, yet it all returns to extinction and decay.

From the day before one entered the womb, how could there have been this male or female form? It is merely because of the temporary conjunction of earth, water, fire, and wind that it has come into being.
One cannot escape the suffering of being worn down by birth, old age, sickness, and death. Above, there is no thread upon which to hang; below, there are no roots from which one is born.
Floating like a bubble on the water, it will soon be dragged away; as precarious and fragile as dew upon a blade of grass, it vanishes in an instant.
Those who live long do not exceed sixty or seventy years before they all perish; those with short lives generally die at three or two.
Ten out of ten die young. Furthermore, there is the matter of not knowing tomorrow when today is still here.

Moreover, how many times do we get up from bed only to part from it once we have descended? When a single breath does not return, one realizes that it is a farewell for all eternity. (Xuefeng’s Verse: A single lamp illuminates the night chamber;

upon the bed, one takes off socks and shoes. The three souls and seven spirits depart in a dream; I know not whether they will return tomorrow. Alas, this body is nothing but a state of instability; alas, who can rely upon it?
It cannot be deceived by others: seven feet of sinews wind around bones; a skin wraps a lump of flesh. The nine orifices constantly discharge impurities;
the six sense-faculties indulge unrestrainedly in ignorance. Hair, body hair, nails, and teeth accumulate like heaps of dust;
mucus, tears, saliva, and secretions are as filthy as a public latrine. Inside, maggots swarm together; outside, mosquitoes and lice cluster in throngs. To touch it even once—
Calamities are manifold; diseases cause all to die. Great heat and great cold hasten one toward old age.

The eye is dragged by forms back to the realm of hungry ghosts; the ear follows sounds away into Avīci Hell. The mouth exhausts a thousand varieties of flavors, yet after death, it only adds a few drops of oil [to the funeral pyre].

(The poem by Chang Kui says: "Whether red or white, do not deceive one another. The Unconditioned True Person is a mass of bare flesh. Its decay is worse than that of a pig or dog; look upon it right now as a corpse.")
This body is not worth cherishing; all people should aspire to renunciation. How can those who are deluded and ignorant still display such affectation?
How can these bewildered ones still give rise to such perversions? Some pin flowers or grass upon their skulls;
others carry musk and incense at the side of their stinking skin-bags. Silk robes cover a sack of pus and blood; brocade garments conceal a mass of excrement.
The urine bucket. Having exhausted every cunning stratagem, one thinks oneself shall dwell in this world for ten thousand years; yet one knows not that the head will ache and the eyes grow dim.
When the King Yama comes to receive the person, how much more so when the hair is gray and the teeth decayed? The Ghost of Impermanence sends word to seek you out.
Each and every one of them is infatuated with sensual desire and greedy for wealth; these are all swift paths to losing one's human form. Day after day they drink wine and eat meat;
nothing but this plants the deep roots of hell. They seek momentary pleasure before their eyes, yet they shall suffer bitter hardship for ten thousand kalpas after death.

[From the *Pure Land Text*: "Skin encases flesh and blood, bones entwined with sinews; the deluded ordinary person recognizes this as his body. Only upon reaching death does he realize it is not himself; the gold and jade of his former life are left to others.

When the life-root is suddenly severed and the four elements are cut by the knives of the winds, externally the limbs are pulled and stretched, while internally the liver and intestines tear with agony.
Even if wife and children cherish one another, there is no way to detain you. Even if your kin fill the space before you, who can take your place?

(An ancient verse says: "The parents' kindness is deep, yet in the end there is parting; the couple's righteousness is weighty, yet they too must separate. Human sentiments are like birds roosting together in a forest; when the great limit arrives, each flies its own way. Those born must only endure bitter weeping and piercing pain;
those who die cannot avoid the wandering of their consciousness. Seeing no light ahead, they raise their eyes in total [darkness].
Without companions, they cross the bridge over the Nai River; there is no one who does not grieve upon seeing them. Upon entering the Pass of the Ghost Gate, all who arrive are utterly desolate.
On this world, barely seven days have passed, yet in the underworld, they are escorted before the Ten Kings. The officials of the various bureaus clutch their ledgers, devoid of human feeling;
the hell-wardens hold their spears, their faces never smiling. Those who practiced goodness throughout their lives are sent back to the Way of Heaven or the Way of the Immortals.
Regarding the human realm: those who committed evil while alive are driven into the realms of boiling water, flaming pits, and blades.

The cauldrons of boiling water seethe as if cliffs were collapsing; the sword-trees tower like mountains. When molten copper is poured over them, their flesh is completely scorched; when they swallow iron balls, smoke billows from their mouths.
When they encounter the crushing and grinding, their blood and flesh flow profusely; when they enter the cold ice, their skin freezes and cracks. Their bodies—
Shattered by the winds of karma, they are blown back to life; when their lives end, the rākṣasas cry out for them to be reborn.

Having exhausted a hundred springs and autumns in the human realm, it constitutes but a single day and night within the hells. (From the *Yanguang ji*: "The boiling cauldrons and glowing coals clamor in the dark ruins; the sword-trees and knife-mountains tower toward the Great Void.

Only after eighty thousand kalpas of suffering have ended do the ox-headed hell-wardens finally allow passage. Though the soul has returned to the realm of ghosts, the physical corpse still lies within the coffin, perhaps separated by three or five days.
In the morning—perhaps in the sixth or seventh month—the corpse rots and worms emerge, blood flows forth, and its stench permeates the earth and sky.
Its bloated state is unbearable to behold; its ugliness is truly terrifying. It is hurriedly consigned to a pyre of wild fire, or sent off to be buried in a desolate mountain ten thousand *li* away.
That which once required such quiet admiration for its crimson countenance has now been turned to ashes; today it lies desolate and white.

The bones transform into a mound of mud. (From a verse by Hanshan: "The rouge upon her face displays a thousand charms; the incense of dragon-camphor perfumes her robes in a hundred ways. Today, all traces of such elegance have vanished;
amidst the green willows and fragrant grasses, the skull lies cold. Former loves and attachments have here become empty. Where are the heroes of old now?
When the rain of tears falls, all is desolate and still; where the wind of sorrow blows, it is chilling and whistling. At the end of the night, ghosts wail and deities cry out as the years pass on.

Crows peck and sparrows scratch; beside the overgrown weeds, the stone monument remains scattered. Amidst the green willows, paper money hangs suspended. At the very end, one cannot avoid being like this.
Reaching this point, how can one not awaken? (Hanshan said: "Sparrows scratch and crows peck until skin and flesh are gone;

wind blows and sun scorches until the skull is dry. Ask those bystanders before your eyes: examine your own physical frame with care. Everyone, possess your eyes! Do not bury your heads further. Turn over and leap!
Depart from the ford of delusion. With a snap of the fingers, tear asunder the net of craving. Do not seek to make your livelihood within the ghost cave;
you must know that the True Person dwells upon the flesh-ball of the heart. Whether man or woman, all are capable of cultivation; whether wise or foolish, all have their share.

Simply request that you turn the light back to reflect within, and you will immediately know that the fundamental substance has always been non-existent. If you are unable to study the Way or practice Chan, for now—
Diligently observe the fasts and recite the Buddha’s name; abandon evil and return to good; reform the past and cultivate the future.

Transform the six thieves into the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and leave behind the eight sufferings to attain the eight masteries (*aṣṭavaśitā*). Then you may serve as a messenger of transformation for Heaven, and it will not hinder you from acting as a representative of the Buddha to receive and guide others.

Before the assembly, proclaim the teaching for the great multitude; upon returning home, explain it for your own family. Thus, cause everyone everywhere to simultaneously attain knowledge and awakening.
Teach others so that all may avoid sinking into the abyss; above, assist the Buddhas in turning the Wheel of Dharma; below, uproot sentient beings from the sea of suffering.
If one does not believe the words of the Buddha, what words can be trusted? If the Way of humanity is not cultivated, the Way of the transcendent is difficult to cultivate.
Do not let a single day pass before you shed your skin; even if there were a thousand Buddhas, they could hardly save you. Make haste to advance; time does not wait for man. Each of you—!

Please accept this directly and immediately; do not let this life pass in vain. (Hanshan said: "When the hundred members of the body disintegrate and depart from the dust and mud, that one thing which remains eternally enlightened—who is it?
If you cannot find the thread of the Way at this moment, how many will know when the skull hits the ground?")
The Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai exhorted practitioners to focus exclusively on the cultivation of the Pure Land, posing this question:

"If Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take great compassion as their primary vocation and wish to rescue and deliver sentient beings, they should simply vow to be born within the triple world, amidst the five turbidities and the three miserable realms, to save those suffering beings. Why, then, do they seek rebirth in the Pure Land?"
They settle themselves in ease and focus solely on their own benefit, thereby obstructing the path to Bodhi. The wise one replied: "There are two kinds of bodhisattvas.
The first are those who have long practiced the bodhisattva path and have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); they truly deserve this reproach.

The second are those who have not yet attained [this state] and have returned [to the world], as well as ordinary (*pṛthagjana*) bodhisattvas who have only recently resolved to attain enlightenment; these must never be separated from the Buddha until they attain patience."
Only when one has achieved power is one capable of dwelling within the three realms and rescuing suffering sentient beings in evil worlds.

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "It is impossible for an ordinary person bound by all fetters, despite possessing great compassion, to vow to be born in an evil world to rescue suffering sentient beings.
Why? Because in an evil world, afflictions are powerful; lacking the power of patience oneself, the mind follows along with external conditions."
Bound by sounds and forms, they fall of their own accord into the three miserable realms; how then could they save sentient beings?

Even if they maintain the precepts and cultivate merit, gaining birth among humans as kings, ministers, or those of wealth and power with complete autonomy, should they encounter virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), they refuse to trust or follow them.
Greed, delusion, and negligence lead them to commit a multitude of transgressions. Driven by this evil karma, they enter the three miserable realms once more, remaining there for immeasurable eons.
Kalpas. Emerging from the hells, one receives the body of a poor and lowly person; yet if one does not encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one falls back into hell.
Such is the cycle of rebirth that continues until this very day; every person is like this. This is called the "difficult path. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"One who cannot save themselves when ill can yet save those who are ill. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "For example..."
It is like two people, each having their own relatives, who are being swept away by water. One person, in a state of urgency, enters the water directly to rescue them;
however, because he lacks the power of skillful means, both he and his relatives sink. The other person possesses skillful means;

he goes to fetch a boat or raft, mounts it, and rescues them all, so that they are all freed from the peril of drowning. A bodhisattva who has newly resolved [to attain enlightenment] is also like this. Not yet...

One may attain the power of patience (*kṣānti*), yet still be unable to save sentient beings; for this reason, one must always remain close to the Buddha. Only after attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) can one truly save sentient beings.
It is like one who has obtained a boat: ordinary people lack the necessary power, and thus they must simply focus their mindfulness exclusively on Amitābha Buddha.
They shall achieve samādhi; at the time of death, by concentrating their mindfulness, they will attain certainty of rebirth and, without doubt, behold Amitābha Buddha.

Having realized the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), they will return to the triple world, riding the boat of non-arising patience to rescue suffering sentient beings and extensively perform the works of a Buddha.
Because they possess sovereign mastery and autonomy, the Treatise states: "Those practitioners who sport within the hells are born in that land;
having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they return to the realm of birth and death to teach and transform those in hell, rescuing sentient beings from suffering.
For this reason, one should seek birth in the Pure Land; this is called the Easy Path."
Chan Master Cijue Ze of Changlu in Zhenzhou exhorts those who practice Chan to concurrently cultivate the Pure Land:
"To take mindfulness as mindfulness and birth as birth is the error of common views;
to take non-mindfulness as non-mindfulness and non-birth as non-birth is the delusion of false views. To be mindful yet without mindfulness, to be born yet without birth..."
That which is "non-arising" is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, on the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a single speck of dust is received;
thus, above, there are no Buddhas to be mindful of, and below, there is no pure land to be reborn in. Yet, within the gateway of Buddha-activities (*buddhakārya*), not a single dharma is abandoned;
thus, all faculties are comprehensively gathered. This is indeed the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, the essential method for returning to the source, which reveals the opening of the past.

They are born through a single gate. Thus, a sutra says: "If a person hears the teaching of Amitābha Buddha and upholds his name, then at the time of that person's death, their mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha."
Generally speaking, those who first enter the Way possess impure powers of forbearance and must rely upon pure conditions as a superior support. Why is this?
In the Sahā world, Śākyamuni has already passed away and Maitreya has not yet been born; whereas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, Amitābha Buddha currently dwells and expounds the Dharma.
In the Sahā world, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are merely admired for their illustrious names, whereas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss...
Those two superior persons will personally serve as your most excellent friends. In the land of Sahā, various māras compete to create disturbances and vex practitioners;
however, within the great radiance of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there will certainly be no demonic affairs. In the land of Sahā, evil sounds are chaotic and distracting.
The seductive charms of women are [a source of affliction], whereas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the waterfowl and the forest trees all proclaim the sublime Dharma.
Their primary retribution is pure, and in truth, there are no women there. Thus, for the cultivation of practice, nothing compares to the Western Land in terms of the completeness of its conditions.

Yet, narrow-minded monastics have willfully given rise to doubt and slander. Allow me to discuss this: among the people of this land, there is none who does not weary of the clamor and bustle of the secular home and yearn for the [solitude of] the Aranya.
If one praises with earnest devotion the act of leaving home and becoming a renunciant because of its tranquility, yet fails to aspire to rebirth [in the Pure Land], that is the first delusion.
For what is the suffering of this Sahā world limited to the clamor of a secular household? And what is the leisurely ease of Sukhāvatī limited to the stillness of an araṇya?

To recognize the excellence of renunciation while remaining unwilling to seek rebirth therein is the first error. Furthermore, to labor diligently for ten thousand *li* to travel afar in search of a spiritual teacher [is the second].
This is because it elucidates the Great Matter and resolves the question of birth and death;

yet, while the vow-power of the World-Honored One Amitābha is vast and profound—such that a single utterance of his perfect voice brings all things into clear accord—there are those who wish to associate with spiritual friends but do not desire to see the Buddha: this is their second delusion.

Furthermore, while the vast assemblies of monasteries all delight in dwelling there, they do not wish to rely upon a small community’s place of practice, even though [the Pure Land of] Ultimate Bliss...
In this world, those who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha) are exceedingly numerous; yet these many superior and virtuous people gather in one place.
That one wishes to draw near to the monastic groves while not admiring the pure assembly of the ocean-like multitude—this is the third delusion.
The people of this land do not exceed a hundred years in maximum lifespan; yet childhood ignorance, senility, illness, and sleep occupy more than half of that time. As for the West—

People have immeasurable lifespans; by merely entrusting themselves to a lotus bud, they immediately attain the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), their status as Buddhas being certain and their liberation from the cycle of rebirth foreseeable.
Yet, in this world of Sahā, where life is brief, people fail to recognize the long-lasting years of the Pure Land. This is the fourth delusion.

If one’s rank has reached the stage of non-retrogression and the fruit has been realized as non-arising—being without desire while amidst desire, and not being defiled while dwelling in the dust of the world—only then can one give rise to unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*) and exercise coessential pity (*sahaja-karuṇā*), returning to enter the toils of the mundane world.

Yet there are those of shallow learning and solitary wisdom, or those who merely correspond with minor virtues, who claim to have forever emerged from the four currents and transcended the ten stages; they disparage the Pure Land and remain attached to [this world].
"Sahā" [world]. Not knowing that this is oneself, one asks, "Who could compare to such a Bodhisattva of Great Power? This is the fifth delusion.
