Now, if one believes the Buddha’s words and is born in the Pure Land, then one cannot be constrained by the bonds of accumulated karma, nor can one be harmed by the passage of kalpas.
One puts an end to the eight sufferings of the human realm and is free from the five signs of decay in the heavens; there is not even the name of the evil realms.
How much more so when there is actual reality? It reveals only the Dharma of the One Vehicle, definitively showing that there are no three.

This is truly the essential gateway to liberation and the swift path for cultivation; nothing surpasses this. Therefore, among the definitive Mahāyāna teachings, there are none that do not point toward the Pure Land as their ultimate goal.
Sages of the past and present, both self and others, all vow to be reborn there. For anyone who wishes to deliver others, they must first [attain rebirth themselves].

This is because they have been delivered. Alas! If a person lacks far-reaching foresight, they will inevitably face immediate distress. Once one loses this human body, there will be deep regret for ten thousand kalpas.
Therefore, if you lead the great assembly of the ocean-like multitude and each recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, then that journey of a hundred thousand leagues will be reached without toil.
Chan Master Yongming Youshou of Hangzhou cautioned those who have not attained realization against disparaging the Pure Land.

He posed a question: "If one merely sees one's nature and awakens to the Way, one transcends birth and death; why then is it necessary to fix the mind on that Buddha and seek rebirth in another realm?
He replied: "A true practitioner should examine themselves. It is like a person drinking water: whether it is cold or warm, they know for themselves."
"Virtuous ones, you should examine your own conduct and understanding, and whether you have seen your nature and awakened to the Way. Are you able to equal Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna?
Have you attained unimpeded eloquence and realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, as did Tiantai Zhiyi?

Are you able to master both the fundamental teachings and their expositions, and cultivate both practice and understanding, as did National Teacher Huizhong? These great beings all clearly transmitted their verbal instructions."
I earnestly exhort you to seek rebirth [in the Pure Land]. This is both for your own benefit and for the benefit of others; how could one be willing to mislead others and mislead oneself?
Furthermore, the *Wangsheng zhuan* (Biographies of Those Who Attained Rebirth) records numerous well-documented accounts of eminent practitioners from all eras.

You should diligently study these to reflect upon your own condition and realize that you must achieve self-deliverance. At the moment of death, will you certainly attain mastery over life and death, departure and remaining? Since beginningless time...
"Come! Since heavy obstacles of evil karma will certainly not manifest before you, will this body of retribution surely be liberated from saṃsāra?
While wandering among various species within the three miserable realms and evil paths, will you have the freedom to appear and disappear at will, surely free from suffering and affliction?

Throughout the heavens, the human world, and the worlds of the ten directions, will you be able to dwell wherever you please, surely without hindrance? If you can attain such clear and confident self-assurance,"

What goodness could be like this? If you have not yet attained it, do not let momentary arrogance cause you to sink into eternal kalpas of delusion, thereby losing the benefit of the good for yourself;
whom else will you blame? Alas, how tragic! What lamentation can avail now?
Preface by Master Lianchi, Exhorting Rebirth in the Pure Land:
When the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, he universally expounded the Buddha Vehicle for the sake of all sentient beings.

Subsequently, as it was difficult for all capacities to be fully accommodated within the Single Vehicle, he revealed the Three Vehicles. Furthermore, from within the Three Vehicles, he brought forth the single gate of the Pure Land. Now...
The sun of the Buddha has long since set. To advance [in practice], one cannot yet develop spiritual insight or transcend to the ranks of the sages;
to retreat, one is left wandering in the dark, facing the peril of falling into ruin. Yet, if one does not rely upon this gateway, from what other source can one swiftly escape birth and death?
How magnificent! It may truly be called the efficacious panacea that rouses the chronic ailments of the degenerate age. Looking back, its efficacy was abundant in antiquity; today, however—
The efficacy is meager. Wherein lies the fault? It is simply that while their mouths recite the Pure Land, their minds remain in Saṃsāra;
thus, their steadfastness, vigor, clarity, and awakening fall short of those of the predecessors. In the past, there were accounts of those who attained rebirth, but over time they have vanished.

From among these fragmented chapters and surviving traces, I have extracted those instances where cause and effect are clearly manifest and compiled them into this volume, so that both the ordained and the laity may gain certain knowledge.
I, [Name], have been born here because of such liberation; I have been born here because of such single-minded purity;
I have been born here because of such ultimate sincerity that moved the divine response; I have been born here because of such great compassion and great vows;
and I have been born here because, not begrudging my reform of faults, I transformed my karma just as I was on the verge of falling. I, [Name], am thus reborn.
Thus [the texts describe] rebirth in the upper realms; such-and-such [describes] rebirth in the middle and lower realms.

This may serve as a left-hand voucher for those practicing the Pure Land path, allowing them to examine the past and verify the present. A visitor who passed by me, having read no more than a few fascicles, suddenly exclaimed: "The Pure Land is but the mind!"
"There is no land outside the mind. This is a metaphorical expression for rebirth in the Pure Land. Do you truly believe that one is actually born there?
Would that not contradict the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*)? I waited until his expression settled, then spoke slowly to him: "How easy it is to talk!
If it were merely a matter of non-arising, then everything would simply cease to exist; it should not still be said that 'mind-only' remains. If one has truly realized non-arising, then—"
"One lives one's entire life yet never truly lives. Moreover, have you already exhausted the mind of outflows (*āsrava*)? He replied, "I am unable. Alas!
If the mind of outflows is not exhausted, then the conditions for birth will not cease. If the conditions for birth do not cease, then one will find a place to entrust one’s substance to existence.
Within the vast ocean of great suffering of the three realms, if one does not give birth in the Pure Land, in what land will one be born? One will merely crawl through the six paths of rebirth.
The distance between the nine grades of the *Xiāoyáo* [Pleasure Park] is almost as vast as that between heaven and the abyss. To adorn empty theories and vie for superiority—I do not do such a thing.
To turn toward the Pure Land and proceed upon the Buddha-vehicle, there has never been an interval of even a hair’s breadth; how, then, could there be any contradiction?
The guest was then left bewildered and lost, and urgently requested that the work be carved into printing blocks.

When Chancellor Zheng Qingzhi encouraged the cultivation of the Pure Land, scholars all said that cultivating the Pure Land was not as good as Chan, Teaching, or Vinaya. I alone maintain that among the dharma-gates of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, none are equal to the cultivation of the Pure Land.
Indeed, true purity, clarity, and wondrousness—empty, penetrating, and spiritually responsive—are possessed by all, whether wise or foolish.
Therefore, the Śākyas established expedient means through Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya to lead people to enter by various gates, so that all might attain transcendental awakening.
Only Amitāyus Buddha has opened a single gate, known as the cultivation of the Pure Land; it is like a singular prescription for curing disease—simple, direct, and straightforward.
Through single-minded devotion for even a single thought-moment, one reaches the other shore. Regardless of whether one is a monastic or a layperson, all may practice it.
[This is] practice. It is known merely as a shallow and mundane teaching for transforming the ignorant and the common folk; in reality, however, it is the swift path to attaining the Buddha-way.
Among those who study Buddhism today, there are generally no more than the schools of Chan, Teaching (Dharma), and Vinaya. As for the ultimate, sudden, and complete [teaching], none is equal to Chan.

Unless one possesses sharp faculties and is a superior vessel capable of spiritual reception and mental comprehension, one cannot avoid falling into the error of "stolid emptiness. Thus, one must investigate the Three Vehicles.

Nothing compares to the Teaching (Dharma). Those who have not yet attained the forgetting of the trap upon catching the fish, or the seeing of the moon through its pointing finger, cannot avoid the malady of poring over old paper.

Nothing compares to the Vinaya for protecting the good and warding off evil. Those whose body and mind are not pure and whose inner and outer selves are not as one, cannot avoid the suffering of self-entanglement.
As for those who attain precepts, concentration, and wisdom without relying on Chan, the Teaching, or the Vinaya, there is only the Pure Land.

This is the gateway. When reciting the Buddha’s name, one chants with the mouth and contemplates with the mind: "Commit not any evil. Is this not binding the precepts to the pure realm of mindfulness?
When illusory dusts are extinguished together, is this not concentration? When the mind-flower is serene and still, is this not wisdom?

If a person can cast aside myriad concerns and direct their single intent toward the Western Land, then they will realize the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden Teaching without the need for staffs or shouts. It is not...
By perusing the Great Tripitaka, one attains the Eye of the True Dharma; without maintaining the four modes of deportment, one attains great sovereignty.
Neither defiled nor pure, neither entangled nor liberated—at such a time, what are precept, concentration, and wisdom?
What are meditation, teaching, and discipline? My own mind and the Buddha-mind are entirely without distinction. This is the ultimate realization of the Pure Land path. (The Eight Meritorious Deeds)
The water of virtue; the golden lotus pedestal—how could one possibly doubt this?
Li Yanbi of Luling recorded his dream:
In the *jiasi* year of the Qiandao era, his family was stricken by an epidemic. On the fifth day of the fourth month, Yanbi himself also fell ill with porridge and medicine [as his only sustenance].

He did not recover. On the nineteenth day, early in the morning, he dreamed of a man in brown robes with a divine and emaciated countenance who stroked Yanbi’s limbs with his hand and called out for him to rise quickly.
Startled, Yanbi asked, "Who are you, sir? The man replied, "I am Longshu.
Yanbi then told him of his illness, saying that although he wished to endure it, he was unable to do so. He was about to—
"How can his illness be cured? The Duke said, "Do you remember that I previously taught you the shortcut?
Yanbi replied, 'Indeed; every day I have recited the name of Amitābha Buddha without ceasing. The Duke said, 'Rise and eat white congee.

As soon as he awoke, he sought out the congee and ate it. His illness was indeed cured accordingly. Later, when he saw the portrait of Longshu, [Yanbi] found him looking solemn and exactly as [in the likeness]."
I, Yanbi, have long heard that the Layman never tires of instructing others; wherever he goes, scholars flock to him like spokes to a hub.
Master Xie has prepared the Jingyi Hall for his reception. On the eleventh day of the first month, I sent my sons and nephews there to receive his teachings.
Before long, he returned and said: "Last night, after finishing my lecture on the scriptures, I recited the mantras and paid homage to the Buddha as usual until the third watch.
Suddenly, in a stern voice, I chanted the name of Amitābha Buddha several times and said, 'The Buddha comes to receive me. Having spoken, I passed away while standing upright.
That evening, the people of the district had a dream in which two youths in blue robes led the Master westward; this was transmitted as a most extraordinary marvel. Thus it was with the Layman.
Three days before his passing into parinirvāṇa, he exhorted everyone extensively to persevere in their spiritual practice, saying that after this they would no longer see him again.
Were it not for one whose power and cultivation were profound enough to have mastered the cycle of birth and death, such a state would be difficult to attain.
When Yanbi was on the verge of death from illness, he was secretly sustained and rescued by the Layman; thus he was able to recover completely. This may indeed be called mastery over birth and death.
This is indeed a matter of bone and flesh. Some may say that dreams are formed through conceptualization; however, how can the efficacy of consuming white congee be denied?

I have therefore carefully carved this portrait of the Master and recorded these accounts of his spiritual responses, so as to broaden their dissemination. It is not my intention to employ flowery language to deceive the eyes and ears.

I humbly hope that all who see or hear of this will respond with reverent faith and together receive its benefits. The Master’s surname was Wang, his given name was Rixiu, and his courtesy name was Xu...
[End of] Middle [Volume]. Titled "The Lay Practitioner of Longshu. Recorded respectfully by Li Yanbi of Luling on the final day of the last month of the year.
*Complete Collection of Pure Land Texts*, Volume Upper;
*Complete Collection of Pure Land Texts*, Volume Lower.
Regarding the realization of the fruit of the Pure Land, Wang Longshu stated: "The Dharma Master Huiyuan of the Eastern Jin initiated the practice of cultivating the Pure Land.
Subsequently, Minister Wang Minzhong and the layman Lu of Qiantang extensively collected accounts of spiritual responses, totaling two hundred cases."
The remaining traditions have all been carved into printing blocks and circulated; I cannot record them all here now.

I shall select those concerning practitioners who observe the precepts and fasts, those of middling capacity, those who practice while burdened by evil deeds, and those who practice amidst illness and suffering.
I have further appended accounts from what I have recently heard and witnessed. Among these, each contains marvelous signs and extraordinary responses.
These are recorded here in order to inspire the faith of others. As for the śramaṇas who attained rebirth in the Pure Land,
they are categorized under the lineage of the ancestral master Huiyuan.
Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty was a native of Loufan in Yanmen. He had extensively mastered the Six Classics and was particularly adept at the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*.

Upon hearing Master Dao’an lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he attained a sudden and profound enlightenment. Consequently, he shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk to serve him. In the sixth year of the Taiyuan era, he traveled to Xunyang.
Seeing that Mount Lu was secluded and spacious, a place where one could set the mind at rest, he was moved by a mountain deity who appeared in a dream.
One night, amidst thunder and rain, timber arrived of its own accord. The Regional Inspector Huan Yi then constructed a hall for him, naming it "Divinely Transported" (Shenyun).

Because Huiyong had previously resided at Xilin, this site was called Donglin (Eastern Grove). Huiyuan lived at Donglin for thirty years; his footsteps never entered the secular world as he fulfilled his resolve.

In the west, he formed a Pure Society with one hundred and forty eminent monks and great scholars. For six periods of time each day, as measured by the lotus-water clock, they engaged in ritual recitation without ceasing.
Huiyuan concentrated his mind on contemplation; for eleven years, he beheld sacred manifestations three times, yet he remained profound and silent, saying nothing.
Nineteen years later, on the evening of the last day of the seventh month, as he was just arising from meditative concentration, he beheld Amitābha Buddha, his body filling the void of space.
Within the halo of light were immeasurable transformation Buddhas, with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta standing in attendance at his left and right.

He further saw flowing water and radiant light divided into fourteen branches; in each branch of water, the currents circled and surged upward and downward, proclaiming the wondrous Dharma. The Buddha...
He told Yuan: "By the power of my original vow, I have come to comfort you; seven days hence, you shall be born in my land.
He also saw Buddhabhadra, Huidi, Huiyong, Tanshun, Liu Yimin, and others standing by the Buddha’s side.
Huiyuan bowed toward him and said, "The Master’s resolve preceded mine; why have you arrived so late?
Huiyuan saw it clearly with his own eyes and spoke of it to his disciples, saying, "I have lived here for eleven years and was fortunate enough to behold the sacred image three times;
now I behold it once more. It is certain that I shall be reborn in the Pure Land. The following day he fell ill, and on the seventh day, he sat upright in meditation.
He entered nirvana at the age of eighty-two on the sixth day of the eighth month in the twelfth year of the Yixi era.
Huiyong (Jin) was a native of Henei; he left home to become a monk at the age of twelve and subsequently followed Master Dao’an together with Master Huiyuan.
At the beginning of the Taiyuan era, he took up residence at Mount Lu. The Regional Inspector, Tao Fan, donated his own residence to become Xilin Monastery for him to dwell in.

He severed all ties with worldly clamor and set his mind upon the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Later, in the tenth year of the Yixi era, he manifested illness. Suddenly, he adjusted his robes, asked for his sandals, and attempted to rise. The assembly was startled and questioned him;
he replied, "The Buddha has come to welcome me. Having finished speaking, he passed away. A wondrous fragrance lingered for seven days before finally fading.
Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Master Jueji.
Tanshun was a native of Huanglong during the Jin dynasty. In his youth, he followed Dharma Master Kumārajīva to lecture on and explain various sutras. Kumārajīva marveled, saying: "This..."

Ziqi was a man of extraordinary capacity. Later, he entered Mount Lu to cultivate the practice of Pure Land. At that time, Liu Zunxiao, the General-in-Chief for Pacifying the Barbarians, founded a monastery in Jiangling and invited Huiyun to initiate its construction.

Huiyun extensively propagated the *Nianfo Sanmei* (Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection). In the second year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he passed away while seated in meditation before the assembly, and a wondrous fragrance filled the chamber.

Sengrui (Sengrui of the Jin Dynasty) was a native of Jizhou. Having traveled for study to various regions and journeyed as far as India, he returned to Guanzhong, where he received the teachings on the meaning of the sutras from Dharma Master Kumārajīva.
Later, he joined the Lotus Society at Mount Lu. In the sixteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he suddenly announced [his passing].
The assembly said, "We shall depart. Facing west with palms joined, he passed away.
The assembly saw a golden lotus flower suddenly vanish before Master Rui’s bed, and five-colored fragrant smoke issued forth from his room.
Daobing of the Jin dynasty was a native of Yingchuan. In his youth, he studied under Master Huiyuan; he was well-versed in the sutras and the Vinaya, and his words accorded with his conduct.

He devoted himself to the *nienfo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi), investigating it with uninterrupted focus. In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, Wang Qian, the Governor of Yuzhang, entered the mountains to pay him a visit and show his respect.

He invited Master Shaoyuan to take his seat; the assembly all revered him with deep devotion. In the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, he gathered the multitude for the practice of Buddha-recollection (*nianfo*), and while seated, he passed away.
Daojing.
Jing Daojing was a native of Langya. His grandfather, Ningzhi, served as the Governor of Jiangzhou, and because of this, Daojing followed Master Huiyuan into the monastic order.

At the age of seventeen, he had extensively mastered the sutras and treatises, memorizing ten thousand words a day. He was devoted to the practice of *nianfo* (recitation of the Buddha’s name), never ceasing from dawn until night.

In the first year of the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, he said to the assembly, "My former teacher has summoned me; it is time for me to depart. Sitting upright, he chanted the Buddha’s name and passed away. The assembly...
He saw a radiance fill the room, which did not dissipate for a long time.
Buddhavarman—Buddhavarman in the Jin language; this means "Awakened Virtue"—was a native of Kapilavastu, [the son] of King Amṛtodana.
Huikai was sixteen years old when he had extensively studied the various scriptures and attained a profound mastery of Chan and the Vinaya.

When the Yao Qin śramaṇa Zhìyán traveled to the Western Regions, he invited the Master to Chang’an to propagate the Dharma at the Eastern Palace. There, he engaged in dialectical debate with the Dharma Master Kumārajīva.
Later, he entered Mount Lu and joined Master Huiyuan’s Lotus Society. He translated various sutras on the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*.
In the sixth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he passed away while recollecting the Buddha.
Sengji was a monk of the Jin dynasty. He entered Mount Lu to study under Master Huiyuan. Huiyuan sighed in admiration and said, "The task of propagating and upholding the Great Dharma rests upon you.

Later, when Sengji’s illness became critical and he sincerely aspired to the Pure Land, Huiyuan left him a single candle, saying, "You may direct your mind toward An-yang (the Land of Peaceful Nurturing)."
Tanyi held a candle and leaned against a small table, his contemplation steady and undisturbed. He also gathered the assembly to recite the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

At the fifth watch, Tanyi handed his candle to his disciple Yuanbi, instructing him to join the assembly in circumambulation. After a short while, he felt as though he were holding a candle himself and was traveling through the air.
He saw Amitābha Buddha receive him, placing him upon the palm of his hand, and traveled thus throughout the ten directions. Suddenly, he awoke from this experience. Furthermore—

Filled with both sorrow and consolation, he examined his own four elements and found himself entirely free from illness or suffering. On the following evening, he suddenly rose and stood up, gazing into the void as if seeing something there;
after a short while, he lay back down, his countenance serene and joyful. Addressing those around him, he said, "I am departing," and passed away lying on his right side.
At that time, though it was the height of summer, three days later his body remained unchanged, and a wondrous fragrance wafted forth.
Hui-gong of the Jin dynasty was a native of Fengcheng in Yuzhang. He studied together with Hui-lan, Seng-guang, and others.

Lian and Guang focused their mindfulness on the Pure Land, and at the time of their deaths, both experienced miraculous responses. Five years later, Gong fell gravely ill; shedding tears like rain, he prostrated himself and made a solemn vow.
He dwelt in peace, his mindfulness uninterrupted for even a moment. He beheld Amitābha Buddha, who came to welcome him with a golden platform.
Respectfully mounting it, he also saw Lan and others amidst the radiance upon the platform, who addressed him, saying: "Elder, you have been reborn and already abide in the highest grade."
We are filled with unsurpassed joy and consolation. Our only regret is that we were late in relying upon you, as the five turbidities have persisted for so long.
[He] respectfully and joyfully exerted himself and passed away. Huìqián.
Huiqian of the Jin dynasty entered the monastic life in his youth. His observance of the precepts was precise and rigorous.
During the Yixi era, he joined the Jiaxiang Temple in Shanyin, where he disciplined himself and led the assembly. Later, he fell ill;

with his thoughts fixed upon the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī) and his sincerity directed toward Avalokiteśvara, a nun named Jingyan—who was of long-standing virtue and steadfast practice—dreamed one night that Avalokiteśvara entered through the western city gate, his pure radiance and wondrous form emitting brilliant light.

It reflected the sun and moon; its banners, streamers, and flower-canopies were adorned with the seven treasures. The nuns were struck with wonder and prostrated themselves, asking, "Where is the Great Being going?
He replied, "I am going to Jiaxiang to welcome Master Qian. Although Qian’s illness was severe, his countenance remained as usual.
His attendants all smelled a wondrous fragrance as he passed away in serene stillness.

Zhi Xian (452–522) was a Dharma Master of the Jin dynasty, styled Zhenjiao. He resided at Bailian Temple for thirteen years, reciting the name of Amitābha ten times while facing westward, never ceasing for even a moment throughout the twelve periods of the day.
One night, he fell slightly ill and instructed the attendants of the meditation hall to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Before it had finished...
He sat upright and passed away peacefully.
Huitong of Jin:
Huitong followed Chan Master Huishao of Liangzhou to inquire about and receive the methods of dhyāna. He prayed for rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing. When he was slightly ill, he...
While in meditative concentration, he saw a person of most upright and majestic appearance who said to Tōng, "The auspicious time has arrived.
Shortly thereafter, he beheld Amitābha Buddha, his radiance blazing brilliantly. Upon emerging from concentration, he informed his fellow students; he then passed away in tranquility.
A wondrous fragrance lingered for three days before it finally ceased.
Falin (Jin dynasty), whose secular surname was Lin, was a native of Linqiong. He specialized in the precepts and resided at Lingjian Temple in Chengdu, where he cultivated the practice of purity.
He constantly maintained the two sutras of Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara; whenever he recited them, he would invariably see a majestic-looking śramaṇa standing firm before him.
Previously, in the second year of the Jianwu era, he fell ill. He focused his mindfulness on the Western Realm and performed rites of repentance without ceasing.
Seeing that various worthies and sages had all assembled, he joined his palms and passed away.
Tanjian (Song dynasty): Throughout his life, Tanjian dedicated every fragment of merit toward the Western Pure Land, vowing to behold the Buddha.

One day, while in meditative concentration, he saw Amitābha Buddha, who sprinkled water upon his face and said, "I wash away the dust and grime from you; I bathe your mental intentions and your body."

His mouth was entirely adorned and purified. Furthermore, from within the flask, he produced a single lotus flower and bestowed it upon him. When his meditative absorption ended, he took leave of the monks of the monastery.
As the night grew deep, he walked alone beneath the corridors reciting the Buddha’s name. By the fifth watch, his voice became even more resonant and intense.
When it grew light, the disciples questioned him as was their custom; he sat cross-legged without moving. Upon approaching to look at him, they found he had passed away.
Sengrouqi, whose secular name was Sengrou, studied the various Mahāyāna sūtras and cherished the practice of pure karma alone. On the day of his death, he beheld a transformation Buddha.
There were thousands [of followers]. Inside and outside the room, everyone smelled a wondrous fragrance. He passed away while performing prostrations toward the west.

Huiguang (also known as Qihuiguang) resided in Luoyang. He authored commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Daśabhūmika* sūtras, exhaustively elucidating the provisional and the ultimate teachings.
The Master’s intent was thus. One day, he fell ill and saw a host of celestial beings coming to welcome him. Zhi Guang said, "My vow is only to return to An-yang (Sukhāvatī).
Shortly thereafter, transformation Buddhas of the Pure Land filled the void. Guang said, "I pray only that our Buddha will receive me and fulfill my original vow.
He then snapped his fingers and cleared his throat; with these words, his speech and breath ceased together.
Huijin of the Southern Qi dynasty was a monk from Yangdu. Over forty years of age, he resided at Gaozuo Temple and vowed to recite the *Lotus Sūtra*.

As soon as he took up the scroll, he fell ill; thereupon, he made a vow to produce one hundred copies of the scripture to repent for his karmic obstructions. Once he had raised the funds and completed the task, his illness likewise subsided.

He recovered. He wished to dedicate the merit from the production of this scripture toward rebirth in the Pure Land. Suddenly, a voice from the air said: "Your task is already accomplished; your vow has also been fulfilled.
As for being born in the Pure Land, who else could it be but you? Jingjin replied:
"I do not dare hope for the highest grade, but even at the very lowest of the lower grades, there shall be no falling back. In the third year of the Qiming era, he was eighty years old.
He passed away without illness.
Dharma Master Daozhen of the Liang dynasty lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. During the Tianjian era, he stayed his staff at Mount Lu, admiring Master Huiyuan’s purity.
While practicing seated meditation, he suddenly saw several hundred people on the sea traveling forward in a precious vessel. The Master asked where they were going;

they replied, "We are going to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. He then requested to be allowed to join them, but they informed him, "Although you, Dharma Master, are skilled at lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,"

However, as he had not yet recited the *Amitābha Sūtra*, how could he go together with them? The Master thereupon suspended his lectures and devoted himself to mindfulness of the Buddha and the recitation of the *Amitābha Sūtra* without ceasing for many years.
On the night before the fourth seven-day period (the twenty-eighth day) prior to his death, at the fourth watch, he saw a silver platform from the West arrive.
In the air, it was as bright as the midday sun. A voice proclaimed, "The Dharma Master shall ascend this platform at the time of his rebirth.
At that moment, the assembly all heard celestial music, and a wondrous fragrance did not dissipate for several days.

Shenluan (later known as Tanluan) was a man of the Later Wei dynasty. In his youth, he traveled to Mount Wutai, where he was moved by its spiritual wonders and left the household life. By nature, he was fond of the pursuit of longevity;
he received the ten fascicles of the *Xianjing* (Scripture of the Immortals) from Tao Hongjing. Later, meeting Bodhiruci, he asked him: "Does the Buddha possess the art of longevity?"
"Is this the art of dying? Zhi laughed and said, "Longevity and immortality—this is my Buddha-way.

He then bestowed upon him the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations*, saying, "If you study this, there shall be no further birth within the three realms and no further wandering through the six paths.

As for its longevity, even the sands of the Ganges or kalpa-stones cannot compare to it. This is the longevity of our Golden Immortal. Sengluan was greatly delighted and subsequently burned [the sutra].
He followed the *xianjing* (immortal scriptures) while cultivating pure karma; through cold, heat, illness, and pain, he never slackened for even a moment. The Wei ruler titled him "Divine Luan.
One night, in his chamber, he saw a Brahman monk who said to him, "I am Nāgārjuna. I have long resided in the Pure Land, and because you share my same aspiration, I have come to meet you.
Luan knew that his time had arrived, so he gathered the assembly and instructed them, saying: "The toil of life is but a weary cycle..."
There was no day he did not stop. He could not fail to fear the various sufferings of hell; he could not fail to cultivate the pure karma of the nine grades.
Consequently, he had his disciples recite the Buddha’s name aloud as he faced westward and prostrated himself until his death.
The assembly heard celestial music coming from the west, which ceased only after a long while.
The Great Master Zhizhe was Zhiyi of the Sui dynasty; he was titled the Great Master Zhizhe. His surname was Chen, and he was a native of Yingchuan. He had double pupils in his eyes.

As a child, upon seeing a Buddha, he would immediately prostrate; whenever he encountered a monk, he would invariably bow. At the age of eighteen, he left the household life at Guoyuan Temple and recited the Lotus Sūtra.

He was also thoroughly versed in the Vinaya-piṭaka. He went to Mount Dasu and paid his respects to Meditation Master Huisi. Upon seeing him, the Master said, "In days past at Vulture Peak, we heard the Lotus Sūtra together;
you have come here once again. Thereupon, he bestowed upon him the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra. After twenty-one days, his body and mind became suddenly clear and expansive.
Later, he entered Tiantai, where he subdued demons and advanced in his practice. When his period of seeking sustenance through teaching had ended, at Xinchang Da...

Before the stone statue, he manifested illness and announced his passing. When his disciples asked about the direction of his rebirth, he said, "My teachers, friends, and attendants, including Avalokiteśvara, have all come to welcome me.
As he approached death, he expounded various Dharma gates and instructed them to chant the name of Amitāyus Buddha.
He then looked toward the assembly, joined his palms, and praised: "The forty-eight vows adorn the Pure Land; its lotus ponds and jeweled trees are easy to access."
When he went there, he saw no people, but the chariots of fire appeared. Yet, by repenting for even a single thought, he was still able to attain rebirth there;

how much more so for one who has cultivated the power of the noble path through the熏習 (*vāsanā*) of precepts and meditative concentration—such merit shall not be in vain. Having finished speaking, he recited the names of the Triple Gem and entered as if into *samādhi*.
Fahxi of the Sui dynasty constantly practiced the Fangdeng (Vaipulya) repentance rites. Suddenly, a pheasant came to claim its life.

A divine being rebuked it, saying, "This Dharma Master is destined for rebirth in the Pure Land; how could he repay your life? Later, while ill, Fahxi made a vow to dedicate his entire life to [the practice].

Yezhi directed his merit toward the Western Paradise and, with a sincere heart, practiced the mindfulness of the Buddha. He immediately saw the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas coming to welcome him, and he passed away while sitting upright.
Daoyu of the Sui dynasty resided at Kaijue Temple; he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha day and night without ceasing, having fashioned [a statue] barely three...

Later, while in meditative concentration, he saw the Buddha, who said to him, "Why have you made my image so small? Daoyu replied, "If the mind is great, it is great; if the mind is small, it is small.
As soon as he had spoken, the form of the image was seen filling the entirety of space. The Buddha told him, "You should bathe yourself until pure;
when the morning star appears, I will come to welcome you. When the time arrived, he indeed saw the Buddha coming, his radiance filling the room.
He then sat and passed away. Zhi Shun (of the Sui dynasty):

Zhi Shun entered Mount Lu and followed Master Huiyuan’s practice of pure karma. At the beginning of the Daye era, immediately after completing his lecture on the *Amitābha Sūtra*, he manifested [his passing].

He fell ill. Seeing that the parrots and peacocks were mindful of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and were uttering sublime sounds, he told his disciples, "I shall attain rebirth in the Pure Land today," and passed away peacefully.
Huihai of the Sui dynasty resided at Anle Monastery in Jiangdu. He was well-versed in the sutras and śāstras and practiced the mindfulness of the Buddha with profound sincerity.
A monk named Daoquan arrived from Qizhou, carrying an image of Amitābha Buddha that was so exquisitely crafted it was unprecedented in the world. [Daoquan] asked:

Regarding this, it is said: A Bodhisattva possessing the five supernatural powers from the Kukkutapāda Monastery in India traveled through the air to that Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) and brought back a painted image.
When Hai encountered it, he was filled with joy and reverence; as he paid his respects with utmost devotion, he beheld a divine light shining brilliantly.

Thereupon, he painstakingly copied the image, vowing to be reborn in that land. Later, while suffering from a slight illness, he suddenly rose in the night and, facing the image as usual, [passed away].
Facing west, he completed his prostrations and sat in the full lotus posture. At dawn, he passed away, remaining as upright as if alive.

As for the two śrāmaṇeras from Wenzhou in the Sui dynasty: these two śrāmaṇeras shared a common aspiration to practice *nienfo*. When the elder suddenly died and reached the Pure Land, he saw the Buddha and said:

He asked, "Is it possible for my fellow practitioner, the young novice śrāmaṇera, to be reborn here as well? The Buddha said, "It was because he exhorted you that you first resolved to seek enlightenment.
You may now return home and apply yourself even more diligently to pure deeds. Three years from now, he shall come here with you.
When the time arrived, both men saw the Buddha coming; the great earth shook, celestial flowers fell like rain, and they were both transformed together at once.
Master Shandao (fl.
Tang Dynasty): During the Zhenguan era, Master Shandao saw the Nine Grades of the Pure Land Practice Hall established by Chan Master Chao of Xihe.
He exclaimed with joy, "This is truly the essential ford for entering the Buddha-way. Cultivating other practices is circuitous and difficult to accomplish; only this Dharma gate is swift."
To transcend birth and death, he applied himself with earnest diligence and ascetic rigor, as if his head were on fire.

Whenever he entered the Buddha hall, he joined his palms and knelt in the *hu* posture, single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha without ceasing even when his strength was exhausted. Even amidst freezing cold, he would cause himself to perspire to manifest his utmost sincerity.
Upon emerging from meditation, he would preach on the Pure Land for the assembly. For over thirty years, he did not sleep even for a moment.
He upheld the precepts, never violating them by even a hair’s breadth. When his food and clothing were in surplus, he dedicated them all as offerings;

he sent fine food to the kitchen to provide for the community, while consuming coarse and simple fare himself. All the alms and donations he received were used to transcribe more than one hundred thousand scrolls of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
He painted more than three hundred wall murals depicting the transformation scenes of the Pure Land. Upon seeing ruined temples and pagodas, he repaired and restored them all;

he lit lamps to maintain continuous illumination, doing so every year without fail. He never had others carry or wash his three robes or alms bowl, nor did he ever travel in the same company as the monastic community.
Fearing that discussing worldly affairs would hinder their practice of the path, they passed [the teachings] down to one another.

There were those who recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* one hundred thousand to five hundred thousand times; there were those who made it their daily task to chant the Buddha’s name ten thousand to one hundred thousand times.

Those who attained the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation and were reborn in the Pure Land are beyond counting. Someone once asked Zhidu: "Can one be reborn in the Pure Land through the practice of Buddha-recitation?"
He replied, "It shall be as you have thought; I grant your wish. Thereupon, Dao recited the name of Amitābha Buddha once, and a beam of light issued from his mouth;
when he recited it ten times, and eventually a hundred times, the light appeared in the same manner.
His verse of exhortation says: "Gradually the skin becomes like that of a chicken, the hair turns white like a crane; look at the gait, how one totters along. If..."
Even if one possesses gold and jade filling the halls, one cannot avoid decay, old age, and illness. No matter how many kinds of happiness you may enjoy, impermanence will inevitably arrive.
There is only the path of cultivation; simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Later, he said to others, "This body is loathsome; I shall return to the West.
He then climbed a willow tree in front of the temple and threw himself down, passing away. Emperor Gaozong...
The Emperor learned of these matters and bestowed the temple’s plaque with the name "Guangming" (Radiant Light).

Zhiqin—of the Tang dynasty, Zhiqin—devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Chan meditation and also performed the ritual of reciting the names of fifteen thousand Buddhas up to one hundred times. Later...
Before the Aśoka Stūpa in Liuzhou, he burned one of his arms, vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land.

At midnight, his disciple Senghu saw an extraordinary light illuminating the courtyard. He asked, "Who is holding this torch? He asked this three times, and a voice from the air replied, "It is to come and welcome Master Qin.
Senghu hurriedly opened the window and beheld the radiance of the Buddha’s body, along with banners, flowers, and jeweled canopies.
Filling the void of space, they followed the Buddha, drifting slowly away.

The Dharma Master Wuhui (Fa-zhao) of the Tang dynasty resided at Yunfeng Monastery in Hengzhou during the second year of the Dali era. He was renowned for his compassion, forbearance, precepts, and meditative concentration. At that time—
Zong once beheld five-colored clouds within his alms bowl, in which appeared a Brahma-palace inscribed with the words "The Great Sage’s Zhulin Monastery.
Later, when he went to Mount Wutai and saw a wondrous light, he indeed found Zhulin Monastery.

Upon entering the lecture hall, he saw Mañjuśrī to the west and Samantabhadra to the east, surrounded by a multitude of ten thousand beings as they preached the Dharma. Zhao prostrated himself and asked: "Ordinary people of the final age have not yet—"
"What dharma-gate should one diligently cultivate? Mañjuśrī replied, "Among all gates of cultivation, none is equal to the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).

By means of the recollection of the Buddha, I have attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). He asked again, "How should one recollect it? He said, "To the west of this world is Amitābha Buddha.
The power of that Buddha’s vows is inconceivable; you should maintain the recollection continuously, without letting it be interrupted. This is certain."

He attained rebirth in the Pure Land. Later, on the first day of the twelfth lunar month, while at the Jingye (Pure Practice) Dojo in Huayan Monastery, he suddenly remembered that the two Great Beings had predicted his rebirth thereupon.
He then focused his mind single-mindedly on the Buddha’s name. Suddenly, he saw the Indian monk Buddhapālita, who said to him, "Your lotus pedestal is already prepared;
in three years, the flower shall bloom. When the appointed time arrived, he said to the assembly, "I am going," and sat upright.

Shi once held five assemblies for the recitation of the Buddha’s name at Lake East Temple. He was moved by auspicious clouds and a jeweled pavilion, and beheld Amitābha Buddha and two Bodhisattvas, their bodies filling the void.
Furthermore, while holding five assemblies for the recitation of the Buddha’s name in Bingzhou, he moved Emperor Daizong such that the sound of the recitation was heard within the imperial palace.
The Emperor dispatched an envoy to investigate, who then witnessed the great scale of the Master’s exhortations and conversions.
He was subsequently summoned to the capital to instruct the palace ladies in the recitation of the Buddha’s name, continuing for five assemblies;
thus he was titled the Dharma Master Wuhui.

As for Dharma Master Kang Taiyan, his secular surname was Tang and his given name was Shangkang. A native of Xindu in Jingyun, he mastered the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* at the age of fifteen. During the Zhenyuan era, he went to...
At Baima Temple in Luoyang, he saw characters within the hall emitting light. Upon examining them, he found they were the "Text on Guiding Others to the West" by the Venerable Shandao.
The Master made this vow: "If I have a karmic affinity for the Pure Land, may the light shine forth once more.
As soon as he had spoken, the radiance flashed brilliantly. The Master said, "Though kalpa-stones may be worn away, my vow shall never change. Thereupon, he proceeded to Chang'an.

While paying homage at the portrait hall of the Venerable Shandao at Ming Temple, he suddenly heard a voice from the air saying, "If you follow my teachings and extensively transform sentient beings, when your merit is perfected in the future, you will surely be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.

Thereupon, he traveled to Xinding to beg for money, using it to entice small children to recite the Buddha’s name, giving one coin for each recitation. After more than a year, people of all ages and social standings—whether young or old, noble or humble—saw the Master.
Everyone there recited the name of Amitābha Buddha, and the sound of their mindfulness of the Buddha filled the roads. Furthermore, at Mount Oryong, he established a Pure Land practice hall;
whenever he ascended the seat, he would chant the Buddha’s name in a loud voice, and the assembly saw a Buddha emerge from his mouth.
When ten sounds were heard, there were ten Buddhas appearing like a string of pearls. The Master said, "Those of you who have seen the Buddhas will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
At that time, among the thousands in the assembly, there were those who did not see them; they felt sorrowful and reproached themselves, subsequently redoubling their diligent practice.

Twenty-one years later, on the third day of the tenth month, he addressed the monastics and laypeople, saying, "You should give rise to a heart of joyful aspiration for the Pure Land, while [remaining] in Jambudvīpa..."
"Ti! Give rise to a mind of weary detachment. You who see my radiance at this moment are truly my disciples.
He then emitted several rays of extraordinary light and departed. His remains were enshrined in a stupa on Taiziyuan, and he was titled the Dharma Master of Taierock.
Zizhao Tang Zizhao resided in Zhenzhou. He constantly made this vow: "By means of Avalokiteśvara, may I behold Amitābha Buddha.
Thereupon, he cast an image of Avalokiteśvara forty-nine feet in height. Once it was completed, he offered prayers. At the third watch of the night, suddenly there appeared golden...
Two rays of light appeared. Amitābha Buddha descended from within the light, with the two Great Beings attending him on his left and right.

The Buddha extended his hand and stroked Zhiqian’s head, saying: "Fulfill your vows without wavering; prioritize benefiting sentient beings. In the jeweled pond where you shall be reborn, how could anything fail to accord with your wishes?
Eleven years later, on the evening of the full moon in the seventh month, he saw a figure resembling a heavenly king appear amidst the clouds.
Shen addressed his disciples, saying, "The time for my rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing has arrived. He then sat cross-legged before an image of Avalokiteśvara and passed away.

Shanzhou of the Tang dynasty was a native of Yingzhou. In the third year of the Wude era, when he was on the verge of death, he said to his disciples, "Throughout my entire life, I have been upright..."
He had faith and did not doubt that he would be born in the Pure Land. He immediately ordered his quarters to be swept and cleaned, burned incense, and waited with solemnity.
Though he had been bedridden for a long time due to illness, he suddenly sat up, joined his palms, and told his attendants, "Prepare a seat for the World-Honored One.

He then personally confessed his transgressions. After a long while, he said, "The World-Honored One has departed," and he lowered his body as if seeing him off. Then, lying down again, he said, "Just now, Amitābha..."
"The Buddha has come; do you all see him? It will not be long before I depart. Shortly thereafter, he passed away. Huaiyu (Tang Huaiyu) was a native of Taizhou.
For nearly forty years, he focused his thoughts on the pure karma of rebirth, wearing plain clothes, eating only one meal a day, and remaining constantly seated.
He did not lie down to sleep. He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* three hundred thousand times and daily chanted the Buddha’s name fifty thousand times.

In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, while he was practicing mindfulness of the Buddha, he suddenly saw Buddhas and Bodhisattvas filling the void of space; one person held a silver platform in his hands.
He presented it to the former [official], who said: "I have spent my life reciting the Buddha's name, hoping for the Golden Terrace; why is it not so?
Thereupon, the holy assembly vanished. The official redoubled his diligent practice, and on the twenty-first day, those who had previously held up the platform returned and told him:
The Master, through his diligent practice, attained the highest grade of rebirth. Those who attain rebirth in the highest grade must first behold the Buddha;
therefore, he sat in the full lotus posture to await the Buddha’s arrival. Before long, a wondrous light filled the room. After three days, the wondrous light appeared once more.
He said to his disciples, "If you smell a rare fragrance, my reward body will have reached its end. The following day, he wrote a verse: "Pure and radiant white."
Free from dust and defilement, born by transformation within lotuses as my parents, I have practiced the Way for ten kalpas.
Manifesting in Jambudvīpa to weary the masses of suffering, through a single lifetime of asceticism I have transcended those ten kalpas; forever leaving Saṃsāra, I shall return to the Pure Land.

When the verse ended, fragrant incense wafted from all directions. Some disciples beheld the Buddha and two Bodhisattvas together riding upon a golden platform, with thousands [of deities] by their side.
A hundred transformation Buddhas descended from the west to welcome Yù. Yù joined his palms in reverence and returned home with a long, smiling gait.
Dào’āng (d.
589), a native of Wèijùn, was a disciple of Dharma Master Língyù. He frequently lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Hánlíng Mountain Monastery.

Regarding the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages): he was profoundly learned and extensively versed, his aspirations reaching in all four directions. He vowed to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*).

Later, knowing his own life was coming to an end, he predicted it would be in the eighth month; others could not fathom this. When the first day of the eighth month arrived, he suffered no ailment. He asked whether the time for the midday meal had arrived, then immediately ascended the high seat.
His body manifested extraordinary marks, and a wondrous fragrance issued from the incense burner. He led the fourfold assembly to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
The words were profound and poignant. Daowang raised his eyes and looked upward, where he saw the celestial hosts amidst a profusion of pipes and strings.
Their music was clear and resonant as they announced to the assembly: "The Tuṣita Heaven welcomes you. Daowang replied, "Yet the heavenly realms are the very root of birth and death.

Since time immemorial, this has not been my wish; I have always prayed for the Pure Land. Why is it that this sincere aspiration has not yet been fulfilled? As soon as he finished speaking, the celestial music ceased. Then he saw—
From the west, incense, flowers, and musical instruments came surging like clouds, swirling above his head; the entire assembly witnessed this.

Daowang said, "Now the spiritual manifestations of the West have come to welcome me; it is necessary that I go there. As soon as he saw the incense burner fall from his hands, he passed away while seated upon his high throne.
Beneath his feet were the characters "Hall of Universal Radiance" (*Puguang Tang*) and others. Far and near, all were struck with wonder and sighed in admiration.

Daocuo (562–645) was a native of Wenshui in Bingzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of fourteen and studied the sutras and śāstras. Later, he served under Chan Master Zhan to study meditation.
Furthermore, he devoted himself earnestly to the practice of the Pure Land according to Shenluan. A monk once saw Daocuo’s prayer beads within his meditative concentration, appearing as...
At his great mountain retreat adorned with the seven treasures, he regularly lectured on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Visualization of Amitāyus) nearly two hundred times.

Each participant would count their prayer beads while chanting the Buddha’s name aloud. Occasionally, when the assembly dispersed, the sound of their voices still echoed through the forests and valleys.

He performed prostrations during the six periods of the day, never failing in his mindfulness of the Buddha, which he maintained at a minimum of seventy thousand recitations daily. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away into nirvana.
Those who heard of this and went there filled the mountain temple; they saw a manifested Buddha dwelling in the sky as celestial flowers rained down.
Wei An of Tang was a native of Bingzhou who specialized in the practice of the Sixteen Contemplations. Once, while he was out, he beheld the two Bodhisattvas, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

Sākyamuni appeared in the air and did not vanish for a long time. Hui'an prostrated himself and wept as he sighed, saying, "Fortunately, by means of my fleshly eyes, I have been able to behold the countenance of the Sage.
What I regret is that there will be no transmission of this image for future generations. Suddenly, two men appeared who called themselves painters;
before their arms had even been extended, the sacred image was completed. Shortly thereafter, the men vanished as well. The disciples marveled at this and questioned Hui'an. Hui'an said:
[The Master] said, "Is this not a work of a master painter? He spoke again, saying, "I shall now attain rebirth in the Pure Land;

who will accompany me as my fellow practitioner? The young boy replied, "I wish to follow my teacher. Dao-an said, "You may return home and inform your parents. When his parents heard this, they laughed and scolded him.
The boy then returned to the temple, bathed in fragrant water before the image of Amitābha Buddha, sat in the lotus position, and passed away. Dao-an stroked his...

The Master turned back and said, "Young man, why have you departed first? He then took up his brush, burned incense, and before the painted Bodhisattvas, composed a verse: "Avalokiteśvara assists from afar to receive me;
Mahāsthāmaprāpta aids from the distance to welcome me. The precious vase is manifest upon the crown; The transformation Buddhas are clear before the usnīṣa.
Together we shall travel through the lands of the ten directions, Holding flowers and awaiting the nine births. I pray that with your hands of compassion, You will lift me up and guide me along."
He traveled westward and then instructed his disciples to join him in chanting the Buddha’s name. Looking up and gazing toward the west, he passed away.
Qifang Yuan’guo (also known as Tang Qifang):
Yuan’guo was a native of Fenzhou. At that time, there was a monk named Xuanchu from Bingzhou who was devoted to Maitreya and vowed to ascend [to Tuṣita].
He was born into the Inner Court (the imperial palace). At the age of ninety, he met the Chan Master Daocuo and first heard of the Pure Land;

he then turned his mind toward the recitation of the Buddha’s name, performing one thousand prostrations daily. Later, when he fell ill, he told his disciples: "Amitābha Buddha has bestowed upon me fragrant robes, and Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta have shown me their jeweled hands.
Having spoken these words, he passed away. For seven days, a wondrous fragrance did not dissipate. The two masters witnessed this with their own eyes.
Regarding this matter, they went to Wuzhen Temple and together plucked willow branches from the hand of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, making this vow:

"If we have an affinity for the Pure Land, these branches shall not wither for seven days. When the period arrived, they grew even more luxuriant; their hearts were filled with joy at this auspicious sign.

With focused minds, they visualized the Pure Land, and within that visualization, they both felt as though their bodies were standing by a pool of the seven treasures. Within the pool was a great treasure...
In the pavilion, he saw Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta seated upon two great precious lotus flowers, beneath which were countless millions of spreading lotuses.
Amitābha Buddha came from the west, seated upon the largest of the lotuses; their radiance alternately shone upon one another.
Fangguo paid homage to the Buddha and asked, "Can the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, by recollecting the Buddha in accordance with the scriptural teachings, attain birth here? The Buddha said:
"Those who recite my name shall all be born in my land; there is not a single person who recites it and yet is not born there.
Furthermore, I heard Śākyamuni World-Honored One and Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva praising the Pure Land with Brahma-sounds.
Ahead was a great hall, with three jeweled stairways leading to it: the first was composed entirely of laypeople; the second consisted of a mixture of monastics and laity; the third...
The three were exclusively monks and none were laypeople. The Buddha pointed to Fangguo and said, "These are all sentient beings from Jambudvīpa in the south who practiced mindfulness of the Buddha;
they have consequently been born here. Once Fangguo had awakened, he recounted this to his disciples.

Five months later, while the two men were free from illness, they suddenly heard the sound of a bell that others did not hear. Fangguo said, "The sound of the bell is my affair," and at that very moment—
Huàqù. Biàncái (Táng Biàncái) was a native of Xiāngyáng.
He cultivated the Pure Land in secret for twenty years without ever claiming it for himself; he lived alone with Hù...
Ren Ren was a man of great virtue. He told [Tanyi] that his talent would surely lead him to be born in the Pure Land, and set a ten-year deadline for this.
One day, he ordered a disciple to inform Ren that the appointed time had arrived. When Ren arrived, Tanyi said, "I am departing. He sat in the lotus position and passed away.
The assembly heard the music of immortals coming from the west, and an extraordinary fragrance wafted through the air.
Faxiang of the Tang dynasty resided at Daxingguo Monastery in the capital of Yangzhou. For thirty years, he cultivated the practices for rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

Whenever he performed any act of benefit, he invariably dedicated the merit toward that goal. Later, while he was ill, his disciples heard Faxiang chanting the name of the Buddha with great intensity; they also saw him in his room...
On the western wall, there was a light like a mirror that manifested the signs of the Pure Land. A *pingga* bird flapped its wings and then suddenly vanished.

Da Xing of Tang resided at Mount Tai and practiced the *Samantabhadra Repentance* for three years; he was moved by the manifestation of the Great Being (*Mahāsattva*) appearing before him in his later years.
He entered the Great Canon Treasury and made a vow to take up a scroll at random; he obtained a copy of the *Amitābha Sūtra*.

He recited it day and night until the twenty-first day, when he beheld the Buddha and the two Great Beings manifesting their forms upon the ground of lapis lazuli. Emperor Xizong heard of this matter.
An imperial edict summoned her into the palace, where she was bestowed the title "Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent. One year later, the lapis lazuli ground appeared once more;
she passed away on that very day. A wondrous fragrance persisted for ten days, and her physical body remained incorruptible.

Mingzhan of the Tang dynasty, in his later years, resolved to seek rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). Some criticized him for doing so at such an advanced age, to which Mingzhan replied, "If ten recitations of the Buddha's name can achieve success and still allow one to see the Buddha, why should I have any concerns?
Later, due to illness, he prepared a vegetarian feast at Xingjiao Temple to bid farewell to both the monastics and the laity.
At that time, the Secretaries Fang Xuanling and Du Ruhui were both present. After noon had passed, he adjusted his dignified demeanor and recited the Buddha’s name.
Suddenly, he said, "The Buddha is coming; the two Great Beings have also arrived. He straightened his body, joined his palms, and passed away.
Zhītōng Shíjìn (志通石晉), styled Zhītōng, was a native of Fǎngxiáng. Upon seeing the *Jìngtǔ Yíshì* (Rituals for the Pure Land) by Master Zhìzhě, he was overcome with joy.

From then on, he never spat toward the west nor sat with his back to the west, but devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Later, he saw white cranes and... [the text continues].
A flock of sparrows flew down in formation toward the west. She also saw lotuses opening and closing before her. Tong said, "The white cranes and peacocks are the scenery of the Pure Land;
the radiant appearance of the lotuses is the place of rebirth. The Pure Land has manifested. Thereupon she rose, prostrated to the Buddha, and passed away.
During the cremation, auspicious clouds of five colors encircled and covered the flames, and the *śarīra* relics were arranged like scales upon her remains.
Chan Master Yongming Shou was of the Qian clan;
he was a Chan master of Wuyue. Yanshou was originally a native of Danyang, later moving to Yuhang. In his youth, he recited the Lotus Sūtra.

Originally serving as a county magistrate’s clerk, he embezzled a great deal of official funds. Upon investigation, it was found that the money had been used solely to purchase and release living beings; his crime merited death.

As he was being led to the execution ground, King Qian Zhongyi sent someone to observe him, instructing that he be executed immediately if his facial expression changed, but reported back if it did not.
At the moment of execution, his expression remained unchanged, whereupon his life was spared. He subsequently became a monk and studied under National Teacher Shao of Tiantai.
The Master elucidated the essential points of the awakened mind. Within his meditative contemplation, he beheld Avalokiteśvara, who poured nectar into his mouth; thereupon, he attained eloquence.

His brush flowed until his writings filled volumes, resulting in the *Wanshan tonggui ji* (Collection on the Convergence of Myriad Goodnesses) and the *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source), totaling several hundred fascicles.
Once, in the middle of the night, he saw Samantabhadra’s lotus flower suddenly appear in his hand. Reflecting that his long-held vow had not yet been fulfilled, he ascended Mount Zhizhe.
Yan Zuo cast two lots: one said "single-minded meditative concentration," and the other said "cultivating the Pure Land through myriad practices.

He focused his mind and prayed with devotion; seven times he drew the lot for the Pure Land. Thereupon, he devoted himself exclusively to this practice. Later, while residing at Yongming, he daily performed one hundred and eight acts of merit.
At night, he would go to a separate peak to practice the Way and recite the Buddha’s name. Those nearby occasionally heard the sounds of conch shells and celestial music.
Upon hearing the sound of his joyful chanting, King Zhongyi sighed and said, "From antiquity, no one has ever sought the Western Paradise with such single-minded earnestness.
He then established the Xifang Xiangyan Hall (Western Paradise Incense-Veneration Hall) to fulfill the master's aspiration.

On the twenty-sixth day of the second month in the eighth year of the Kaibao era, he rose at dawn, burned incense, addressed the assembly, sat in the lotus position, and passed away. After the cremation was completed, a stupa was erected for him. There was...

The monk circumambulated the stupa and prostrated every day. When people asked him the reason for this, the monk said: "I fell ill and went to the underworld, but as my life span was not yet exhausted, I was released and returned.
There, I saw a scroll-painting of a monk in the left side of the hall whom King Yama himself came to bow his head before.

When I asked who this person was, the chief clerk replied: 'This is Chan Master Shou of Yongming Temple in Hangzhou. For all those who die as humans..."* *(Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at this point.)*
While everyone else passes through this place, only this person does not; they have already attained the highest grade of rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
The King honors such a person and provides offerings here, thereby showing that those who cultivate the West with diligence are held in high esteem by the underworld authorities.

Master Shengchang of the Song Dynasty was the son of the Yan family of Qiantang. He left home at the age of seventeen and received full ordination; his observance of the precepts was meticulous and rigorous.

He was thoroughly versed in the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* and practiced the *Tiantai* system of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. He continued the legacy of Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu. During the Chunhua era, he resided in Hangzhou.
At Zhaokong Temple on West Lake in the prefecture, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism and established a society for pure conduct (*śuddhacaryā-saṃgha*).

The Chancellor Xiang Gong and the Duke Wen Zheng Gong Dan served as the heads of the society. Among the scholar-officials who joined the assembly, there were one hundred and twenty people, all of whom styled themselves disciples of pure conduct.
At that time, the number of bhikṣus reached nearly a thousand. The Master then made a vow, saying: "I and..."
A great assembly of one thousand people, from this very day forth, shall resolve to attain Bodhicitta and practice the deeds of a Bodhisattva until the end of the future.

They vow that when this retributive body is exhausted, they shall be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī). Song Bai, Imperial Commissioner for the Hanlin Academy, composed the inscription for the stele;
Su Yijian, Academician of the Hanlin Academy, wrote the preface to the "Chapter on Pure Conduct," in which he stated: "I shall spread my hair to receive his feet."
He even did not decline when asked to gouge out his own flesh to request the Dharma. Yuanzuan Sunhe inscribed this account as a guest on the back of the stele.
Master Yuanshi of Gushan composed the biography of the Master’s deeds. On the twelfth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Tianxi era, he sat upright reciting the Buddha’s name.
After a short while, he called out in a forceful voice, "The Buddha is coming! and then passed away peacefully.

Jingguan of the Song dynasty resided at Jiguang Hermitage in Jiahe. Having practiced the Pure Land repentance rites for over ten years, he said to his disciples, "Twenty-seven days from now, I shall depart.
On the second day prior to the appointed date, he saw a red lotus flower; on the following day—
Furthermore, he saw yellow flowers filling the room, each with a spontaneously born infant sitting upon a flower, dressed in immortal sashes and girdles.
On the third day, he entered his shrine and sat upright, commanding the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name. After a short while, he passed away.

Ciyun Chanmaster Song Zunshe was a native of Linhai County in Taizhou. His learning and conduct were lofty and ancient, his reputation preeminent throughout the two Zhejiang provinces. He dedicated himself exclusively to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
He once practiced the Pratyutpanna Samādhi for ninety days; through his arduous studies, he vomited blood. Upon entering the dharma hall, the skin on both his feet [became calloused].
His body broke out in sores. He made a solemn vow to die. Suddenly, as if in a dream, he saw Avalokiteśvara extending his hand and pointing his finger;

from his mouth, the Bodhisattva drew out several worms. Furthermore, nectar flowed from the tip of the finger and was poured into his mouth. Upon awakening, his body and mind were refreshed and cool, and his illness was subsequently cured.

He composed the *Jingtu jueyi xingyuan* (Resolving Doubts about the Pure Land through Practice and Vows) and the *Jingtu chanfa* (Pure Land Repentance Method), which circulated in the world. During the Tiānshèng era, on the day he was about to pass away—

He burned incense and paid homage to the Buddhas, vowing that all Buddhas would bear witness to his rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). That evening, he sat in meditation and passed away.
People saw a great star fall upon Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa). At that time, he was titled the Repentance Master Ciyun.
Zongtan of Lufu: Master Song Zongtan was a native of Licheng in Luzhou.
His surname was Shen. At the age of sixteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination. From a young age, he was well-versed in the study of Buddhist doctrine;
for nearly fifty years, his reputation spread throughout the monastic academies. In his later years, he lectured on the Pure Land teachings in the regions of Tang, Deng, Ru, and Ying.

He preached the *Amitābha Sūtra*, exhorting people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and seek rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). Those who listened gathered like clouds, all undertaking the pure practices (*śukla-karma*).
On the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Zhenghe era, he dreamed that Amitābha Buddha told him: "Your preaching of the Dharma shall last for only six days;

you shall then be born in the Pure Land. Upon waking, he informed the assembly, saying: "I have cultivated the path seeking rebirth in An-yang; it seems I have now attained the necessary conditions (*pratyaya*)."

"You should come at the appropriate time. The Buddha told him, "I have attained birth in the Pure Land; how could you dare not believe this? Although he felt unwell the following day, he did not cease his preaching and chanting.

At the hour of *chou* on the fourth day of the fifth month, knowing that the time had arrived, he struck the bell to assemble the congregation and said, "The gathering and dispersing of causes and conditions must indeed occur at their appointed times;
however, the supreme conditions for the Pure Land depend solely upon the moment. I hope you will [bear witness...]"
The assembly recited the Buddha’s name to assist him in his departure. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away. Thunder rolled through the sky and white clouds covered the earth;

it was only after three days that they subsided. The Master had previously possessed a string of agate beads, which he held between his fingers at the time of death; the multitude was ultimately unable to remove them.
The Patriarch Cizhao Song Ziyuan, whose style name was Wanshi Xiu, was the son of the Mao family of Kunshan in Pingjiang. His mother dreamed one night that a Buddha entered her door;
the following morning, he was born, and for this reason he was named Fulai. At the age of nineteen, he shaved his head and practiced *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. One day, while in meditative concentration...
Upon hearing the cry of a crow, he attained enlightenment and composed a verse, which says: "For over twenty years I sought on paper; Seeking and seeking, I grew ever more despondent.
Suddenly I heard the compassionate crow call out, And only then did I believe my former efforts were in vain. Thereupon, his altruistic resolve became most earnest.

Admiring the legacy of Master Huiyuan’s Lotus Society, he universally exhorted others to practice *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) and to receive and uphold the five precepts. First, [the precept against killing...]

First, do not kill; second, do not steal; third, do not commit sexual misconduct; fourth, do not lie; fifth, do not harbor thoughts of intoxication. These five sounds of Amitābha Buddha serve as testimony to the Five Precepts.
They universally establish pure conditions, intending to cause the people of the world to purify the five faculties, attain the five powers, and emerge from the five turbidities.
Thus, I have excerpted essential passages from the Great Canon and compiled them into this White Lotus Repentance Ritual for the sake of all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm.

Every morning he performed repentance and prayed to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). At the age of forty-six, while facing the circumstances of adversity and favor at Linjiang Prefecture, he never once allowed his thoughts to waver.
In the second year of the Qiandao era, Emperor Gaozong summoned him to the Deyou Hall to expound upon the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, bestowing upon him the title of Patriarch Cizhao.
On the twenty-third day of the third month, at the residence of Ni Jian in Duocheng, he announced [his passing].

His disciples said, "Our Master's transformative conditions are now exhausted; it is time for him to depart. Having spoken these words, he joined his palms in salutation to the assembly and suddenly manifested parinirvāṇa.
On the twenty-seventh day, his body was cremated, yielding countless śarīras, which were enshrined in a stupa at the residence of Wu Juechang in Songjiang.
The Emperor bestowed upon him the title of "Most Victorious Stūpa.
Fazhi of the Song dynasty resided at Huadu Monastery, where he practiced the Amitābha Repentance and Vows; thus shortening his lifespan in Jambudvīpa, he was born early into peace.
While she was in her later years, she fell slightly ill. She wept rain-like tears and wailed in grief, praying for the Buddha’s compassionate guidance.

As she recited the Buddha’s name with a resolute voice without ceasing, she suddenly saw the Buddha’s body, sixteen feet tall, standing upon a pond. She then said to herself, "I have attained rebirth in the middle grade," and passed away while facing west.
Benru was styled Shenzhao. He resided at Chengtian Temple on Mount Dongshan and established a religious society with Zhang Xun, the Prefectural Governor.
One day, he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, bid farewell to the assembly, and then withdrew to sit in meditation until his passing. At that time, fishermen on the river saw clouds...
At that time, there was a monk who traveled westward. The following year, the stupa was opened; his countenance was as if he were alive, and lotus flowers grew before the stupa.

Dharma Master Ji of the Song dynasty—Dharma Master Ji of Taiping Xingguo Temple, who had studied under Baoyun—dwelt there and applied himself with focused devotion to the practice of *nianfo*. One day...
He manifested illness and extensively expounded the profound mysteries for his disciples. Suddenly, the assembly saw light appear in the west and music resound through the air.
The Master said, "Amitābha Buddha has arrived together with two Great Beings. He then passed away reclining on his right side facing west.
His disciples dreamed that Amitābha Buddha conferred upon him the prophecy of becoming the Tathāgata Chao-shi (Transcending the World), or they dreamed of the Master seated upon a blue lotus flower.
As for Tae, Master Seon Cheon of Beopji sighed and said: "To discuss the profound mysteries while lying ill and to behold the Buddha at the moment of death—this is truly worthy of reverence.

As for Yo Yu and So Yu, they resided at Seondam Hermitage in Ungcheon, constructed the Muryangsu Pavilion, and diligently exhorted both monastics and laypeople to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
For thirty years, he was a friend to the two masters Daoqian and Zechang. Qian was skilled in poetry and sought fame, whereas I and Zechang were devoted solely to the practice of the Way.

As we were about to pass away from this world, I dreamed that a divine being told me: "Your fellow student Zechang has attained the Samādhi of Samantabhadra’s Vows and Practices and has already been reborn in the Pure Land;
he is currently waiting for you. Thereupon, I bathed, changed my robes, and summoned the assembly.
While reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra*, he sat upright in silence. Suddenly, he said, "The Pure Land appears before me; I shall now depart.
He wrote a verse and passed away. The verse says: "A thousand-flowered jeweled net in the void, A lotus pond of seven treasures within a dream.
Having trodden the path to the Western Land with stability, There is not a single trace of doubt remaining."
Shouzhen of the Song dynasty was a native of Yongxing. He lectured on the *Qixin lun* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith) and the *Fajie guan* (Contemplation of the Dharma Realm).

Regularly during the middle of the night, he would form the secret mudrā for rebirth in the presence of Amitābha Buddha and fix his mindfulness upon the Western Pure Land. One evening at dawn, he perceived himself ascending to that pure land.
Upon reaching the earth, he raised his eyes and beheld the Buddha; thereupon, prostrating himself before the image, he suddenly said, "If the Forty-eight Vows are indeed able to deliver me.
He then took incense and flowers, entered the hall to make offerings, and passed away while seated.
Yanyan of the Song dynasty resided at Chongshan Temple on Mount Chicheng in Taizhou. He studied the Tiantai teachings under Shenzhao.

In his later years, he built a thatched hut beneath a jujube tree and named it Zhuan’an (Jujube Hermitage). Throughout his life, he was devoted to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism and harbored a deep aspiration for the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
