The "Poem on Returning Home" was widely circulated during his lifetime. In the fourth month of summer in the first year of the Jianzhong Jinggu era, as he approached the end of his life, he beheld a jeweled pond with a great lotus flower and celestial music arranged in four rows.
He then composed the "Poem on Departing for the Pure Land" and showed it to the assembly. Seven days later, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
A light like the moon appeared above his stupa, remaining until three o'clock in the afternoon before finally fading.
Master Zanzong was a native of Yongzhou. While still a novice monk, he recited the name of the Buddha without ceasing at the age of fourteen. He suddenly fell ill and passed away abruptly;
however, he soon revived and said to his master, parents, and others: "Amitābha Buddha has come; this child shall follow him."
As he was walking, a neighbor saw a jeweled terrace in the sky emitting five-colored, extraordinary light that vanished toward the west.

Zhili (Song Zhili) resided at Huadu Monastery in Shangyu. Initially, he traveled extensively to study under various masters of the Chan school; in his later years, he focused his mind single-mindedly on the Western Paradise.
In the first year of the Qinyuan era, in the eighth month of autumn, he addressed the assembly, saying: "In my dream, I saw Amitābha Buddha preaching the Dharma while surrounded by a great multitude.
The Buddha said: 'All you virtuous people, you must single-mindedly cultivate pure karma so that you may be reborn in my land.'"
"I have seen a superior sign; my rebirth there is certain. He then wrote a verse, saying: "A wild goose flies across the vast sky, its shadow sinks into the cold water;
neither ceasing nor arising, it dwells within the Land of Lotus Flowers. Having finished writing, he turned his body toward the west, performed a mudrā, and passed away.

Ji-shin (1508–1592), whose courtesy name was Ji-shin and pen-name Ci-chuan, studied under Hai-yue. He returned to Jiahe, where he established the Changtang Monastery and served the community for twenty years.
He was single-mindedly devoted to the practice of nianfo and constantly used the Pure Land path to transform others; many attained rebirth there. Suddenly, he manifested illness.
When a guest arrived to inquire after his well-being, they conversed as usual; at the very moment the guest was about to depart, he passed away.
Those present saw purple clouds vanish toward the west.
Zongli of Song lived at Bishao (Emerald Pond) in Xincheng, where he practiced the *nienfo samādhi* for ten years.
Later, he entered Daowei Mountain and built a hermitage named Yixiang (Single Aspect). Fifteen years later, he suddenly said to his disciples: "I see blue lotuses."
Flowers filled the air. On the third day, he said again, "The Buddha is coming. He then wrote a verse, saying: "My age is ninety, my head is white as snow;
In this world, there should be no guest of a hundred years. A man who has realized the One Mark is returning home;
Seated upon the Golden Terrace, heaven and earth are cut off and grow narrow. Suddenly, he passed away.
Qi Yu, surnamed Song Qi Yu, whose style name was Huijue, initially established a Pure Land assembly at Baozang Temple in Xiachuan.

Later, while residing at Upper Zhunti, he would take the statue of Amitābha upon his head at midnight and practice walking meditation while reciting the Buddha’s name. One day, he said to the head seat: "There are many [signs] before my bed..."
"The appearance of the jeweled stupa was not my wish; what I desired was the pure land. He then instructed them, "Gather the assembly to recite the Buddha's name.
The head seat struck the bell, and more than a hundred monks assembled. Yu said, "I have now seen the Buddha," and he sat upright and passed away.

Chuqian (處謙), a monk of the Song dynasty, was dedicated to the cultivation of the Pure Land. One night, having finished reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra*, he extolled the virtues of the Pure Land and addressed the assembly, saying, "I shall be born in the Pure Land through the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Then, as if entering a state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he suddenly passed away.

Chan Master Yuanzhao Zongben was a native of Wuxi, Changzhou, during the Song dynasty. Initially, he studied under Chan Master Tiandi Huai; through the practice of nianfo (buddha-recitation), he attained realization.

Later, he moved to Jingci Monastery and was summoned by imperial decree to enter HuiLin Monastery in the Eastern Capital. He was granted an audience at the Yanhe Hall and pleased the Emperor’s mind. In his daily life...
He practiced pure deeds in secret. When Dharma Master Cai of Leifeng traveled spiritually to the Pure Land, he saw an exceptionally beautiful flower.

Upon being questioned, it said, "It awaits Chan Master Ben of Jingci. Furthermore, when Master Xi of Zifu went to Huilin Temple to pay respects at the feet [of the master] and departed after offering gold, people asked him the reason.
He replied, "In my meditative absorption, I saw a golden lotus flower; people say it was to await Master Ben."
Furthermore, there were countless lotus flowers. It was said that those who were to be saved would receive them; if some were withered, it was said they were people who had regressed and fallen away.
Someone asked: "The Master’s transmission is the direct pointing; why then do you use the realm of the lotus as a designation? He replied:

"Although we belong to the School of the Patriarchs, we also cultivate the Pure Land in conjunction with it. Later, when his end approached, he passed away while sitting peacefully. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Yuanzhao.

The Vinaya Master Qingzhao, surnamed Song, was named Huiheng. He resided at Yanshou Temple in Wulin. Initially, he relied upon Lingzhi to study the Vinaya, and for sixty years he specialized in the cultivation of Pure Land practices.
Whenever he encountered others, he invariably exhorted them to recite the Buddha’s name. He constructed a precious pavilion and established images of the Three Sages, which were most excellent.
It was truly extraordinary. There was one named Jiang Ziren who suddenly dreamed that a jeweled throne descended from the sky, saying, "Master Heng shall ascend this throne.
At that very moment, his fellow practitioner, Layman Sun, came to inform him of his departure; Master Heng immediately performed the seal of renunciation while still at home and passed away.
The Master went to offer incense. Upon returning, he said to his disciples, "Master Sun has already departed; I too shall go.
He then gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name and spoke this verse for them: "Recite the name of Amitābha with every word; contemplate his white ūrṇā-hair with every thought.
By maintaining this heart of non-retrogression, one will certainly be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing. He sat upright and passed away, and was posthumously titled Vinaya Master Qingzhao.
Xi Zhan of the Song dynasty was a native of Shanyin. In his youth, he was a Confucian scholar, but suddenly grew weary of the world and left the household life.

Together with the lay practitioner Ying, he constructed a hall for Amitābha Buddha at Ruandu and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the Pure Land. He never sat with his back turned toward the west. After a long time, he constantly beheld [the Buddha].
The images of the Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas remained as they were. One night, he faced west and recited the Buddha’s name; sitting upright and motionless, he performed a mudrā and passed away.

Dharma Master Zang (Song Sengzang) was a native of Fenzhou. Throughout his life, he did not accept prostrations from either monastics or laypeople, devoting himself exclusively to the practice of the Pure Land. As he approached his end:
Heavenly music arrived in succession to welcome him, yet he did not go to any of them. When the Buddha of the West arrived, he departed from the assembly to undergo transformation.

Master Yuan of Gushan, Song Zhiyuan, resided at Gushan on West Lake; he provided extensive commentaries on various sutras and devoted his heart to the Pure Land, composing a sub-commentary on the *Amitābha Sūtra*.

As well as the *Xizi chao*, he exhorted others toward rebirth in the Pure Land. When he was about to pass away, he had his remains interred in a clay vessel. Fifteen years later, during a period of heavy rains, the mountain collapsed.
Upon opening the vessel to inspect it, the physical form remained perfectly intact; even the nails and hair had grown long.

Yumi (Yùmí) of the Song dynasty was surnamed Yù. A native of Qiántáng, he styled himself the "Son of the Pure Land. In his youth, he attended Master Yīng’s lectures on the *Lotus Sūtra*. Later, he devoted himself exclusively to the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
In his leisure time, he would paint images of the Buddha; whenever he painted, he would do so in a pure chamber while maintaining a state of tranquil contemplation. He saw [the Buddha in vision].

The light of Amitābha then appeared, and he began to write. In the Dingyi year of the Shaoxing era, he sat upright for seven days, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name, and then passed away peacefully.
Taimi Song Taimi.

In his childhood, he entered the monastic life under Dharma Master Fajian of Qiantang after offering a coin as an act of devotion. Initially, when he was first taught the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, he was able to recite it from memory.

Upon receiving full ordination, he shut the door and practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name with such diligence that he never slackened. He often took long walks on the mountain behind the monastery, when suddenly—
Upon hearing the sound of a flute, he attained sudden enlightenment. Consequently, he kept a flute for his own amusement. There was a certain Magistrate Ling who shared his devotion to the Pure Land;
he referred to Zhiwei as the "Village Headman of the Pure Land. One day, Ling knocked on the door and said, "A fellow brother from the Village of the Pure Land has come to visit you."
Wei said, "We shall meet tomorrow in the Pure Land; for now, reciting the Buddha’s name is merely a distraction. The following morning, people marveled that he had not come to the morning gruel.
When they went to look, they saw that his flute, alms bowl, and meditation chair had already been burned, and he had passed away while sitting in the full lotus position upon the ground.
Jiufahua (Long-Living Lotus) was surnamed Kejiu and resided in Mingzhou. He constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and vowed to be reborn in the Pure Land; thus, he was known as Jiufahua.
In the eighth year of the Yuanyou era, at the age of eighty-one, he passed away while seated in meditation. Three days later, he returned and said to people, "I have seen the Pure Land."
The realm [revealed] accords with the scriptures. Upon the lotus pedestals, the names of those destined for rebirth therein were inscribed:

one golden pedestal bore the name of Monk Xun of Guangjiao Monastery in Chengdu Prefecture, who had already been born there; one bore the name of Mr. Sun, the twelfth son of the Mingzhou family, who was destined to be born there;
one bore the name Kejiu; and one silver pedestal bore the name of the Daoist nun Xu of Mingzhou. Having finished speaking, he transformed once more.
In the fifth year, the nun Xu passed away; a wondrous fragrance filled the room. In the twelfth year, Sun Shierlang passed away;
celestial music welcomed him into the void. Both events were exactly as had been foretold long ago.

Yongqin of the Song dynasty resided at Qiantang Qibaoyuan. He studied the Vinaya under Dazhi. Hearing Dazhi address the assembly, saying, "If one propagates the *vinaya* in life, one shall return to An-yang after death;
when one has completed the essential tasks of leaving home to study the Way, one should then direct the mind toward purity. Yongqin immediately set his heart upon this.

Tuoyi never wavered in his resolve. He recited the Buddha’s name thirty thousand times daily. Once, while his spirit wandered through the Pure Land, he beheld the Buddha and various bodhisattvas manifesting diverse and extraordinary signs.
He said to his attendant, "I shall depart for the West tomorrow. He immediately gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name.
At dawn, with palms joined and gazing toward the west, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away.
Shanzhu Yuan was styled Yunwu; he was a native of Suzhou. He remained in seclusion for six periods of the day and night reciting the Buddha’s name, never wavering despite his long illness.
At the time of his death, a rare fragrance filled the room. His work, *The Oral Tradition of Peaceful Nurturing: A Collection of Resonant Echoes*, is still in circulation today.
Miaowen Yuan was the son of the Sun clan of Wei Prefecture. He left home at the age of nine and received full ordination at eighteen.

At twenty-one, he traveled to the capital and relied upon Master Dade to study the Perfect and Sudden Teachings for eleven years before finally entering the world [of public ministry]. Although he was without...
He was obstructed from speaking. When the mountain torrents were in spate and the rivers rushed forth, yet when he dwelt in leisure and silence, his words were not uttered recklessly.

His cultivation was humble and modest; he had no desire for haste and did not advance with impetuosity—his great character was largely like this. Emperor Shizu summoned him for an audience and, turning to his attendants, said, "This is a monk of great merit.
By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Baoji Temple. When he exceeded eighty years of age, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the *nienfo* samādhi.
In the sixth year of the Yanyou era, knowing that the time had come, he instructed his disciples to loudly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Facing west, he sat cross-legged, his hands forming the *samādhi* mudrā, and passed away with serene composure.

Xing Chengyuan, whose courtesy name was Zantang, was surnamed Sun by birth and was a native of Kuaiji. His mother, Lady Jiang, dreamed that a solar disc fell from the sky, and subsequently gave birth to the Master.
At the age of four, he would often play with a brush, drawing images of the Buddha; when given Buddhist scriptures to read, he was immediately able to master them.
Recitation. In the year of the Bingzi cycle of the Zhiyuan era, he shaved his head under Master Shu of Shimen and received full ordination.

He studied the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school. In the year of the Xinyou cycle of the Zhizhi era, he was suddenly summoned to the capital. When the Emperor visited Wenshu Ge, he was introduced for an audience and received inquiries regarding his well-being.

The Emperor bestowed upon him scriptures such as the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. Upon hearing of this, the Chancellor, Prince Dongping Zhongxian Wang, requested that he ascend the seat to preach the Dharma. This matter was reported [to the throne], and he was thus honored.

The imperial favors bestowed upon him were exceptionally abundant, and he was granted the title of Great Master Fohai. Later, he returned to Foguo Monastery in Yue, where he devoted himself earnestly to the Pure Land.
For seven days and nights, he practiced the "three contemplations in a single mind," during which he repeatedly experienced auspicious omens.

One morning at dawn, when the assembly came to inquire after his well-being according to custom, the Master suddenly said, "Please take the time to inspect my robes and bowl; let this serve as a sign of impermanence. The assembly recited the Buddha’s name for him, and he stopped them, saying:
The Buddha thought to himself: "I shall see him off tomorrow morning. At dawn, the assembly gathered; [the Buddha] sat upright and passed away.

Pan Gu was originally named Pan Gu; he was a native of Haiyan. Though his physical appearance was not striking, his spirit and resolve were transcendent. He had read widely through the classics and histories, and his nature...
He was devoted to mountains and waters. During the Zhizhi era of the Yuan dynasty, he traveled extensively among the Five Terraces, Mount Emei, Mount Funiu, and Shaoshi—various famous sacred peaks.
He once remarked, "My footprints have covered half the world; my poetic fame fills the realm.

At that time, Prince Shen of Goryeo, a son-in-law of the Emperor, having heard of the Master’s virtue and reputation, invited him to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Huīyīn Temple in Jiangxi. There, the Master displayed his fourfold unimpeded eloquence before the seven assemblies.

He was deeply moved and submitted himself [to the teachings]. The King was greatly pleased. Later, he went to Song County and constructed a vihāra, where he diligently cultivated the practice of purity.

He recited the name of Amitābha Buddha daily. When he was over seventy years old, he fell ill; however, he announced his passing in advance at the appointed time and passed away peacefully while sitting upright.
Bi Caiyuan, courtesy name Dayong, was surnamed Qu and was a native of Linhai in Taizhou. His mother was Lady Zhao, who delighted in goodness and revered the Buddha.

Ten months after Master Cai’s conception, his mother dreamed that a Buddhist monk entered the hall shaking a *khakkhara* staff; she awoke and gave birth to him. At the age of seven, the Master became proficient in...
He composed verses spontaneously as they flowed from his mouth. At the age of twelve, he took up the scriptures and followed Master Ju of Jiangxi to receive the tonsure and the full precepts.
He was grave and silent, diligent in contemplative practice, and pursued his cultivation with tireless effort, never relaxing for even a moment.
He received others with compassion and taught them without weariness. By imperial decree, he was specially granted the title "Fujian Yuanzhao. One day, he suddenly attained awakening.
His head and eyes became fixed and motionless. He then said to the assembly, "My karmic conditions have come to an end.

He then burned incense, sat upright facing west, and recited the Buddha’s name in a loud voice for an entire day and night. Again he told the assembly, "Do not say that the practice of cultivation yields no results;
my conditions for the Pure Land have ripened, and samādhi has manifested before me. He then requested a bath, changed his clothes, and wrote a letter to bid farewell to his acquaintances.
He then passed away with his palms joined. Upon cremation, light of five colors issued forth from the funerary chamber.
Among the remains of the fire, his tongue was like a red lotus and his teeth were like white conch shells; śarīras filled the ground. The multitude gathered them, exhausting them all at once.

Master Yuan Zhiguan, whose courtesy name was Biezong, was a native of Hangzhou. His observance of the precepts was extremely strict. He established a meditation hall on the southern slope of Longshan Mountain and practiced the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi).
Even while fleeing from military conflict, he did not abandon his practice for even a moment. At the time of his death, he passed away without illness.
He bathed, sat upright, and passed away.
Zu-hui and Yuan Zu-hui resided at the Buddha Pavilion in the city of Siming County; whenever they encountered people, they would simply say, "Amitābha Buddha. They also preached [in this manner].
He could not speak; thus people called him the "Monk Who Cannot Speak" (Shuobude Heshang). Wang Yongxiang, the Magistrate of Yinqian County, and his wife served him with deep reverence.
One day, he went to their home to take his leave, saying, "I shall depart tomorrow. When morning came and the assembly had gathered, he entered his coffin and sat upright.
He requested a sweet melon, ate one whole, and passed away while reciting the Buddha's name.
Chu Qiming was a native of Shu who possessed profound faith in the Western Regions. He traveled to Yanjing, where he attained great enlightenment upon hearing the sound of the drum atop the tower.

At the beginning of the Hongwu era, he was summoned three times by imperial decree to preach the Dharma in the capital, which greatly pleased the Emperor. Later, he built a residence called Xizhai (Western Studio) and devoted himself single-mindedly [to his practice].
Jingye once saw a great lotus flower filling the world, with Amitābha at its center, surrounded by a multitude of sages.
As he was about to pass into parinirvāṇa, he wrote a verse for the assembly, saying: "I am going. Someone asked where he would be reborn; he replied, "The Western Land. They asked again.
"There is a Buddha in the West; is there no Buddha in the East? With these words, he let out a piercing shout and passed away in stillness.

Baizhu Ming lived constantly between the regions of Hangzhou and Jiahe. Wearing but a single robe throughout both winter and summer, he sustained himself by begging for food. He had no fixed dwelling.

Hengju constantly resided [there]. In his daily life, he would recite the Buddha’s name without ceasing, even when called by others; he would only respond briefly, immediately continuing to chant the Buddha’s name with an uninterrupted voice, never uttering any other words.
Later, at Haimen Temple, he suddenly acted like one who was insane for more than half a month.
A monk scolded him, saying, “Your lifelong practice has been genuine and should serve as an example for the world; why have you come to this? Zhuzhu replied:
Having spoken thus, he prepared for his departure. After completing his bath, he passed away peacefully.
Huiri Minghuiri, whose courtesy name was Dongming, was surnamed Jia; he was a descendant of Jia Sidao, the Chancellor of the Song dynasty. Sidao...

During the period of his banishment to the frontier garrisons, the Master was still young, yet his resolve was set on seeking ordination. At the age of twenty-two, he followed Bazi Ting to study the teachings of the Tiantai school, through which he thoroughly mastered their great principles.
During the Zhizheng era, the Lower Tianzhu region suffered a disaster; the Yuan official Gao Nalun requested that the Master rebuild it.

When Emperor Shundi heard of this, he specially conferred upon him the title "Ciguang Miaoying Pujie" (Compassionate Light, Wondrous Response, Universal Salvation). In the second year of the Hongwu era, he was summoned [to the capital].
He was summoned to the Fengtian Hall, where his vermilion face and white eyebrows were presented; his performance of the ritual was entirely to the Emperor’s satisfaction.

Emperor Taizu turned to the assembly of monks and said, "For you who study Buddhism, such works as the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* are all essential scriptures for the cultivation of the mind.

Why do you not consult the Master with the White Eyebrows? Thereafter, whenever he was summoned for an audience, the Emperor addressed him simply as "the White-Browed One. In the fifth year, he took his leave and returned to the mountains.
Zhú daily practiced the *Miaoyin Amitābha Sūtra* repentance to perfect his pure karma.

On the evening of the seventh month in the twelfth year, he dreamed of a blue lotus flower growing from within a square pond, its fragrance pervading the air. Upon waking, he told the assembly, "The auspicious sign of my rebirth in the Pure Land has appeared.
Four days later, he sat in the lotus posture with palms joined and passed away at the age of eighty-nine.

Zhenqing Mingzhen was the son of the Luo family of Xiangtan. From birth, he was exceptionally gifted; at fifteen, he was enrolled as a scholar in the local district school, and at nineteen, he left the household life.
He took up the "Mu" (No-Word) koan, and upon hearing the sound of a boat striking the shore, he attained realization. Later, he moved to Mount Huading and Tianzhu.

Feng practiced the Great and Small Amitābha Repentances. He privately maintained the "Mind-Ground Chapter" of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and the *Sūtra of the Sixteen Contemplations* as his regular daily recitations.
One night, he dreamed of a magnificent and elegant temple with rows of precious trees. There he beheld Amitābha and the Three Holy Ones.
Just as the Master was about to prostrate himself, a novice monk appeared beside him and handed him a plaque inscribed with the words: "Perfumed by the Incense of the Precepts. (Wanli guisi).

In the first month, he suddenly fell ill. He then addressed his disciples, saying, "My karmic conditions for the Pure Land have ripened, and a sacred realm has manifested before me in the unseen world.
I shall pass away on the twenty-ninth day. At evening, he rose and took leave of the assembly, saying, "I shall depart this life immediately.
The assembly asked, "To which of the nine grades of rebirth will the Master go? He replied, "It is the middle grade of the middle birth. They asked, "Why not be born in the upper grade?"
"Yes," he replied. "I have been perfumed by the fragrance of the precepts, and my station remains at the middle grade. Having finished speaking, he passed away in serene stillness.
Master Lianchi—his courtesy name was Fohui; his surname was Shen. He was the son of a prominent family from Renhe. From childhood, he was brilliant and quick-witted. At the age of... [text ends]

At seventeen, he topped the list of candidates in the local school examination; nevertheless, his aspiration was set upon transcending the world, and he would invariably write the four characters "The Matter of Birth and Death is Great" upon his desk.
At thirty-one, he went to the monk Xingtiantilü of the Western Mountains, where he received the tonsure and the full precepts.

He traveled through various regions, visiting and studying under numerous spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*). While traveling north to Mount Wutai, he was moved by the manifestation of Mañjuśrī’s radiance.

Upon passing through Dongchang, he suddenly attained a profound realization and composed a verse: "Events from twenty years past remain suspicious; What marvel did I encounter three thousand *li* away? Incense burned and spears cast—all like a dream;
Demons and Buddhas vainly contend over right and wrong. In the *Xinwei* year of the Longqing era, he went to beg for food at Fannian Temple.
In the village, he saw that the mountains and waters of Yunqi were secluded and tranquil; he thereupon leaned against a cliff wall and sat in meditation for seven days without food.

The local people, including Chen如玉 and others, constructed a thatched hut for him to dwell in. As the village was plagued by many tigers that frequently harmed people, the Master recited sutras and performed the ritual of offering food (śrāddha), whereupon the tiger menace subsided.
During a severe drought that year, the villagers earnestly requested him to pray for rain; the Master struck his wooden fish (mokugyo) and walked through the fields.

As they recited the Buddha’s name, rain poured down in accordance with the extent of their footsteps. The assembly was moved by this marvel and, working shoulder-to-shoulder with axes and hoes, they vied with one another to clear the ground.
There they discovered a stone stele and foundation block, which read: "This is the former site of Yunqi Temple, belonging to Master Fuhu.
We vow to renovate it for you. In no time, the monastery (ārāma) was completed. From then on, disciples from all quarters flocked there daily to practice the six periods of contemplation.

He was mindful. During the middle watch of the night, he exhorted himself with vigilance. Initially, Master [Yunqi] gained realization through the practice of investigating *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation).
He subsequently devoted himself exclusively to the Pure Land gate, composing the *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* (*Míto shūchão*) in over one hundred thousand words.

Furthermore, he recorded the essential instructions and kōans of ancient masters, compiling them into the *Chánguān cèjìn* (Exhortations for Advancement at the Zen Barrier) to demonstrate the methods for investigative study. This was intended to manifest the principle of the dual cultivation of Chan and Pure Land. Moreover,

He strictly observed the monastic precepts as his primary practice. He composed the *Essentials for Śrāmaṇeras* (*Shami yaolüe*) and the *Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra Unveiling the Hidden* (*Fameng jingshu fayin*), among other works, to elucidate the teachings.
The Master’s reputation for the Way spread daily, transforming both the court and the common people.

When Empress Dowager Cisheng saw the Master’s essay on releasing living beings, she marveled at it greatly and dispatched an inner attendant with a purple cassock and provisions for a vegetarian feast to present to him.

He was asked about the essentials of the Dharma, and the Master answered him in verse. As he was about to enter nirvana, he entered the city in the middle of the sixth lunar month to bid farewell to his disciples.
He did not wish to speak plainly, as it would have seemed strange or forced; he merely said, "I am going elsewhere.

Upon returning to the mountain, he descended from the hall in succession to provide offerings for the assembly, saying, "I shall not remain here; I am going elsewhere. The assembly could not fathom this, as it was contrary to the usual custom.
The alms bowls for the Ullambana festival were set out. The Master said, "This year, I shall not attend the assembly. He had a register of names, which he inscribed in secret, stating:

"A monk serving as the Head of the Administrative Office at Yunqi Monastery acts on behalf of Master Lianchi to offer posthumous offerings for the late ancestors of the Shen family. Later, [the Master] reviewed the register.

Only upon seeing this did they realize that he had previously left behind these parting words. On the evening of the first day of the seventh month, he entered the hall and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Tomorrow I must travel far away. I spoke to you all, but you would not listen; you waited until I stumbled and fell before you finally believed me.
The assembly tried to detain him, so the Master composed "Three Things to Be Regretted" and "Ten Things to Be Sighed Over" to admonish them. That following night, he entered his private quarters.

He manifested a slight illness and closed his eyes, remaining silent. When the assembly requested him to speak, the various disciples from within the city arrived. The Master opened his eyes and said, "The great assembly, be sincere and mindful of the Buddha.
Having spoken these words, he ordered his seat to be moved toward the west; then, while reciting the Buddha’s name in the full lotus posture, he passed away.
Previously, he had seen a great lotus flower in a vision, and thus could not conceal the signs of his rebirth in the Pure Land. At that time, Wan...
It was the year of Yimao (1275), the fourth day of the seventh month at the hour of the horse. His worldly age was eighty-one.

The Master himself selected a site for his temple at the foot of a ridge and subsequently enshrined his entire remains in a stupa there. He is widely acclaimed as the eighth patriarch of the Lotus School.
Foshi Ming, whose alternative name was Layman Fayu, was the son of the Dai family of Qiantang. His mother dreamed that a monk covered her body with a *kāṣāya* robe before he was born.
From infancy, he loathed the smell of meat and pungent foods. At the age of fourteen, he went to pay his respects to Chan Master Jingming and received the tonsure and precepts.
At eighteen, he received the precepts from Master Lianchi. He traveled extensively among lecture halls, studying the teachings and contemplative practices of the Tiantai school.

In the year Jia-wu, he visited Chan Master Zibo in Jinling and personally received his transmission. As he was about to depart, the Master instructed him, saying, "A skilled merchant hides his treasures deeply.
Upon returning to Wulin, he immediately took up a single umbrella and a straw mat on his shoulder, entering the mountains as a means of deep concealment. When he reached...

In the eighteenth ravine, the forests and valleys were secluded and extraordinary; the Master was greatly delighted by this. He then tied his umbrella to a short pine tree and sat cross-legged upon a lotus-cushion.
As evening fell, two tigers roared and circled the Master without leaving. The Master addressed them, saying: "If I have a karmic affinity with this place..."
"You must depart quickly. Having spoken these words, the tiger nodded its head, tugged at its tail, and left. Thereupon, he cleared away the brush and piled up stones to construct a small hermitage.

Prominent monastics followed one after another to visit him. One day, while digging the earth, he discovered fragments of an ancient stele and broken foundation stones, realizing that this was the site of the ancient Liran Temple;
consequently, he reconstructed it. By nature, the Master was solitary and eminent, remaining unmoved by worldly conditions. In his later years...

At the end of the year, he dismissed his guests and retreated to the mountain peak, where he constructed a single room and excavated a burial pit, saying, "This shall serve as my dwelling when alive and my tomb when dead.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the ninth year of the Chongzhen era, he suddenly manifested slight illness.

It was the beginning of autumn, and he said to his disciples, "Today the weather is clear; I wish to depart for far away. The disciples replied, "The Master is currently ill; where do you wish to go? The Master—
He said, "Do you think I am ill? He rose from his bed leaning on a staff, washed his face, and sat in the lotus posture.

He gathered the assembly to entrust them with his final affairs. Just then, the layman Cai arrived; the Master clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "Layman, bear witness. There is no need to wait for anything else.
The disciples requested that he leave behind a verse, and the Master wrote it with a swift brush: "One phrase of Amitābha for fifty years—clearly evident."
"Digging into the earth to seek the blue sky. Now there is a truly excellent news: at midnight, the sound of the bell reaches the traveler’s boat.
Having finished writing, he looked around him, threw down his brush, and passed away.
Zuxiang Mingzuxiang was a native of Xinyu, Jiangxi. At Longtan Temple in Shandong, he diligently cultivated the Pure Land practices.
A layman named Wang Jie built a hermitage to invite him; after a short time, he told Jie, "On such-and-such a day, I shall return home. The assembly was distressed.
He remained there. His fragrant cloud returned to the family of An-yang. When the appointed time arrived, he spread his seat and sat facing west, passing away.
When his coffin was carried into the mountains, it ignited spontaneously and burned itself to ashes.
Juzong, the Great Qing monk Juzong, was a native of Wuxi. He lectured on the Tiantai *Zhi guan* and the *Nianfo Sanmei*. He exhorted others without weariness.
During the Jihai year of the Shunzhi era, he manifested illness. He arranged for a bath at the appointed time and, wearing only a single sandal, presented his secret memorial.

Regarding the meaning of returning to the West with a single sandal: having finished reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra* and chanting the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times, he took up his brush and wrote in large characters:
"Vast and empty is the numinous void; there is no place of coming or going. He then threw down his brush and departed. He sat in the lotus position for three days.
His countenance remained unchanged. Moved by this, those who were faithless turned their minds to serve the Buddha.
He was a new and great Qingxiu; his posthumous name was Dazhen. He left home as a youth at Lianju Hermitage in Wulin and received ordination from Master Shaojue.
He practiced the Pratyutpanna Samādhi. At the time of his death, his disciples all saw him together in a dream at night:

celestial beings filling the sky held incense and flowers and proclaimed, "We come to welcome the Great Master; he has been born in the Western Land. When morning came, the disciples gathered to wait for him;
the Master’s body was healthy and he was mindful of the Buddha, appearing as usual. Three days later, at noon, he suddenly passed away while sitting in meditation.

Linggu Daqing of Linggu was a native of Shaoxing. He resided to the southwest of Luoshan, wearing tattered robes and hempen sandals. He exhorted people only that the essential practice was to recite the Buddha’s name.
At the time of his death, he saw a white cloud and a standing Buddha coming to welcome him, and he passed away. The local people changed [the name of] his...
An said, "White Clouds. Daoshu was a native of Dading;
he was a person from Renhe who, whenever he lectured on the sutras, took the fundamental tenets of Tiantai as his primary framework and exhorted others [to follow them].
He took the practice of Buddha-recitation as his vanguard. In his daily life, he recited the Buddha’s name with vigor and did not exert himself in worldly affairs.

In the year of Yiwu (1655) during the Shunzhi era, he dreamed that he ascended the summit of Mount Yuping together with a divine monk. In the sixth month of the year of Bingshen (1656), he fell slightly ill.

On the twenty-sixth day, early in the morning, he said to the assembly: "Last night I dreamed that a divine monk came to welcome me; could this be the same one from when we previously ascended Mount Yuping?"
On the evening of the Bingfeng day, at the hour of Xu (7–9 p.m.), she suddenly saw banners and canopies filling the sky and lotus flowers carpeting the ground.
She immediately sat cross-legged with palms joined and recited the title of the *Lotus Sūtra* seven times and chanted the name of Amitābha Buddha more than a hundred times.
She then passed away peacefully, her countenance unchanged. Between the shrine and the table, there was a pervasive fragrance, as if from some extraordinary incense.
Wanyuan Daqing:
His secular surname was Qiao, and he was a native of Changxing. By nature, he was dull-witted; when reviled in his daily life, he did not become angry, and when praised, he felt no joy.
For several decades, he had single-mindedly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha. In the sixth month of the second year of the Kangxi era (1663),...

He was free from illness. Suddenly, he bound himself within a grass hut. A man named Yin Ren, who had long been on friendly terms with the Master, said to him, "Since you have already bound yourself in this hut, I am going to Suzhou to sell tea;
upon my return, I shall provide you with a mat. The Master replied, "I appreciate your generous intention, but I fear I may not wait for you.
On the first day of the ninth month, he suffered a slight ailment and took nothing but plain water. At noon on the sixth day, he himself—
He entered a grass hut and passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. His senior brother, Qiao Zhongwo, had already attained rebirth in the Pure Land;

they were of the same clan. Benchong was the Chan Master of Zhangjiasi Temple in Hangzhou during the Qing dynasty. Benchong had long been dedicated to presiding over the Dharma seat, guiding the ignorant masses.
In the ninth month of the eleventh year of the Kangxi era, he manifested illness. After turning his head back, he regained consciousness after a short while and said to the assembly:
"I have lacked the practice of reciting the Buddha's name in my daily life. Now, as I depart, I have no seat upon which to sit. You all should assist me in reciting the Buddha's name."

The assembly joined their palms and recited [the Buddha's name] together; after some time had passed, he passed away. Observing this, one knows that the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha leads from the mundane to the transcendent, and its benefits are extraordinary.
It is absolutely certain that one must not allow even a moment’s delay. Recorded specifically by the practitioner Baolian.

This serves as a definitive proof. Future students should, with earnestness, suddenly awaken to firm faith and perform the recitation of the truth. Do not regard the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) as something trivial.
[The following are] examples of kings and ministers who attained rebirth.
The King of Ujjayinī, during his leisure from the myriad affairs of state, was deeply devoted to the Buddha-dharma. He once said to his attendants:
"Though I am a king and enjoy blessings and pleasures, I cannot escape impermanence. I have heard that the Pure Land of the West is a place where one may lodge the spirit; I shall [go there]."

He made a vow to seek rebirth in that land. Thereupon, he practiced the Way and meditated on the Buddha during the six periods of the day. Whenever making offerings to the Buddha or providing meals for the Sangha, the King and his consort personally served the food.
He did not cease this practice for thirty years. At the time of his death, his countenance was serene and joyful;
transformation Buddhas came to welcome him, and auspicious omens appeared in great numbers.

The Crown Prince of Song and the Crown Prince of Wei of Song—these three, father and sons, all practiced the Way of the West. Only their wife did not practice it. They had a daughter who died at the age of fourteen;
seven days later, she was reborn. She informed her mother, saying, "I saw the West. Upon a pond made of the seven treasures, my father and two elder brothers were there."

There was already a lotus flower; she who had sunk [into the mire] shall be reborn there. Her mother alone did not possess this [lotus], so the daughter returned for a moment to inform her, saying, "I pray that you, Mother, will take heed.

Moved by her daughter’s words, the mother immediately gave rise to faith and recited the Buddha's name without weariness. Later, when her life ended, she too was reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
Thus it is said.

Liu Yimin (also known as Liu Chengzhi), a military aide from Pengcheng during the Jin dynasty, lost his father while still young and was renowned for his filial devotion to his mother. Confident in his own talent, he refused to conform to worldly customs.

He initially served as a military aide to the provincial administration but soon withdrew into seclusion. Despite the joint recommendations of Xie An and Liu Yu, he did not accept their appointments; thus, they honored him [with the title of "Retired Official"].

He styled himself a "Remnant" (Yimin). He entered Mount Lu and relied upon Master Huiyuan, where they together cultivated the Pure Land and specialized in seated meditation and the practice of visualization.
Within half a year, while in samādhi, he saw the Buddha’s light illuminating the ground, all of which turned the color of gold.

After fifteen years of dwelling in the mountains, he again beheld Amitābha Buddha, his body the color of purple-gold, with the light of his jade-like brow-hair radiating forth as he lowered his hands to receive him.

As he approached his chamber, the surviving people were comforted and fortunate, yet they wept with grief. They said to themselves, "How might the Tathāgata come to rub the crown of our heads and cover us with his robe?
The Buddha then rubbed their crowns and drew his *kāṣāya* over them.

On another day, they saw him again, his body entering a great pool of seven treasures where lotuses of blue and white were interspersed; the water was so clear and deep it was like the boundless ocean.
On the bank was a man with a halo around his neck and a *svastika* on his chest. Pointing to the water in the pond, he said, "This is water of eight virtues;
you may drink from it. Yirmin drank the water, and its sweet flavor filled his mouth. Upon waking, he still perceived a wondrous fragrance emanating from his pores.
He then addressed the assembly, saying, "The karmic conditions for my rebirth in the Pure Land have arrived. Thereupon, the monks of Mount Lu all came to him.
He did so. Yimin faced the Buddha image, burned incense, and prostrated twice, making this vow: "Because of the bequeathed teachings of Śākyamuni, I know that Amitābha Buddha exists.

This incense should first be offered to Tathāgata Śākyamuni, next to Amitābha Buddha, and then to the assembly of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the Lotus Assembly, extending to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions. May it be granted that..."
"May all sentient beings be born together in the Pure Land. Having finished this prayer, he took his leave of the assembly, sat upright facing west, folded his hands, and passed away.
He was fifty-nine years old; it was the sixth year of the Yixi era.

Zhang Kang, a scholar of the Jin dynasty—his given name was Kang—accumulated great merit. He turned toward the Buddha and vowed to recite the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* one hundred thousand times, vowing to be reborn in the Western Land.
When he was over sixty years old and fell ill, he focused his mind single-mindedly on the Buddha. Addressing his family members, he said, "The Pure Land of the West..."

It was located solely within the western wing of the main hall. Amitābha Buddha sat upon a lotus flower, while the old man’s grandson played and paid homage to the Buddha on the golden sand of the lotus pond.
Having finished speaking, he recited the Buddha’s name for a long while and then passed away.
"Old man's son" (*wēng'ér*) is a term for a grandson; he had died at the age of three.

Ma Ziyun, the County Magistrate of the Tang Dynasty, was a candidate for the "Filial and Incorrupt" (Xiaolian) examination. Serving as the County Magistrate of Jing, he was escorting grain taxes to the capital when his boat was lost at sea due to a storm. He was subsequently imprisoned;

thereupon, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. After five years, he encountered a general amnesty and retired to live in seclusion at a mountain temple in Nanling. One day, he said:
A man said, "Throughout my life I have been diligent in reciting the Buddha's name; now my karma for the Western Land is fulfilled, and I shall soon be reborn in An-yang.
The next day, having bathed and put on new clothes, he sat upright with palms joined. A wondrous fragrance filled the room, and he joyfully exclaimed, "The Buddha has come to welcome me!"
Having spoken thus, he passed away.
Bai Juyi, the Junior Tutor of the Tang Dynasty, held the official rank of Zhongdai Fu and Taizi Shaofu. He donated his residence to establish Xiangshan Temple, which was named Xiang...

The layman Shan suffered from wind-paralysis in his later years. He contributed thirty thousand coins of his stipend to commission a painting of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, Adorned with the Primary and Secondary Features.
He followed the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* in every detail, leaving nothing unrepresented. He prostrated himself and made a vow.
He praised it with a verse, saying: "In the Pure Land of the World of Ultimate Bliss, There are no evil realms nor manifold sufferings.
I pray that those like me, aged and infirm, May be reborn together in the presence of Amitāyus Buddha. Furthermore, his previous poem in response to Inspector Li says:
Recently, someone returned from the sea and saw pavilions deep within the ocean mountains. There, a celestial youth opened a chamber and said, "All these are prepared to await the arrival of Li Bai.
I study the Gate of Emptiness and do not seek immortality; I fear your words are but a false report. The ocean mountains are not my place of return;
if I were to return, I would surely return to Tuṣita Heaven. (This poem was composed in his middle years.)

Throughout his life, Le Tian had devoted himself to the study of the inner scriptures (Buddhist texts) and diligently cultivated the Supreme Vehicle (Mahāyāna). With a single-minded resolve, he sought liberation from the cycle of rebirth and rebirth in the Pure Land. At that time, Li Shiji was serving as an Inspector of Zhedong. There was a merchant in Mingzhou, under Li’s jurisdiction, who had set out to sea with a group of others.

They were caught in a storm and drifted until they reached a great mountain adorned with auspicious clouds, wondrous flowers, white cranes, and extraordinary trees—none of which were seen in the human world. A person came from the side of the mountain to greet them and asked, "What kind of people are you that have managed to reach this place?

The merchant explained in detail that they had been blown there by the wind. The man on the shore said, "Since you have arrived at this land, tie your boat fast and come ashore to see the Celestial Master. The other passengers on the same boat were timid and did not dare go up; only [the merchant]...

The merchant followed him up to the bank, where a man led him to a place that resembled a great monastery or temple. The merchant followed this man as he proceeded along the path. There they saw a Daoist whose beard and eyebrows were entirely white, seated upon a great hall with dozens of attendants flanking him on both sides.

He addressed the merchant, saying: "You are originally a person from the Middle Kingdom; it is by karmic affinity that you have reached this land. This mountain is the Mount Penglai spoken of in the secular world.

Now that you have arrived here, would you like to tour the various places? The merchant replied that he wished to see them. The Daoist immediately commanded his attendants to lead him on a tour of the palace grounds. There were jade terraces and verdant trees, their brilliance dazzling to the eye. There was...

There were dozens of courtyards and buildings, many bearing famous names; however, there was only one courtyard that was tightly locked. Peering through a crack in the door, he saw that the entire courtyard was filled with extraordinary flowers.

Inside the hall stood an empty throne, upon which lay cushions and rugs. Below the steps, clouds of incense smoke billowed, striking the nose. A merchant asked, "What place is this? Why is it so empty and locked up? The man replied, "This is the very monastery where Bai Juyi resided in a previous life.

Since Juyi is currently in China and has not yet returned, it remains closed here. The merchant already knew in his heart that Bai Juyi was an honorary title for the Vice Minister Bai. He then described these various sights and scenes in detail.

He made a mental note of it. Taking his leave of that man, he stepped down from the ship and, with the wind filling the sails, arrived at the coast of Yue within ten days. The merchant reported in detail all that he had seen.

Upon learning that this was the domain of Inspector Li, Li Gong recorded everything the man had said and sent a letter to Master Bai. When Master Bai finished reading it, he laughed and said, "I have cultivated the Pure Land practices for many years; the Western Paradise is my own world. Why would I go to mountains beyond the sea to become an immortal?"

Therefore, I offer these two *jueju* (quatrains) in response to Master Li, to demonstrate that the direct path for dedicated cultivation lies within the Chan school; one need no longer seek the immortal isles of Penglai.

Those who discerned this all agreed that Master Bai had cast off the dust of the world and discarded his carriages and robes, possessing a singular and extraordinary spirit and bone—surely he must be a "banished immortal. Yet, if in this life he further applies himself with diligence and directs his single mind toward the West, he will surely transcend the profound gates and proceed directly to the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
this requires no further words. I append this note here as proof of Master Bai’s latent roots from past lives.
Jiang Gongwang, the *Sijian* (Censor-in-Chief), was a native of Diaotai.

He held the office of *Jianyi* (Palace Counselor). He maintained a vegetarian diet and practiced pure cultivation, composing the "Essay on Bodhi" and the "Essay on the Expedient Means of Buddha-Recitation" to exhort both the clergy and the laity.
His son died young, and in a dream he appeared and said: "My lord practices the Way; your meritorious achievements..."

It was already completed. On the golden plaque in the underworld, it was inscribed: "Yan Zhou Prefecture, Jiang Gongwang. Though his station required him to hold office as a censor, his aspirations were set upon the realization of suffering and emptiness.
He personally engaged in cultivation and meditation; his mind was free from attachment. In both movement and stillness, he did not violate the Buddha-dharma;

whether speaking or remaining silent, he always accorded with the spirit of the school. His name has already been liberated from Jambudvīpa; his body shall surely return to the Pure Land. This was at the end of the Xuanhe era. The Prefectural Administrator...
Guangde Army. One day, without prior illness, he sat upright facing west and passed away.
Ge Fan, a Great Officer (Dafu), was a native of Chengjiang.
Having attained the imperial examination at a young age, his official rank reached that of Chao-san. In all public offices and private residences, he invariably...
He established a pure chamber and installed a Buddha image; whenever he entered a room to perform liturgical recitations, śarīra relics would descend from the sky.

In his daily life, he universally exhorted both monastics and laypeople through his pure karma, and many were moved by his transformation. Once, while in meditative concentration, a monk traveled spiritually to the Pure Land and saw Fan there.
Later, without illness, he sat upright facing west and passed away.
Zhang Di, Assistant Instructor.

A native of Qiantang during the Song dynasty, he served as an Assistant Instructor (Jiàozhù). He received the Bodhisattva precepts from Vinaya Master Yuanjing and inquired about the Dharma-gate of Pure Practice (*śubhakarma*).

With resolute devotion, he cultivated these practices and vowed to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). Whenever he practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, he would chant with a loud and courageous voice.
His voice failed him, yet he did not cease his practice. One day, he said to Yuanjing, "In meditative concentration, I saw white kalaviṅka birds dancing and fluttering before me.
After another three years, he sat upright facing west and passed away while reciting the Buddha's name.

Wang Zhonghui, a *sishu* (Assistant Magistrate) under Emperor Song, served as the *Sishu Canjun* (Assistant Magistrate) of Guangzhou. He asked Master Yang, the "Master of Non-Action" (*Wuweizi*), saying:
"The scriptures teach people to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, yet the Patriarch said, 'The mind is the Pure Land; there is no need to seek it elsewhere. How is this so?"
Master Yang replied, "Try to reflect upon this for yourself: if you are already within the realm of the Buddha, there is neither purity nor defilement; what need would there be to seek rebirth?
If you have not yet emerged from the realm of sentient beings, how can you fail to recite the Buddha's name with a sincere heart, forsaking this defiled land to seek rebirth in a pure land?
The Director of Personnel was moved to realization and departed with great joy. Two years later, while Master Yang was serving as the governor of Danyang, he suddenly...
The Dream Officer said: "I previously received your instructions and have now attained rebirth; I have come specifically to express my gratitude. A few days later, the news of his passing arrived.
It was reported that seven days prior, the Officer had foreseen that his time had come; he took leave of his kinsmen and passed away precisely at the moment he had experienced the dream.
Li Bingzhong was an official of the Song dynasty;
he served during the Shaoxing era. He held the post of Director of the Imperial Pharmacy. Initially, he studied Chan under Master Hui of Jingci Monastery and attained a realization.

Later, upon reading the *Longshu Jingtuzhuan* (The Pure Land Text of Longshu), he began to recite the Buddha’s name as his daily practice, serving alongside Yuanmei, the Head of the Pavilion, in the palace halls.
Chang-lin, Shi-wen, and several dozen others held a pure assembly at Chuanfa Temple. Suddenly, Chang-lin fell ill and dreamed that Amitābha Buddha placed a golden circular halo upon his head.
Seven days later, he again saw golden light filling his room;
he then took leave of his relatives, sat upright with his hands in the mudrā of meditation, and passed away.
Hu Yin Xuan-yi of the Song dynasty:
Hu Yin held the office of Xuan-yi. Although he had long believed in the Buddha-vehicle, he was not yet familiar with the Pure Land teachings.
At the age of eighty-four, when his illness became critical, his son invited the Vinaya Master Qingzhao to request his guidance. Qingzhao said to Yin: "You know that..."
Zhao asked, "Is this where you have established your person and settled your life? Dongshan Yunyan replied, "If the mind is pure, then the Buddha-land is pure.
Zhao asked, "Have you yourself, throughout your daily life, ever been defiled by impure thoughts? Yunyan replied, "Since one dwells in the world, how could one possibly be without impure thoughts?
Zhao said, "If that is so, then how can you attain a pure mind and a pure land? Yunyan replied, "By reciting the name of the Buddha once, how can it not extinguish [them]?"

Regarding the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas, [Vimalakīrti] said: "Amitābha Buddha, through his great vows and cultivation over kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, possesses vast majesty and virtue;
his radiance and spiritual power are inconceivable. Therefore, by reciting his name even once,"
It extinguishes immeasurable sins, just as the blazing sun melts frost and snow; how could there be any further doubt?
Zhaoyin then attained realization and that very day invited monks to recite the Buddha’s name. On the following day, Zhao arrived again. Zhaoyin said, "Why have you come so late?
The two Great Beings have already descended. Thereupon Zhao led the assembly and recited the Buddha’s name with a resolute voice. Zhaoyin then joined his palms and passed away.
Wen Yanbo, Duke of Lu (Song Wenlu Gong):
His name was Yanbo. Throughout his life, he pursued the Way with great diligence, single-mindedly reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha and vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land.
He burned incense at dawn and sat in meditation at night, never neglecting these practices for even a moment. He would frequently make this vow: "May I always remain diligent."
Diligently cultivating all virtues, I vow to realize the essence of the mind and widely deliver all sentient beings.
Whenever I see anyone, I urge them to practice the recitation of the Buddha's name. In the capital, I gathered with the Dharma Master Jingyan ten thousand people for a Pure Land assembly.
The Layman Ruru composed a verse in praise, saying: "I know your courage is as vast as heaven; I vow to form a bond with the Western Paradise."
With a hundred thousand karmic conditions, they do not make a living for themselves alone; everyone together boards the ferry at the crossing.
At the moment of death, they pass away peacefully, reciting the Buddha’s name.
Regarding Minister Ma Xu of the Song dynasty:
when his ancestor, the Duke Zhongsu, was governing Hangzhou, he instructed the Abbot of Ciyun Monastery to lead the family in the practice of Buddha-recitation.

The entire household followed this with devotion. Xu himself recited the Buddha’s name with a sincere heart for twenty-five years. During a minor illness in the Chongning era, he changed his clothes, sat upright, and passed away.
A vapor like a blue parasol emerged from his door, ascended into the air, and departed. All the members of his household dreamed that Xu had been reborn in the Upper Grade.

When Zhongli Shaoshi (Zhongli Jin of the Song dynasty) was serving as the Judicial Commissioner of Zhexi, he encountered the Master of Repentance Ciyun; consequently, he came to place profound faith in the Pure Land. Later...
He was appointed Governor of Kaifeng. When he went out, he exhausted himself in the affairs of state; when he returned home, he would not sleep, reciting the Buddha’s name.

On the night of his passing, he urged his family members to rise, seek a bath, and change his clothes. He then sat upright and passed away. The entire family saw that Jing was riding upon a blue lotus, being welcomed and led westward by celestial music.
The Court Gentleman Yan Bangrong was a native of Chizhou.
For twenty years he had maintained the practice of reciting the *Nianfo* (Buddha-remembrance) and the *Wangsheng zhou* (Rebirth Mantra).

As his end approached, his family members dreamed that the Buddha emitted light to welcome Bangrong. At dawn, Bangrong sat cross-legged facing west; suddenly, he rose and walked several paces before standing upright and passing away.
Wang Zhongchao, Prince of Song, was a native of Jiahe.
He established a religious society on West Lake and invited anyone who wished to be reborn in the Pure Land to join, regardless of whether they were wise or foolish, noble or humble, monastic or lay.
He composed a "Treatise on Encouraging Practice" that circulated throughout the world. Later, he passed away peacefully while seated facing west, free from illness.
Zhongli Jingrong, Grand Master of the Song Dynasty:
Zhongli Jingrong held the official rank of Chaoqing Dafu. He constantly recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* and never ceased his mindfulness of the Buddha. He subsequently resigned from office.
He thatched a hut beside the East Garden in Yizhen. He once said, "If you do not recognize Amitābha, Amitābha remains beyond the Western Pure Land;
if you recognize Amitābha, Amitābha is simply within your own home. One night, he instructed the monk Miaoying to recite the *Bhadracari-praṇidhāna*.
He lit incense and listened with reverence, and while forming mudrās with both hands, he passed away.

Qian Xiangzu, Prefect of the Commandery during the Song Dynasty, styled Zhian (Cottage of Cessation). While serving as the governor of Jinling, he took the true cultivation of the Pure Land as his constant contemplation.
He frequently established ten reception centers throughout his home region and prefecture, all of which were named after the Pure Land and Sukhāvatī. He founded the Zhian Gao... [text fragment].

The Monks’ Quarters (*sengliao*). This was a place for inviting monks to discuss the Way. Since the Left Prime Minister retired from office, he had increasingly advanced in his pure practices (*śukla-karma*).
In the second month of the fourth year of the Jiading era, he fell slightly ill. He wrote a verse, saying: "The fragrance of the lotus comes from the Buddha-land;

Upon the ground of lapis lazuli, not even a speck of dust remains. My mind is pure and transcends that realm; Today, I know from afar that one flower has blossomed. Three days later, [he passed away].
When a monk came to inquire after his health, the Duke said, "I do not crave life, nor do I fear death. I shall not be reborn as a deva, nor as a human;
I seek only birth in the Land of Purity. Having spoken these words, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
Later, someone dreamed that a voice from the sky proclaimed, "Prime Minister Qian has already been born in the Lotus Palace of the Western Paradise as the Bodhisattva Ciji (Compassionate Aid)."
Xianling Mei Ruren was a native of Changshu who served as a county magistrate. He was devoted to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.
One night, he suddenly dreamed that a monk gave him a hundred sheets of paper, which he tore into sixteen pieces. He asked Master Dong Lingzhao about this, who replied, "Two eights make sixteen."
Could this not be what is meant by the *Sixteen Contemplations Sutra*? One day, a monk gave him a copy of the sutra, but it suddenly vanished.
From then on, he recited the sutra and practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, considering himself destined for rebirth in the Pure Land as his primary aspiration.

Later, when Master Zhong of the district commissioned a sixteen-foot statue of Amitābha, he contributed one million coins to have it adorned. Suddenly, a pair of [lotuses] emerged from the pond in front of the hall.
His hair turned white like a lotus flower. Its petals numbered one hundred. In the winter of that year, he passed away without illness.
Zan Dingguo, styled Shengzhai, served as a lecturer at the prefectural school. He constantly recited the Buddha’s name and read various sutras concerning the Pure Land. Every...

On the eighth and thirteenth days of every month, he gathered monks and laypeople to chant sutras and recite the Buddha’s name. In the fourth year of the Jiading era, he dreamed of a youth in blue robes who told him, "The Buddha has summoned you;
on the third day from now, you shall be reborn in that land. On that day, he bathed, changed his clothes, and while reciting the Buddha’s name, he passed away while seated.
Counselor-in-Waiting Feng Jichuan was surnamed Feng and styled Jichuan;

he was a native of Suining. Having passed the examinations at the Imperial Academy, he initially sought the Way within the Zen forests, but in his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the Pure Land practice.

He composed the *Xifangwen* (Text for the Western Quarter) and the *Mituo Chan yi* (Ritual for the Repentance of Amitābha). Later, he served as a Reminder (*Ji shi zhong*) and was subsequently appointed as a Regional Commander (*Shuai*).

In Lunnan, he led both monastics and laypeople in holding a "Concentration of Mind" assembly (*xièniàn huì*). Later, while serving as the Governor of Qiong Prefecture, he arranged a high seat in the rear hall;

facing the imperial palace, he performed a solemn prostration. Donning his monastic robes, he ascended the seat to thank the officials. Then, leaning his staff across his lap and resting his hands upon his knees, he passed away.
Minzhong Wang Gu, courtesy name Minzhong, was a native of Dongdu.

He served as the Minister of Rites (Libu Shilang). Compassionate and benevolent toward all living beings, he was deeply attuned to the Chan school and further realized the excellence of the Pure Land dharma-gate.
He composed the *Direct Pointing to the Pure Land: A Collection for Resolving Doubts* in three fascicles.

Throughout his life, he was diligent in the practice of Buddha-recitation (*nienfo*). His prayer beads never left his hand, and whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he performed all his religious duties through the pure contemplation of the Western Paradise.
When a monk traveled spiritually to the Pure Land, he saw Gu and Ge Fan there together;
thus, his rebirth was clearly verified.

Scholar Su Shi of the Song dynasty, styled Dongpo, served as a Hanlin Academician. During his banishment to the south, he painted a single scroll of Amitābha Buddha and wore it with him wherever he went.
When people asked about it, he replied, "This is my official passport for rebirth in the Western Paradise. His mother, the Lady... [text ends]

After Lady Cheng passed away, her surviving assets—her hairpins and earrings—were used to commission the artisan Hu Xi to paint an image of Amitābha, in order to dedicate the merit for her rebirth in the Pure Land.

She then offered this hymn: "The Buddha, with his Great Perfect Enlightenment, fills worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Yet I, through inverted thoughts, am born and die within the cycle of birth and death.
How can I, by means of a single thought-moment, attain rebirth in the Pure Land? I have created karma since beginningless time; its root..."

They arise from a single thought; having arisen from a single thought, they likewise perish within a single thought. At the place where arising and perishing are utterly extinguished, I and the Buddha are one and the same.
Like water cast into the sea, like air blown through a bellows, even with the great wisdom of a Sage, one cannot distinguish them.
May my former parents, wherever they may be, find the West as their realm, and may all whom they encounter dwell in Ultimate Bliss. People—
"Human beings have immeasurable life; they lack inherent nature and there is no coming.

This was written by Chancellor Zhang Wujin (Zhang Shangying) of the Song dynasty. Initially inspired by his wife, Lady Xiang, he applied his mind to the Inner Canon and took the monastic name Wujin (Inexhaustible). He resided at [the monastery].

The Master once composed a *Pranidhāna* (Vow Text) which says: "Reflecting upon this world, where the five turbidities disturb the mind, one lacks the power of right contemplation and the power of the cause of realization.

Since the nature of reality is but mind, one cannot awaken to it. I respectfully follow the golden-mouthed teachings of Śākyamuni Bhagavān, single-mindedly reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha and seeking the compassionate reception of that World-Honored One’s vow-power. When my retribution is fulfilled, I shall go..."
To be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is like riding a boat downstream; one arrives without the exertion of personal effort.

Wei Wenjin, the Surveillance Commissioner of Song, established his conduct in solitary purity and founded a Pure Land practice hall to universally deliver all sentient beings. On the [day] of the sixth month...
One day, he suddenly sat cross-legged facing west with palms joined, recited the Buddha’s name, and passed away. A wondrous fragrance was perceived both inside and outside [the room].
Jia Chunren, the District Magistrate of Song, was a native of Xiachuan;
he served as the Vice Governor of Yingzhou. He devoted his heart to the Pure Land practice and maintained a lifelong fast while reciting the Buddha’s name. Because of this—

Suffering from a slight illness, he sat in meditation facing west and passed away. A circular halo of white light appeared above his crown, and an extraordinary fragrance filled the room, lingering for a night without dispersing.
(Recorded by the Jinshi degree-holder Wu Xinsou.)
Wu Zicai of the Song dynasty, whose courtesy name was Xinsou, after retiring from official service, had a coffin prepared in advance.
He would lie within it at night and have a youth strike upon the coffin while singing: "Wu Xinsou, go back! Go back! There is no peace in the three realms; there is nowhere to dwell."
"In the Pure Land of the West there are lotus wombs; turn back and return home as early as possible. He himself then joined in with these words.
When his conditions were ripe, he passed away without illness.
Du-xuan Zhang Lun (Song dynasty).
He served as the Regional Commander-in-Chief of the Two Zhejiang Provinces. He vowed to be reborn in the Pure Land and was diligent and self-urging in his recitation of the Buddha’s name.

His entire family embraced the realization of the illusory nature of existence, and none failed to follow his transformation. He excavated a pond and planted lotuses; every day he led his wife and children to recite the Buddha’s name ten thousand times. Emperor Xiaozong...
The Emperor personally inscribed the two characters "Lotus Society" (Lian-she) and bestowed them upon him.

Zhu Gang, the Junior Minister of Works, was a native of the capital who studied Confucianism. Having passed the provincial examination, he attempted the imperial examinations three times without success; he subsequently took up his official post.

He served in two government offices before retiring from his post to devote himself exclusively to the Pure Land practice. He recited the Buddha’s name thirty thousand times daily for fifteen years without the slightest negligence or weariness.

At the time of his death, while sitting upon his bed, he held a rosary in both hands and continued chanting the Buddha’s name without ceasing. A wondrous fragrance filled the room, and he said, "The Buddha is coming.
He passed away while repeatedly invoking the Buddha’s name with a continuous voice.

Dai Baixu Ming was the hereditary holder of the Baixu (Hundred-Household) rank. He served as a front-line guard and assisted Tao Baixu in administrative affairs under the jurisdiction of the Provincial Governor’s headquarters.
At that time, there was a notorious murderer and great thief on the Qiantang River known as Manjianghong; his faction was powerful and flourishing, and local officials...
They did not dare to arrest him. The Provincial Governor secretly summoned the two men and handed each of them a warrant, instructing them:
"I have a secret and urgent matter for you two to handle. If you cannot accomplish it, you shall come to see me carrying coffins. Having finished speaking, he withdrew and entered his inner office.
The two men unfolded the warrants and looked at them; they were warrants for the arrest of Man Jiang Hong. Facing one another, they had no strategy left and resolved to risk their lives.

He entered the bandits' den, employing various means to lure them out, and immediately executed them according to the law. As he faced the execution on the banks of the Manjiang River, he harbored deep resentment toward the two men, vowing to exact their lives in retribution.
The two men were terrified; they resigned their posts, observed the precepts, recited sutras and the Buddha’s name, and performed many acts of merit to resolve this karmic grievance.
Although the two practiced in different locations, they simultaneously turned back toward the truth. Dai Baibu [was thus saved].

He bid farewell to his relatives and, when the appointed time arrived, sat down and passed away. After a long while, he revived and said to his relatives, "Brother Tao, at the critical moment, my mindfulness faltered and I took a wrong path;
therefore, I have come to inform you all. Tomorrow, I shall depart. The following morning, he again sat down and passed away.
His nose hung down like a jade pillar, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room without dispersing.
Jinguang was the son of a former official of the Daqing period. He was a member of the Zhenghuang Banner and rose from the ranks of the military; he was illiterate.

Nevertheless, whenever he encountered a matter of righteousness, he would invariably apply himself with keen resolve. His wife, Lady Gong, was said to be the daughter of a filial and incorrupt scholar from Luzhou.

She was the daughter of a noble family who suffered greatly during the upheavals of war and turned her heart toward the Western Paradise. Having acquired a rudimentary knowledge of books and history, she would recite Buddhist scriptures morning and night whenever she encountered them;

even those of former times were moved by her light, and she maintained a profound faith. In the winter of the *Guisi* year of the Shunzhi era, while serving in the campaign against the rebellious, she traveled to Min with her husband.
On their way, they passed through Wulin and heard that the Venerable Juede was preaching the Dharma at Lingyin Temple.

They went together to pay their respects and personally received his instructions. From that time on, they devoted themselves to the practice of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name), becoming increasingly earnest and steadfast.
In the summer of the *Xinchou* year, he returned to the capital and stayed by the banks of the Qiantang River. Suddenly, Jin fell ill;

Gong summoned a physician, but Guangqian stopped him, saying, "In the past, you and I visited Lingyin Temple together in person; now I wish precisely to perform my 'turning-over' (*zuoshen*) right here."
"I merely sought for my preceptor one witness; why would I need medicine? Gong laughed loudly and said, "I did not expect that even Guangqian would reach such a state.
He then moved his tent into Chongsheng Hermitage, desiring that she might die where she belonged.
After staying in the hermitage for ten days, Gong had two coffins made and said to those around him, "I and Master Jin shall depart together. Looking back...
"There is no one to complete the Master's final affairs. Once the rites are concluded, I shall depart. When Guangqian heard this, he immediately passed away with a serene expression.

Gong then wrote a letter to Lingyin Monastery, requesting that they provide the torches for both men and further entrusting them with matters such as providing meals for monks and performing repentance rituals.
Upon reaching the seventh day, he ceased all food and drink, remained awake day and night, and focused his mind single-mindedly on the Buddha’s name.

Many female companions came to urge her to desist, but she remained firm and would not listen. Again, on the evening of the seventh day, she observed the position of the sun to determine whether it was morning or evening;
feeling her body slightly weary, she leaned against the coffin and dozed. After a short while, she awoke and said, "The time has come.

She then passed into stillness with dignified composure, her countenance appearing as if alive. As for the sharpness of her courage and agility, even the woman of the Pang family could not surpass her. Master Guifeng said:
To perform deeds of meaning is the awakened mind; to perform deeds of meaninglessness is the deluded mind.

The deluded mind revolves according to emotions, and at the moment of death, one is dragged away by karma. The awakened mind does not follow emotions, and at the moment of death, it can transform karma.
Is this not what is meant by "Guangqian"? When Master Lingyin offered the funeral pyre for Guangqian, he said: "When a person is in the perilous instability of birth and death..."
The Master was sovereign over life and death. This very sovereignty is the handle for becoming a Buddha or a Patriarch.
All people of the world gaze up at him with reverence; after a thousand years, he shall remain as a fine legend at Chongsheng Hermitage.
Furthermore, he performed the cremation for the Gong family, saying: "While the world is entangled by emotional attachments, you alone have decisively severed the bonds of birth and death."

To cast off this body as if discarding worn-out sandals; to fix the date of one’s return as if recording it on a formal contract—such a virtuous woman is truly diligent, truly making a Dharma-offering, and is the foremost among those of great practice and great vows at the assembly on Vulture Peak.
Master Lianchi said: "I have heard the ancient virtuous ones say that among the scholar-officials, those whose brilliance and acuity surpass others mostly come from the ranks of the monastics.
Yet, nineteen out of twenty are deluded and do not return [to the path], while only eleven do not obscure their past causes.
What is the reason for this? In this world of five turbidities, there are many conditions for regression; even the worthy cannot avoid them. Therefore, Master Jie..."
The later incarnation of [Master] Qing became Dongpo; the later incarnation of Master Zeng became Duke Zeng.

Master Zhe’s later incarnation was deeply attached to wealth and status, yet suffered much anxiety and pain. Among them, Dongpo was the most intimately connected to the Dharma gate, whereas Duke Zeng could not even compare to him.
As for the later incarnation of Old Master Zhe, his delusion and suppression were even more extreme. This is why the wise of past and present exhort people [to practice].
