They abandoned the five turbidities to seek the Pure Land. Thus, what the various gentlemen, beginning with Liu Yimin, have attained is already considerable.
They belong to the class of recluses who attained rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Zhang Ye, a man of eminent talent during the Jin dynasty, resided in Xunyang.

He was proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit literature and was particularly skilled in literary composition. Having been nominated as a "Man of Eminent Talent" (Mocaicai), he was repeatedly summoned to serve as an Attendant Cavalier (Sanqichangshi), but declined both appointments.
He entered Mount Lu to join the Lotus Society (Lianshe) and cultivated the practices of Pure Land Buddhism. In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, together with...
He bid farewell to his family, entered his room, sat upright, and passed away.
Que Gongze—Que Gongze of Jin—was a member of Master Huiyuan’s White Lotus Society; he had already passed away. His friend [resided] at the White Horse Temple in Dongjing.
At the temple, while performing a memorial service for him, the forest trees and the temple buildings suddenly turned entirely golden. A voice from the air said, "I am Gye Gongjeok.
I have now reached the precious land of Ultimate Bliss, the place to which I prayed to be reborn; therefore, I have come to inform you.
Having spoken these words, he vanished.

Zhang Jian of Jin was a descendant of Zhang Ye. He was lofty and reclusive, yet fond of learning; even amidst his plowing and weeding, he never laid down his scroll. Although summoned repeatedly for office, he did not accept.
Yu Yue, noting his poverty, recommended him for the post of Magistrate of Xunyang. Zhang laughed and said, "The ancients [sought only] enough space to rest their knees..."

For the sake of peace, he humbled his aspirations to accept a stipend; what glory was there in this? He subsequently entered Mount Lu and relied upon Master Huiyuan’s Lotus Society, where he investigated the inner scriptures (Buddhist texts) with great depth, attaining numerous insights and realizations.
In the first year of the Jingping era of the Song dynasty, without any illness, he faced westward to recite the Buddha's name and passed away while sitting upright.
Zhou Xuzhi of the Song dynasty was a native of Yanmen. At the age of twelve, he had mastered the Five Classics and the Five Supplements (Wuweī), earning him the title "The Ten Classics Boy.

He cultivated his mind in seclusion; though high officials repeatedly offered him invitations, he declined them all. He served under Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu and joined the Lotus Society. [End of] Text.

When the Emperor ascended the throne, he summoned [him] for an audience and engaged him in debate; the Emperor was greatly pleased. Someone asked, "It is said that one who serves as a retired scholar (chushi) should not frequent the royal court.
Is this permissible? He replied, "For those whose hearts race toward the imperial palace (Wei-que), the rivers and lakes are but shackles. For those whose emotions have transcended both extremes—"

The marketplace and the court were, for him, no different from mountain caves. He was known in his time as Master Tongyin (the Recluse of Penetration). Later, he resided on Mount Zhong, where he devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name;
as he grew older, his practice became increasingly earnest. One day, facing the sky, he said, "The Buddha has come to welcome me," and with palms joined, he passed away.

Yu Xian (of the Liang dynasty). A native of Xinye, he was summoned by Emperor Wu to serve as a Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gate, but he did not go. Six times a day he recited the name of the Buddha.
One night he saw a practitioner who called himself Master Yuan and addressed Yu Xian as "Master Shangxing. He bestowed a fragrant incense upon him and departed.

Four years later, he wished to return once more, but then passed away through transformation. A voice spoke from the air, saying: "Master Shangxing has already been reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
Gao Haoxiang of Liang was a native of Dongping. He lived in seclusion, sitting in quietude, and devoted himself exclusively to reciting the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. He once stayed at Guan...
In the midst [of her dream], she perceived herself floating upon a red lotus on the surface of a pond. At first, she did not see the Buddha;

she then immediately bowed her heart in worship toward the Buddha atop the flower, gazing afar at his golden countenance, its radiance shining from a distance. One night, she saw a multitude of bodhisattvas coming to welcome her, and she instantly transformed away.
Song Man of the Sui dynasty was a native of Changzhou. He calculated his beans and recited the Buddha’s name, accumulating thirty *shí* of them.

In the ninth month of the eighth year of the Kaihuang era, after providing a meal for the monastic community, he sat in meditation and passed away. People saw celestial flowers and extraordinary fragrances filling the air as he ascended into the void and departed toward the west.

Zheng Muqing of Tang was a native of Xingyang. His entire family recited the Buddha’s name. During the Kaiyuan era, when he was critically ill, someone urged him to consume fish and meat, but he resolutely refused.
Holding a censer in his hand, he vowed to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. Suddenly, a wondrous fragrance filled the air, and in an instant—
However, as he was passing away, his uncle, the Minister of State Su Ting, dreamed that lotuses were blooming in a jeweled pond and that the Prefectural Governor was sitting upon them.

As for Zhang Yuanxiang of the Tang dynasty—Zhang Yuanxiang lived constantly reciting the Buddha’s name without ceasing. One day, he summoned his family members and said, "The Sage of the Western Land..."
"Wait for me until my meal is finished, and we shall go together. When the meal was concluded, he burned incense, sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), and passed away facing west.
Yuanzicai of Tang lived at Guanyin Temple in Runzhou; he recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* and practiced the mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*). Suddenly, he fell slightly ill. One night...
He heard the fragrance of incense and the sound of music in the air, as if someone were saying, "The coarse pleasures have passed; subtle pleasures follow in succession.
You should now depart. He passed away while recollecting the Buddha, and a rare fragrance did not dissipate for several days.
Later, Yuanziping of the same monastery also heard musical sounds in the air and immediately sat facing west to pass away.

Li Zhiyao of the Tang dynasty was a native of Chang’an. He was skilled in the teachings of the Pure Land and practiced the *wuhui nianfo* (five-assembly recitation of the Buddha), serving as a model for the masses.

Later, due to illness, he suddenly said, “The Buddha has come to welcome me. He washed himself, changed his clothes, requested an incense burner, and went out of the hall to prostrate in worship. Then—
A voice from the air was heard reciting a verse: "I announce to you, Li Zhiyao: your merit has borne fruit and you have summoned this result yourself.
I shall lead you to be born in the Pure Land and carry you across the Golden Bridge. Thereupon, he sat upright upon his bed and passed away; the assembly smelled a wondrous fragrance.
The Elder of Fenyang lived during the Tang dynasty.
At Mount Farin, he borrowed an empty room for his lodging and recited the Buddha’s name day and night.

In the fifth year of the Zhenguan era, when his life came to an end, a great light shone everywhere; facing west, he passed away. People saw him ascending upon a lotus pedestal, saying: "He has gone."

Fang Zhu of the Tang dynasty died suddenly. He arrived at the Underworld and saw King Yama. The King said, "According to the records on this desk, you once exhorted an elderly man to recite the Buddha’s name;
he has already been reborn in the Pure Land. By virtue of this merit, you too ought to be reborn there. Fang Zhu said:
Previously, he had promised ten thousand copies of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and intended to tour Mount Wutai rather than seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.

The King said, "While touring the mountains and reciting the sutras are certainly virtuous deeds, they are not as good as being reborn in the Pure Land early. Knowing that his resolve could not be swayed, the King released him to return home.
From this we know that those who exhort others to practice do so not merely for the sake of rebirth, but also to move the spirits of the netherworld.
Sun Liangsong was a native of Qiantang. He lived in seclusion and studied the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*), attaining a profound mastery of the essential principles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Following the Vinaya Master Dazhi, he received the Bodhisattva precepts. Every day he recited the Buddha’s name ten thousand times, never ceasing for twenty years. One day, he suddenly summoned his family...

The person requested the monks to recite the Buddha’s name to assist him in his rebirth. After the assembly of monks had been reciting for about half a meal-time, he joined his palms toward the sky and said, "Buddha and Bodhisattvas, you have already graciously descended. He then withdrew his seat and passed away.

Wang Tian (also known as Song Wangtian) was a native of Siming, who styled himself the "Old Man of No Merit" (Wugong Sǒu). He possessed profound mastery of all the fundamental tenets of the Chan school and the teachings of the Tiantai school.

He authored the *Jìngtǔ Zìxìn Lù* (Record of Self-Confidence in the Pure Land). In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Buddha-recitation; facing west, he passed away in a state of spiritual transformation. This was extraordinary.
The fragrance was rich and pervasive. When the shrine was cremated, one hundred and eight grains of *śarīra*, each the size of a soybean, were obtained.
Fan Yan of the Song dynasty was a native of Renhe. He had severed his ties to worldly affairs; when his son could not manage the household, Yan paid him no heed.
He simply said, "I am merely a guest here. Daily he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and meditated on Amitābha Buddha with single-minded devotion and without slackening.
Suddenly, he saw Samantabhadra Bodhisattva riding a six-tusked white elephant, emitting golden light, who told Yan:
"Tomorrow at the hour of the Rabbit (卯), you shall depart. After one night had passed, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas came to welcome him; he sat upright, joined his palms, and passed away.
Lu Yuandao of the Song dynasty, styled the Layman Sheng’an, resided at Hengxi in Mingzhou. Rising at dawn, he would burn incense and sit in meditation with his eyes fixed, never glancing elsewhere.
He first composed a verse, which began: "Washing my hands at early dawn, the *palm-leaf* scriptures unfold; I seek no worldly blessings..."

To avert calamities, he severed his worldly ties through others. He performed a single dance amidst the flames of the kalpa-ending fire, and thereafter recited mantras, neither too slowly nor too hurriedly, with a voice like a string of pearls.
Every day he completed one recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and ten thousand invocations of Amitābha, directing his mind single-mindedly toward the West.
On the sixth day of the fourth month at the age of eighty-five, he bathed, adjusted his robes, and passed away. Upon his enshrouding, a sudden sound was heard.
The fragrant scent of lotuses was such that no one knew its source. Upon approaching to inhale it, they found it was indeed emanating from his mouth.
Sun Zhong, known as the "Twelfth Young Master Sun," was a native of Siming. Having long admired the Western Paradise, he constructed a hermitage to the east of the prefectural city.

He practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Later, falling ill, he invited one hundred monks to focus their mindfulness upon him. Suddenly, he looked toward the sky with palms joined, his hands forming a dual mudrā, and passed away with a serene expression.

The entire city heard celestial music and a wondrous fragrance, which gradually faded as they vanished toward the west. His two sons followed in succession by practicing the recitation of the Buddha’s name and likewise passed away while seated in meditation.
Shen Quan of the Song dynasty was a native of Qiantang. Together with his wife, Shi, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the Pure Land. He dedicated all his ordinary acts of merit toward this goal.
Later, when both husband and wife passed away, they were each moved by the appearance of a transformation Buddha holding a monk’s staff, who came to welcome and lead them away.
Tang Shiliang of the Song dynasty was a native of Kuaiji. He maintained the precepts and recited the Buddha’s name. Though he was old and afflicted by illness, he would not yet lie upon his pillow.
Having recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* one hundred thousand times, he said to his family members, "The Buddha has come to receive me. Having finished speaking, he prostrated himself and immediately—

He passed away while seated. At that time, the practitioner Li Xingren was at Mount Daowei. During the night, he dreamed of extraordinary light from the west, along with banners, flowers, and celestial music.
A voice in the air proclaimed: "Tang Shi-liang has already returned to the Pure Land."
Ji Gong and Song Ji Gong were both ironworkers from Taoyuan in Siming. At the age of seventy, both had lost their sight.

A local school inspector named Zan distributed "block-print" charts to encourage people to recite the Buddha’s name. When Ji Gong first received one of these charts, he completed the full count of recitations.

He recited the name thirty-six thousand times until he reached the fourth diagram, at which point his two eyes became clear and bright. He continued in this manner for three years, completing seventeen diagrams in total.

One day, while reciting the Buddha’s name, he suddenly passed away. After half a day, he revived and said: "The Buddha has ordered that one diagram be divided and given to the Imperial Instructor Zan;
he was the foremost in providing exhortation. Another diagram is to be divided and given to the two gentlemen Li; they were the ones who distributed the diagrams."
He entrusted his son with the task of going to offer thanks. Having finished speaking, he bathed, turned toward the west, and passed away.
Shen Sanlang (the Song Dynasty Shen Sanlang) turned his heart toward the Buddha in his later years; when he fell ill, he invited a monk to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* for him as he changed his robes.
He passed away. As he drew up his knees and attempted to rise, his two sons—constrained by the formalities of the Name-and-Teaching (míngjiào)—deemed it difficult to move the coffin.

They dragged his legs to straighten him. Just as they were about to place him in the shroud, he suddenly raised his head and emerged from the coverings; he sat up alertly. The entire family was greatly alarmed.

His two sons hurried forward to support and guard him, but he struck them with his elbows and knees. His sons said, "We were merely assisting our father to sit and depart," and in the end, he remained seated.
He passed away. His body was cremated, whereupon twenty-nine white cranes flew and cried out in the clouds; after a long while, they departed toward the west.

Lu Jun (also known as Song Lu Jun) was a native of Qiantang. In his youth, he served at the imperial court, but after a time, he abandoned that life to devote himself to the practice of the Pure Land. Every...
He repented before the Buddha, tears falling down to his chin. When he met with his dharma friends, they spoke of the causes and conditions for the Pure Land;
after only ten or so sentences, he was overcome with grief and sighed deeply. At the time of his death, he requested Vinaya Master Yuanjing to instruct him regarding the Western Paradise.

As they recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* up to the section on the Highest Grade, Yuanjing said, "You may go. Zongjun replied, "The assembly of holy ones has not yet gathered; let us wait for a moment. After a short while...
Suddenly he rose, went to his bamboo bed, sat upright facing west, and passed away.
Regarding Xu Liugong:
Xu Liugong of the Song dynasty was a native of Jiaxing. He made his living by farming; husband and wife lived on a vegetarian diet and were diligent in the practice of Buddha-recitation.
At forty years of age, he prepared a funerary niche in advance. As his end approached, he changed into coarse cloth robes and grass sandals, entered the niche, and sat upright.
After a short while, he said, "The Buddha has come to welcome me," and immediately passed away.

Whenever he worked with tongs and hammer, he would recite the Buddha’s name without ceasing. He said, "Steel has been forged; peace is near. I am going to the Western Land," and he immediately passed away. This verse spread widely throughout Hunan, leading many people to recite the Buddha’s name.
What a marvelous trace!

Originally named He TANJI, he was eighteen years old when he observed the Bodhisattva precepts and practiced mindfulness of the Buddha. At the fourth watch of one night, he rose immediately to recite the Buddha’s name.
Others said it was too early, but he replied, "I see the golden form of the Buddha coming to welcome me with banners and flowers," whereupon he passed away.
Wu Zizhangyuan was a native of Suzhou. His family had practiced medicine for generations. Together with his elder brother’s son, Zicai, he studied under Master Yunwu.

He was diligent in the practice of Buddha-recitation, and his entire household followed the Dharma. During the Zhizheng era, he passed away without illness, passing into nirvana while joining his palms and reciting the name of the Buddha.
The Layman Hua, Minghua, was a man from the banks of the Yangtze River. He was honest, simple, and without pretension; he did not engage in elaborate social courtesies with others.

In his middle years, he entrusted his affairs to his sons and lived alone in a single room, avoiding all worldly matters. Morning and evening, he did nothing but diligently recite the Buddha’s name. Later...

When his end drew near, the Master knew the time had come. He changed his robes, retired to his main chamber, adjusted his crown with his own hands, and sat upright to bid farewell to the assembly before passing away.
His son had already prepared a coffin; they then replaced the reliquary shrine (kaṅ) according to the established rites for śramaṇas.
On the day the shrine was carried forth, spectators lined the streets like a wall, and people from far and near looked toward him with deep admiration.
Regarding Renhua Taigongming:
Renhua Taigong was a man from Yue who throughout his life was simple and unrefined. He spent his days and nights reciting the Buddha’s name without ceasing.
After his death, a single branch of a lotus flower suddenly sprouted upon his coffin. His relatives were filled with wonder and admiration, and for this reason he was called "Lotus Taigong."
The Master said:
"The layman Gu Minggu Yuan was a native of Jinling. He styled himself Layman Baocang. In his youth, he was able to compose poetry and was skilled in cursive calligraphy. In his middle years..."

He was single-mindedly devoted to pure karma. Later, when he was slightly ill, he gathered his monastic and lay dharma-friends to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times, chanting in unison and continuously.
He said to those present, "I shall certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

When asked why, he replied, "I see Amitābha Buddha, his body filling the void of space and the world turning golden. The Buddha has covered me with his *kāṣāya*, and my body is already seated [upon the lotus throne]."
Within the lotus, at that time, the entire assembly smelled the fragrance of the lotus. The sons grieved and longed for him incessantly.
The layman said, "Where do you think I have gone? Where else could it be but right here? If this place is clear, how could any other place not be so?

Then, setting aside the others, he said, "Say no more, lest it disturb my mind. The Buddhas of the ten directions are welcoming me; I shall depart at the third watch. When the appointed time arrived...
He passed away with a serene expression and a smile on his face.
Guo Dalin (d.

537) was a native of Tangyin. Throughout his life, he was upright, pure, elegant, and simple; his heart was set on transcending the mundane world. Whenever he encountered monks, he would instruct them.

Practicing mindfulness of the Buddha, he eventually became single-mindedly devoted to the Pure Land. At the age of seventy-six, one day, being free from illness, he bid farewell to his son, saying, "I shall depart at noon tomorrow.
When the time arrived, he sat upright and passed away.

The Elder of the Sugar Cart was Ming Tangdan (Bright Sugar-Cart). He lived within the Genshan Gate in Hangzhou City. He made his living by selling sugar as usual, while constantly reciting the Buddha’s name without ceasing.
One day, he went out carrying his sugar cart; whenever he saw someone, he would say, "Eat my [sugar] early!"
"Sugar. I shall now return home. I will visit several more houses of my acquaintances and say to them: 'Please trouble yourselves to come tomorrow to help me carry my coffin;
I wish to return home. Those who knew him were astonished, feeling both belief and doubt.
The next morning, he said to his wife: 'Prepare wine and food to await those coming. At the appointed hour, the acquaintances all arrived, and the old man led them to carry [the coffin]."

The coffin was prepared. Upon arriving home, he bathed, changed his robes, and stood with hands clasped before him. He addressed the assembly, saying, "I shall sleep within this coffin by myself; do not trouble yourselves.
He sat down inside the coffin and settled into sleep with a serene expression, whereupon he passed away forever. The assembly was filled with wonder and amazement.

Liu Tongzhi’s Biography. Liu Tongzhi was a native of the capital. He was diligent and sincere in his recitation of the Buddha’s name. At the age of fifty-two, he fell ill; his mindfulness grew increasingly intense.
His neighbor Li Buzhai had previously passed away. When Tongzhi’s breath ceased, from dawn until noon, he revived and said to his family members:
I happened to see a boat said to be bound for the Pure Land. There were thirty-six people aboard, including Bai Zhai; I was also counted as one among them.
However, my clothes were not fresh and clean, and I had forgotten to bring my prayer beads. They told me to change my clothes and retrieve the beads, and that the boat would wait for me at the quay.
My family members hurriedly changed my clothes and hung the beads around my neck. A short while later, I passed away.

Tiruo (體如) was a native of Lanxi in Zhejiang, serving as an official in the Tang court. He styled himself the Layman Tiruo. His filial piety and fraternal kindness were pure and sincere, arising from his innate nature.

In his youth, he frequented the schools and gained a reputation for scholarship; subsequently, realizing the impermanence of the world, he devoted his heart to the Ultimate Way and studied under Master Yun.
He dwelt in the practice of the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) and pursued it with diligent effort for thirteen years, as if they were but a single day.

He was solely devoted to the Western Pure Land as his ultimate refuge. In the year Wuli (1603), upon reaching the age of sixty, on a morning in the second month of winter, he suddenly said to his sons:
"On the eleventh day of the New Year, I shall depart. Several days prior, his ritual recitations had been no different than usual; when the appointed time arrived—

He washed his hands and rinsed his mouth, adjusted his robes, and sat upright. With his hands forming mudrās and his lips reciting the Buddha’s name, he passed away with a smile, as if entering meditative absorption.
(Recorded by) Yang Jiabei, a scholar-official.
Ming Yang Jiawei, courtesy name Banghua, was a native of Taihe County. He was the son of a distinguished family. At the age of thirteen, he observed the precept against killing;

even fleas and lice were never harmed by him. At twenty-three, while studying at the Southern Capital Academy (Nanyong), he suddenly fell ill and passed away on the nineteenth day of the second lunar month in the year Wanyli Basi (1585).
Prior to his death, he had dreamed of wandering through hell, where he beheld the Great Being Kṣitigarbha.
At the Mingyang Hall, he awakened to the truth and released all living beings. He invited monks to recite sutras and chant the Buddha’s name, saying to his attendants, "I am about to depart.
A blue lotus flower has appeared before me; could this not be the realm of the Pure Land? Thereupon, he chanted the Buddha’s name day and night without ceasing.
He ordered the candles to be extinguished, saying, "You rely on candles for light, but I have no need for them; I am always within the radiance."
[The Master] said, "I heard it. He was asked, "What did you see? He replied, "Lotuses opening in four colors. He was asked, "Did you see Amitābha?

He replied, "I saw Amitābha manifesting a body one thousand *zhang* tall. He was asked about Avalokiteśvara; he replied, "His body is equal in size to that of Amitābha. He was asked about Mahāsthāmaprāpta; he replied, "I did not see him.
Having finished speaking, he suddenly leaped up and offered incense, saying repeatedly: "The merit of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* is unspeakable and beyond description."
He said, "The unspeakable has been spoken; I have already attained the highest grade. Then he passed away in silence.
Hao Xizai (literary name Minghao) was a native of Qiantang.
His Dharma name was Guangding. Throughout his life, he was loyal, trustworthy, and free from deceit, distinguished for his virtuous conduct.

He was highly esteemed within the academies. Later in life, he returned to the Buddha, dedicating himself to meditation and recitation, never flagging day or night. In the second month of spring in the *Xinhai* year of the Wanli era, he fell ill.

Every time he awoke from sleep, he would say, "In my dreams, I have sought an audience with the Buddha in the mountains; yet the Buddha has not appeared, though I see hundreds of birds gathering there. This continued for several days.
On the twenty-seventh day, at the hour of eating, he suddenly raised his head to look out the window and said to him:
His son, Shi Han, said: "Today is a different world altogether. He looked at his family members and had them prepare silver coins. After a moment, he said:
"I was previously afraid that I might need these for official expenses; now they are of no use. At the third watch, he said: "Two youths have come to welcome me.
A Buddha is seated upon a lotus pedestal, appearing before me. I am going. He passed away in auspicious peace.
Go Guangtai Ming:
Go by name for the sake of peace. His Dharma name was Guangtai. A native of Qiantang, his nature was one of supreme filial piety.

Having long accumulated virtuous deeds, he remained deeply self-effacing and sought no recognition from others. In his later years, he served the Buddha with refined sincerity and formed a bond with the Lingzhi monk Xuansu.

During the two seasonal festivals of spring and autumn, he practiced *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) and recited the five scriptures of the *Avataṃsaka*. Suddenly, he said to those around him, "My great life-limit is approaching;
I must prepare the provisions for my journey to the West. Thereupon, he engaged in private recitation within his chamber, never ceasing from dawn until dusk.

He predetermined the date of his departure for the evening of the twenty-first day of the twelfth lunar month. His mother and son gazed upon him, their voices choked with grief, but the Layman smiled and said, "Life..."
"Since there must inevitably be extinction, why grieve? I am now concentrating my spirit in the Pure Land to behold Amitābha face-to-face.

You all must carefully refrain from disturbing my right mindfulness with worldly attachments. I entrust this to you most earnestly. While his companions assisted him in reciting the Buddha's name, they maintained silence without any idle chatter.
When the appointed time arrived, he passed away in profound stillness.
Sun Dayu was the son of Sun Shuzi. His Dharma name was Dayu. From childhood, he was alert, intelligent, upright, and resolute.

At the age of twelve, he accompanied his father, Layman Jingwu, to Yunqi to pay homage to the image of Amitābha Buddha according to the Forty-eight Vows; there, he received the five precepts. Upon returning home...

He abstained from meat and blood, ceased socializing, and put an end to his scholarly pursuits. Vowing to recite the Buddha’s name and aspiring to reach the Golden Terrace, he practiced with such diligence that he disregarded even his own life.
Suddenly, he saw two bhikṣus holding lotus flowers, who confirmed his single-minded devotion to the Pure Land.

Furthermore, he saw a manifested person reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for a full day and night. Thereupon, he suddenly rose from his seat and said, "Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara have both come to welcome me.
He then formed the *vajra-muṣṭi-mudrā*, called out "Amitābha Buddha" several times, and passed away in profound stillness.
This was on the eleventh day of the eleventh month in the Xinhai year of the Wanli era.
Yu Xianyang was a scholar of refined literary talent. His courtesy name was Rulian.
In his youth, he was enrolled as a student at the Renhe Academy. He applied himself diligently to his studies and gained a reputation for his scholarly excellence.

During the Wanli era, while serving as a proctor for the provincial examination, he intended to recommend Yu as the primary candidate for the top rank; however, the presiding examiner slightly demoted him in the rankings. Unable to prevail through argument, Yu resigned rather than remain.

In the following year, he failed the examinations; at the age of thirty-one, on the anniversary of his father’s death, he followed eminent monks and wept blood as he transcribed sutras to repay his filial debt to his parents.
Consequently, he immersed himself in the Buddhist scriptures, observed a lifelong fast in devotion to the Buddha, and practiced the teachings of the Pure Land.
From dawn until dusk, he recited the Buddha’s name without ceasing. In his later years, he often carried a staff and a basket of food to provide for insects and birds;

whenever a monk arrived, he would offer his own clothing to provide a meal. On the first day of the first month of the *guihai* year of the Tianqi era, when friends came to congratulate him on the New Year festival, he said to them immediately, "I shall now bid you a final farewell on this Day of the Lantern Festival.
On the sixth day, he painted his own portrait, and two days later, he made preparations.

Regarding the coffin, shrouds, and various funeral implements: at the hour of the Tiger on the fifteenth day, she summoned her daughter-in-law to the bedside and said, "A divine monk has come to welcome me;
I shall depart at the hour of the Dragon. Having personally risen to bathe and finished arranging her robes and cap, she ascended the bed, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away.

At that time, he was seventy-two years old. Later, his grandson Hao passed the provincial examination in the *Xinmao* year of the Shunzhi era and subsequently attained the top rank in the imperial examination;
thus, it was not in vain that Yang’s learning was held in high esteem.
Han Chengshan was a native of Chuhu Jing in Pinghu County during the Great Qing dynasty.

He was a man of sincerity and simplicity who devoted himself to agriculture and sericulture, accumulating family wealth until his estates were worth approximately one thousand taels of gold. In his daily life, he did nothing but observe the fasts and recite the Buddha’s name.
At the age of eighty-one, on an evening in the fourth month of the first year of the Kangxi era, he suddenly said to his son:
"Tomorrow you should invite all your relatives to our home; I wish to bid them farewell. Following these instructions, the son invited them to arrive, where they were received with seats prepared.
Facing the assembly, he declared: "I have only seven days remaining in this world; I have come specifically to part from you all."

They should part while at the height of their joy. When the appointed time arrives, he bathes, changes his robes, and sits upright. He instructs his children, relatives, and kin to sit in a circle around him reciting the Buddha’s name;
he himself also recites the Buddha’s name. After a long while, he remains motionless. Upon looking closely, one finds that he has already cast off his mortal coil.
Qiao Zhong, of our Great Qing, Qiao Zhong, a native of Huan-dian Ferry at Ximen Lake in Changxing, made his living by selling bamboo wares.

With both hands he carved bamboo, while never ceasing to recite the Buddha’s name with his mouth. He paid homage to the Venerable Master Wuzhan Pumen, and whenever he visited the mountain, he would... [kneel/perform prostrations].

At the time of his passing, he also entered the meditation hall to observe the seven-day retreat. On the third day prior to the first month of the first year of the Kangxi era, he announced to his relatives, friends, children, and grandchildren:
"I am about to depart. On the first day of the tenth month, he changed his robes, turned toward the west, and sat upright reciting the Buddha’s name.

To those who came to visit him, he instructed them all to recite the Buddha’s name in support of him. Addressing his fellow practitioners and monks, he said: "Now that we part forever, it should be..."
"We shall meet in the Lotus Pond. Having spoken these words, he passed away with serene composure. Zen Master Zhan-shan was a long-time friend of mine;
his disciple Fa-ying (Gu-fan) came to reside there. When I questioned him regarding the Pure Land, he spoke to me as follows:
As for those who personally escorted me, they did so to strengthen my faith. It has been barely half a year since I first made this vow in the fifth month;
yet here we have Han Chengshan of Pinghu and Qiao Zhongwo of Changxing—two men from different places returning together.
That they should appear simultaneously is truly extraordinary. Thus I know that the entire great earth is the Western Land.
This applies to all sentient beings; it is only that those who are human and followers of the Buddha have not yet attained sufficient self-confidence.

I universally pray that all who read this book shall give rise to faith and joy, and together proceed to the Lotus Pond, so that we may, in some small measure, look up to and fulfill the great vow of Amitābha Buddha.

Zhai Mengli (Da Qing Zhai Mengli), whose Dharma name was Jingzhen, was a native of Linjiang in Renhe. His conduct was consistently sincere and simple, and he possessed profound faith in the Pure Land.

He never failed in his ten recitations of the Buddha’s name and also chanted the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Although he had surpassed the age of eighty, his spirit remained vigorous and robust. He lived in good health.

In the seventh month, during the latter part of the intercalary month of the year Wushen of the Xi era, he suddenly manifested a slight illness. On the thirteenth day of the eighth month, when monastics and laypeople, as well as his relatives and friends, all came to visit him, he said to the assembly:
"I am deeply grateful for your concern; you must recite the Buddha's name to assist me in my rebirth in the Pure Land."

With his own hands he rotated the prayer beads without the slightest sign of weariness. After a short while, he said, "I originally intended to depart immediately, but alas, I have missed my chance. I shall go tomorrow morning.
At the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m. the following day, the assembly gathered once more, and he passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name.
Shen Yangsu of Daqing:
His Dharma name was Zhien. A native of Linjiang in Renhe, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism, never ceasing regardless of cold or heat.

Having reached the age of seventy-five or seventy-six, he traversed perilous terrain as if on level ground. At that time, he was renowned for chanting the Buddha’s name and reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Once...
In the eighth month of the Wushen year of the Kangxi era, while he was lecturing on thirty-odd sections of the *Lotus Sūtra*, he suddenly fell slightly ill.
He then spoke to himself, saying, "I shall follow in the footsteps of Zhai Mengli. He then said to his disciple, Yunzi: "On the fifteenth day of the ninth month, I shall depart.
Yunzi replied, "The fifteenth is not auspicious; the sixteenth would be better. [He] spoke in a loud voice: "It is better to go forward than..."
He was asked to withdraw, but on the fourteenth day, he passed away while recollecting the Buddha. His body emitted a wondrous fragrance that did not dissipate for several days.
He had practiced together with Master Zhai in the same village; now, their departure and remaining have followed one after the other.
That they were able to exercise such self-mastery is truly rare. May all who read this be moved to inspiration and resolve to practice.
Dai Tongzi (戴童子), also known as Daigong Lie (戴公烈), was a native of Xiuyi County in Huizhou. He lived as a sojourner in the northern sector of Tangqi Town.
Born into a Confucian family, he lost his mother at the age of one. Even during his childhood play, he never transgressed the bounds of ritual propriety. At the age of twelve, he first...
He studied the curriculum for the imperial examination system. His brilliance was already manifest, and by the age of thirteen he had become even more intelligent;
his deportment resembled that of an adult. However, his physical constitution was naturally delicate and weak; due to a medical treatment for smallpox, his stomach qi was impaired.

He subsequently sought medical care at his residence in Wumen, where there were several volumes of Master Lianchi’s *Zhuchuang suibi* (Random Notes from the Bamboo Window). Whenever he took up these books, he would read them repeatedly and minutely, as if there were something he understood.
At the hour of noon on the sixth day of the seventh month, his mind suddenly became settled as he sat upright. He said to his grandfather, "Help me recite the Buddha's name.

Thereupon, he clearly and loudly chanted the Buddha’s name, and his grandfather joined him in harmony. At first the voices were loud, then they gradually grew fainter, until finally there was no sound at all.
For a short while his lips still moved, but after a moment they ceased to move as well; he passed away in a state of profound stillness. This occurred in the *guichou* year of the Kangxi era.
This child must have possessed roots of goodness from previous lives; at the time of death, his right mindfulness was so vividly manifest that it was something truly unprecedented.
As stated in the Forty-Eight Vows: "If sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions, with sincere faith and joy, desire to be born in my land..."
In this land, if there were anyone who recited my name ten times and yet was not reborn [in my realm], may I not attain Buddhahood. As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says:
"When such a person reaches the end of life, their mind shall not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Believing these words, I consider this child to be of that same lineage; therefore, I have specially recorded him so that his memory may endure imperishably.
Since my sixtieth birthday, I have only now begun to make vows and practice with devotion. My wife, Zhuo Ji, has followed my path with steadfast steps.
In a little more than five years, she passed away with such serenity that she even entrusted her dream-vow to be reborn in heaven;
this has already been recorded at the end of the volume to encourage the faithful. This is the year Kāngxī 8, the cyclical year Jǐyǒu.

On New Year’s Day, before the Buddha, the lamps and candles were lit and the four limbs [of the ritual] were fully performed. An extraordinary, massive flower appeared; three of its petals resembled lotus pedestals.
From behind one petal, a statue of the Buddha suddenly manifested, sitting cross-legged upon a mountain-like base.

His features were solemn and vivid, and the folds of his robes were clearly defined. Just then, relatives came to offer New Year’s greetings, and I had them all pay their respects and worship it. All...
I sigh at how rare this is! This is surely the manifestation of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to strengthen my faith. From this point forward, I shall redouble my diligent efforts.
I respectfully inform all virtuous believers everywhere: you must earnestly exert yourselves; be careful not to treat this with negligence. Recorded specifically by the Man of the Precious Lotus.
The *Nizhong wangsheng lei* (Classifications on the Rebirth of the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha), the *Nidaming* (Great Illumination of the Bhikṣuṇīs) from the Sui Dynasty, and the *Nidaming* [of the present].
Whenever entering a room to perform prostrations and recitations, one should first don clean robes and hold incense of *xiangchen* (Aquilaria agallocha) in the mouth. — Emperor Wen’s Empress Dowager.
He held him in the highest esteem. On the day he was about to pass away, the assembly suddenly smelled the fragrance of agarwood filling the entire chamber.
Shortly thereafter, a radiance like clouds appeared, which gradually faded away toward the west.

The nun Jingzhen of Tang lived at Jixian Temple in Chang’an. Wearing patched robes, she sustained herself by begging for alms. She recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one hundred thousand times and was devoted to the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.
She said to her disciples, "Within this fifth month, I have seen the Buddha ten times, and twice I have seen the [Buddha’s] precious [relics]."

"The Youth Who Plays upon the Lotus has appeared; I have already attained rebirth in the highest grade. Having spoken these words, she passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture, as auspicious light filled the hermitage.
Thus did the nun Wuxing attain enlightenment.
Tang Ni was a person of great intelligence who resided on Mount Lu, where he recited the Buddha’s name with devotion, vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land.

Suddenly, he heard the sound of celestial music in the air and said to those around him, "I have already attained rebirth in the Middle Grade. I see that for all my fellow practitioners who have been diligent in their recitation of the Buddha's name, there are lotus flowers awaiting them.
You must each strive with earnest effort. Having spoken these words, he passed away.

Ninengfeng (also read as Ninengfeng), a native of Qiantang, was a nun who devoted herself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism. She once dreamed that the Buddha’s light shone upon her body and heard virtuous words from the air offering her consolation.
She told her disciples, "The time for my rebirth in the Pure Land has arrived. Shortly thereafter, she was heard chanting the name of the Buddha.

Her voice was extremely forceful. He rushed to see her and found her sitting facing west with palms joined, having passed away. A wondrous fragrance filled the room, and the sound of music drifted toward the west.
This was the nun Fazang.

The Song dynasty nun Fazang resided in Jinling. She was diligent in her resolve to practice the recollection of the Buddha. One night, she saw Buddhas and Bodhisattvas arrive, their radiance illuminating the temple;
she then suddenly passed away.
The nun Wuming was the daughter of the Li family from Xiaoshan. From her youth, she vowed not to marry; she maintained a vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name.

At the age of twenty, she shaved her head and built a thatched hut, where she devoted herself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism. At thirty, she traveled to various regions to study under different masters. In every place she visited, for those suffering from illness and pain, she provided assistance according to their needs.

He took the substance and decocted it in water; upon consuming it, he was immediately cured. During the Jiajing era, there was a widespread epidemic within the palace that reached the imperial court by rumor.
He was summoned and his treatments proved effective, whereupon he was granted the title "Chan Master Wúwéixīn" (Wuwei Xin Chan Master) and sent back to his former dwelling.

As he was about to pass away, a divine monk arrived seeking lodging. Although Wúwéi declined him repeatedly, the divine monk urged him with exhortations and insisted on entering, eventually taking temporary residence upon Wúwéi’s meditation seat.
Upon waking, he did not see him. Realizing he was a divine monk, he rose and sat up, composing a verse that said:

"Sixty-four years of worldly affairs; this morning, I cast them aside and return to the West. Having attained the samādhi of Bodhi, there remain only the bright moon and the clear breeze. He then passed away.
His body was cremated, yielding a mass of śarīra relics, which were enshrined in a stupa on Guanshan.
Niyuelang Daqing was the daughter of the Wu family, a prominent clan of Songjiang. Her parents wished to arrange a marriage for her, but she resolutely opposed it and refused to be betrothed.

At the age of seventeen, she encountered the nun Qianjiang in Hangzhou while she was soliciting alms to provide a vegetarian feast for the monastic community; she earnestly requested ordination. Subsequently...

In the spring of that year, he accompanied his grandmother and various kinsmen on a pilgrimage to India to offer incense. Taking advantage of the journey, he traveled all the way to Qianjiang Hermitage, where he took up residence and showed no intention of returning.
His kinsmen all went to urge him to go back, but he remained firm in his resolve and would not consent. Realizing they could not prevail, the assembly accepted his decision.
Regarding women who attain rebirth,
consider Empress Wendi of the Sui Dynasty, Lady Gudu. Although she resided within the royal palace, she deeply loathed her female nature and constantly kept Amitābha in mind.
The Buddha passed away on the first day of the month of August (Jiazi).

At that time, to the north of the Yong'an Palace, various kinds of music spontaneously resounded, and extraordinary fragrances filled the chamber, arriving from the sky. The Emperor asked Jñānagupta, "What auspicious omen is this?
He replied, "In the Pure Land there is a Buddha named Amitābha. Because the Empress’s merit is sublime, she has transcended to that realm; therefore, these signs have appeared."
Auspicious Account of Old Lady Yao.
Old Lady Yao of Tang was a native of Shangdang. Encouraged by the nun Fan Xing, she recited the name of Amitābha Buddha. At the time of her death, she beheld the Buddha.
The Bodhisattva came to welcome them and said to the Buddha, "I have not yet taken my leave of Lady Fan Xing; I request that the Buddha stay for a short while.
The Buddha remained suspended in mid-air for a time, waiting for Lady Fan to arrive. Lady Yao then manifested her transformation and passed away.
Tang Wenjingwen’s wife was from Bingzhou.
She had been bedridden for a long time due to illness. Wenjingwen exhorted her to recite the Buddha’s name without ceasing for one year.
Consequently, she beheld the Pure Land and told Wenjingwen, "I have already seen the Buddha; I shall certainly depart in the coming month. Furthermore...

She offered food to her parents, saying, "I shall now attain rebirth following the Buddha. I pray that you, my parents and husband, will single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name so that we may meet in the Western Land.
Having spoken these words, she passed away. Three days prior, she had seen a lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel.

During the Yuanyou era of the Song dynasty, there was the Consort of the Prince of Jing, Lady Wang. She and her handmaidens cultivated the pure practices with great diligence. There was, however, one handmaiden who was indolent;
the Consort rebuked her, whereupon the handmaiden felt remorse and awakened to the truth. After practicing with vigor for a long time, she said to the other handmaidens: "Tonight, I—"
She was to be reborn in the Western Paradise. That night, a rare fragrance filled the room, and she passed away without illness. The following day, another concubine informed the lady:
"The one who departed yesterday in a dream entrusted me with her greetings, saying, 'By virtue of your instructions, Lady, I have already attained rebirth.'"
Her gratitude was immeasurable. The lady said, "If I too were to have such a dream, then it could be believed.

That night, the lady dreamed that her deceased maidservant appeared and offered thanks as before. The lady asked, "Can the Western Region be reached? The maidservant replied, "It can be reached; simply follow me.
The lady followed her and saw a vast pond where red and white lotuses of various sizes were interspersed.
Some were flourishing while others were withered; they differed in all sorts of ways. The lady asked, "Why is this so?

Her handmaid replied, "These are all people of the world who have conceived the aspiration to cultivate the Western Paradise. As soon as they conceive a single thought, a lotus flower immediately grows within the pond.
If their vow and resolve are diligent, the flower will bloom and flourish day by day until it becomes as large as a chariot wheel. If their vow..."
As his mind regressed, the lotus withered day by day until it finally perished.
Next, he saw a person sitting upon a lotus flower, with celestial robes fluttering about and adorned with a jeweled crown and necklaces. The lady asked, "Who is this person?"
The handmaid said, "This is Yang Jie. She then saw another person sitting upon a lotus flower, dressed in court robes; the handmaid said, "This is Ma Yu. The lady asked, "Where shall I be reborn?
The handmaid led her forward for several li until they gazed in the distance at a golden altar, shimmering with gold and lapis lazuli.
The handmaid said, "This is the place where the lady will be born through transformation; it is the highest grade of the highest birth. The lady—
Upon waking, he inquired as to the whereabouts of Yang and Ma; it was found that Jie had already passed away, while Yu remained unharmed.
From this, one may know that for those whose diligent practice does not regress, although their bodies remain within the Sahā world, their consciousnesses have already entered the Pure Land.

Later, on the anniversary of his wife’s birthday, he held the incense burner and burned incense, standing before the Pavilion of Avalokiteśvara while his descendants were just beginning to present their offerings of longevity.
The ritual protocols for this have already been established through transformation.

Lady Feng, the Lady of Songguangping Commandery, was of the Feng clan; her name was Faxin. She was the daughter of Xu Xun, who was posthumously honored as the Junior Mentor, and she married [the son of] Cheng...

The imperial envoy Chen Sigong had been frequently ill since his youth. He went to visit Chan Master Cishou Shen, who instructed him to observe the fast and recite the Buddha’s name, diligently cultivating the Pure Land practice.
The official completely eliminated meat and blood from his diet and wore the robes used for sweeping stupas. He focused exclusively on the Western Paradise;
whether walking, sitting, rising, resting, eating, or breathing, he was ever mindful of the West. His speech was likewise of the West.
Silence, movement, and stillness are also the Western Land. Drawing water and offering flowers are also the Western Land. Reciting sutras and practicing the Way are also the Western Land.
Every thought in a single kṣaṇa and every virtue as small as an autumn hair—all are taken as bridges and rafts to the Western Land.
For ten years, he showed no sign of indolence; his mind was at peace and his body robust. One day, he suddenly wrote a verse, saying: "Following conditions and yielding to karma..."
For many years, you have laboriously served as an old ox to till the fields. Settle your body and mind and return home at once, lest your nostrils be pierced by others.
Her kinsmen were indignant at this, but the lady said, "My karmic ties to China are exhausted; I am returning to the West. Why should you be indignant?
She then lay ill, but suddenly rose with a start and said, "My spirit has traveled to the Pure Land, where I pay homage face-to-face to Amitābha."

Amitābha Buddha looked toward the left; Avalokiteśvara gazed to the right; and hundreds of thousands of millions of pure sons of the Buddha prostrated themselves, rejoicing that they would be born in his land.
Its palaces, groves, and ponds were radiant and divine in beauty, identical with what is described in the *Sixteen Contemplations Sutra* of the Avataṃsaka.
The next day, he passed away peacefully. His family members smelled a wondrous fragrance for three days.
Upon cremation, the corpse was found to be as if alive.

Lady Song and Lady Wu, both titled Guānjīn (Countess), and their husband, Lǚ Hóng, an Official of the Bureau of Military Affairs, were likewise enlightened in the principles of Buddhism; thus, the couple...
Each observed the fasts and maintained pure cultivation. Lady Wu had two female attendants who also abstained from meat and blood, diligently assisting her in performing meritorious deeds.
One of them was particularly fond of the principles of Chan; even when ill, she remained composed, passing away with a smile and conversation as if casting off a discarded shell.
The other strictly observed the precepts and practiced asceticism, sometimes not eating for an entire month, drinking only the water consecrated by Lady Wu’s recitation of the Avalokiteśvara mantra.
There was only a single bowl of pure water. Suddenly, he saw three golden lotuses supporting his feet.
After several more days, he saw his knees; after several more days, he saw his body; and after several more days, he saw his face and features. Within them was Amitābha Buddha.
To his left and right were Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Furthermore, he saw all their halls, palaces, and realms as clearly as if looking at the palm of his hand;
he understood with perfect clarity that this was the Pure Land. When he asked for further details, they replied, "They are all pure men who walk, stroll, and enjoy themselves;
there are no women there. He asked again, "How does that Buddha preach the Dharma? They replied, "I have attained the divine eye, yet [I have not yet seen him]."
She had attained the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*). Therefore, she could only see their questions and answers and their gestures, but she could not hear what was being said.

This continued for three years, and there was not a single day that he was not before her eyes. Suddenly, she fell ill and said of herself, "I shall be reborn [in the Pure Land]," and then passed away.
The Lady of Wu served Avalokiteśvara with such efficacy that she possessed spiritual responses; every day in her pure chamber, she would arrange dozens of jars and pots and fill them with water.
Filling his hands, he held willow branches and recited the mantra; he would certainly see Guanyin emit light that entered into jars and vessels.

Those suffering from illness who drank the water were immediately healed. The consecrated water remained undeteriorated for years and did not freeze even in great cold. The world thereafter called him the "County Lord Guanyin."
Lady Lu and Lady Song were both from Qiantang.

Lady Lu was the wife of Wang Yu, a Court Petitioner (*chaoqing*). She had long recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and devoted herself to the practice of repentance for the Pure Land, chanting the Buddha’s name ten thousand times in a single session.
She maintained this practice for thirty years. When she was afflicted by a slight illness, she suddenly heard a celestial voice.
The drum sounded spontaneously. Those present were startled and marveled at this. She then sat facing west in a dignified posture, joined her hands in mudrā, and passed away.

Hu Changpo (Song) was surnamed Hu and styled Changpo; she was of the Li clan and a native of Shangyu. After her husband’s death, she recited the Buddha’s name aloud day and night and chanted the [scriptures].

For more than ten years, she had been reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra*. One day, she saw a monk holding a vermilion canopy over her and said, "On the fifteenth day of this month at the hour of the rat, you shall be reborn in the Pure Land.
When asked who he was, he replied, "He is the one you have been mindful of. She then took leave of her relatives.

When the appointed time arrived, amidst extraordinary fragrances and radiant light, she passed away while sitting upright. Seven days later, when her body was cremated, her teeth were found to be like white jade.
His tongue was like a red lotus and his eyes were like grapes; all were exquisite, firm, and indestructible. His *śarīra* relics were beyond counting.
On the following day, a flower grew at the site of the cremation, resembling white *xun-su* (a type of grain).

The Gong family belonged to the Gong clan of Qiantang during the Song dynasty. Day and night they recited the Buddha’s name and chanted the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Later, when one member fell ill, they invited Vinaya Master Heng to provide spiritual guidance.

Before he had even finished explaining the teachings, the patient sat upright and passed away. An elderly maidservant, surnamed Yu, likewise never ceased her recitation of the Buddha’s name. One— [end of fragment]
One evening, she dreamed that Lady Gong told her, "I have already been reborn in the Pure Land; you shall be reborn there in seven days. When the appointed time arrived, Zheng also passed away.
Lady Song Zheng was a native of Qiantang who daily recited the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra and never ceased her mindfulness of the Buddha. Later, while ill, she requested a bath.
After finishing his bath, he sat facing west and asked his family members, "Do you hear the sound of the *ghaṇṭā*? The various sages of the Pure Land are arriving.

Shortly thereafter, with palms joined, he leaped for joy and said, "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have come! Avalokiteśvara holds a golden platform in his hand, and the Tathāgata receives me to ascend it.
Thereupon, he passed away peacefully.
Lady Huang was a native of Siming during the Song dynasty. Having lost her husband early in life, she returned to her father’s home, where she devoted herself to the practice of the Pure Land.

At the time of her death, she saw the Buddha coming to welcome her; she formed mudras and walked slowly, remaining upright and serene as she passed away. Her family sifted ashes upon the ground to verify that she had been reborn.
At her dwelling, she saw a single lotus flower grow from within the ashes.

Zhu Shi, a native of Xiaochuan in the Song dynasty, had practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name for thirty years. Suddenly, she ceased eating for forty days, consuming only water while continuing her recitation.
The Buddha dreamed that three monks each held a lotus flower and said to him, "We previously planted these flowers for you; now you shall be reborn [in the Pure Land].
Upon waking, he invited the monks to assist him in recitation, and he passed away while sitting upright.

Xiangshi was from the Song dynasty; her secular surname was Xiang and her name was Miaozhi. A native of Ning County, she lived as a widow and had two daughters, both of whom she ordained as nuns. They were diligent and devoted to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. One day, she suddenly said, "I wish to depart while seated; do not mistakenly prepare a coffin for me. Her daughter replied, "The Buddha used a golden coffin. She said, "That is so. That night, she sat upright and passed away. Her daughter then prepared a small coffin and placed her within it. When they opened the lid the next morning, they saw that she had vanished, leaving behind only her sitting mat. This occurred during the reign of Emperor Gaozong of the Song dynasty.
